title: Quantum Networking At The Speed Of Quantum Computation: Kilohertz Entanglement In A Heterogeneous Quantum System
authors: Lukas Hartung, Pierre Barral, Noah Glachman, George Toh, Jacob H. Davidson, Sagnik Saha, Alexander Chuang, Matthew C. Cambria, Madison Sutula, Alexander Abulnaga, Julia Breevord, John Chiaverini, Ian Counts, Aos Dabbagh, Christian Dangel, Skylar Deckoff-Jones, Chawina De-Eknamkul, Jonathan Dietz, Riley Forst, Prithvi Gundlapalli, Jeonghoon Ha, Michael Haas, Ezekiel Meulbroek, Andrea Mucchietto, Daniel Riedel, Jonah Sachs, Jeremy Sage, Mikhail Shalaev, Harriet Shi, Denis Sukachev, Yichao Yu, Johannes Borregaard, Christopher Monroe, Nicholas Mondrik, Mihir Bhaskar, Bart Machielse, Matteo Pompili, Carsten Robens, David Levonian
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed quantum computing requires rapid, high-fidelity entanglement between qubits in separate processor modules. Photonic links between single-atom qubits provide switchable, long-range connections, but photon loss limits their entanglement rate. Here we entangle a trapped [MATH]Ba[MATH] ion with a silicon-vacancy (SiV[MATH]) center in a diamond nanophotonic cavity. A photon emitted by the ion is converted in wavelength and encoding, reflected from the SiV[MATH]--cavity system and detected, so that a single detected photon heralds entanglement. Including all conversion losses, we generate ion--SiV[MATH] Bell pairs at an average rate of 1.03(1)\,kHz with a fidelity of 87.9(7)\%. This is four times the rate of the fastest photonic link between two trapped ions and corresponds to one Bell pair per millisecond, matching the cycle time of planned trapped-ion processors.
tldr: Entangled a trapped Ba ion with a SiV center in diamond via a photonic link at a rate of 1.03 kHz and a fidelity of 87.9%.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing requires rapid, high-fidelity entanglement between qubits in separate processor modules, but photon loss limits entanglement rates over photonic links.
method: A photon emitted by the trapped ion is converted in wavelength and encoding, reflected from the SiV-cavity system, and detected, so that a single detected photon heralds entanglement between the ion and the SiV center.
result: Generated ion–SiV Bell pairs at an average rate of 1.03(1) kHz with a fidelity of 87.9(7)%, four times the rate of the fastest photonic link between two trapped ions and matching the cycle time of planned trapped-ion processors.
conclusion: This demonstrates a high-rate heterogeneous quantum network link suitable for distributed quantum computing and advances experimental quantum networking between different physical platforms.

title: Coherence-assisted Quantum State Preparation And Thermal Control Through Repeated Interactions
authors: Dvira Segal Alessandro Prositto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the relaxation dynamics and steady state of a qubit interacting with a coherent environment through an energy-conserving flip-flop interaction within the Markovian repeated-interaction framework. We derive an exact analytical solution for the evolving and stationary state, nonperturbative in the environmental coherence. We show that environmental coherence provides a resource for dissipative state preparation by expanding the set of accessible steady states. In particular, coherent ancillas can increase the system ground- state population beyond that of the bath, corresponding to an effective temperature below the bath temperature, and enhance its steady-state purity, with these effects controlled by the interplay between the system energy scale and the system-ancilla coupling. Nevertheless, we prove that the purity of the system can never exceed the purity of the ancilla. We further analyze the thermodynamics of the protocol and show that environmental coherence can modify and even reverse the natural direction of heat transfer, giving rise to anomalous heat flow. Remarkably, for fixed interaction parameters, the direction of the coherence-induced heat transfer is governed by the relative phase between the system and ancilla coherence, whereas their magnitudes determine the amount of heat exchanged. Our results establish environmental coherence as a resource for controlling steady-state preparation and energy transfer in repeated-interaction dynamics.
tldr: Environmental coherence in a repeated-interaction model enables dissipative state preparation and anomalous heat flow in a qubit, with an exact nonperturbative solution.
motivation: Understanding how quantum coherence in an environment affects relaxation and steady-state properties is central to quantum thermodynamics and dissipative state engineering.
method: The authors study a qubit coupled via an energy-conserving flip-flop interaction to coherent ancillas in a Markovian repeated-interaction framework, deriving exact analytical expressions for the evolving and stationary states.
result: Environmental coherence expands the set of accessible steady states, can lower the effective temperature below the bath and enhance purity (bounded by ancilla purity), and can modify or reverse heat flow depending on the relative phase between system and ancilla coherence.
conclusion: Coherence is established as a resource for controlling steady-state preparation and energy transfer in repeated-interaction dynamics, with phase governing the direction of anomalous heat flow.

They show that environmental coherence acts as a resource for dissipative state preparation: it expands the set of accessible steady states, allowing the system's ground-state population to exceed that of the bath, which corresponds to an effective temperature below the bath temperature. title: Susceptibility Of Qudit-qudit Entanglement To Quantum Noise: Insights From The Negativity Rank
authors: Natalie Klco Matthew Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One aspect of complexity for quantum many-body systems resides in their ability to exhibit entanglement, uniquely quantum correlations central to quantum computation. To quantitatively explore the diminishing effect that quantum noise has on entanglement resources, we focus on the negativity witness, an entanglement measure based on local time reversal transformations that provides a perfect witness in simple physical contexts. Beyond calculation of the negativity, we analyze the associated eigenvalue spectra of partially transposed density matrices for qudit-qudit bipartitions, finding that higher negativity rank provides greater(reduced) robustness to targeted(depolarizing) noise. In particular, we extend the maximum number of separable states that can be arbitrarily mixed into an entangled pure ensemble while retaining negativity to be exactly equal to the original negativity rank. Furthermore, we report how understanding the role of the negativity rank with respect to the completely depolarizing channel allows direct calculation of (1) certain noise boundaries for the Absolutely Positive Partial Transpose (APPT) subspace beyond which no unitary operator is capable of generating negativity and (2) the maximum qutrit-qutrit APPT purity. Beyond proving tight bounds and contributing to the ongoing search for APPT entanglement, these results expand our understanding of the nuanced relationship between computation with entanglement and practical environments for operating quantum devices.
tldr: The paper analyzes how the negativity rank of qudit-qudit entanglement determines robustness to targeted and depolarizing noise, with bounds on APPT subspaces and qutrit-qutrit APPT purity.
motivation: Understanding how quantum noise degrades entanglement is crucial for operating quantum devices, but the role of the negativity eigenvalue spectrum in noise resilience is not fully characterized.
method: The authors study partially transposed density matrices for qudit-qudit bipartitions, using the negativity witness and its rank to derive bounds on mixture with separable states and on completely depolarizing channels.
result: Higher negativity rank yields greater robustness to targeted noise but reduced robustness to depolarizing noise; the maximum number of separable states mixable while retaining negativity equals the negativity rank, and tight APPT bounds and qutrit-qutrit APPT purity are obtained.
conclusion: These results clarify the nuanced relationship between entanglement resources and noisy environments, contributing to the search for APPT entanglement and practical quantum device operation.

title: Markov Length Can Diverge In Systems Whose Universal Physics Is Spatially Markovian
authors: Tarun Grover Yu-Hsueh Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conditional mutual information (CMI) probes spatial non-Markovianity and plays a central role in a recently developed framework for defining mixed-state phases based on local reversibility. This framework sharply distinguishes exponentially decaying from algebraically decaying CMI, since the latter obstructs equivalence to a state with finite Markov length. Here we show that states that flow to the same renormalization-group (RG) fixed point can nevertheless exhibit qualitatively different CMI. Starting from a critical Gibbs state of a finite-range local classical Hamiltonian, whose CMI vanishes beyond the interaction range, we show that an RG-irrelevant perturbation that breaks detailed balance generically generates algebraically decaying CMI. Crucially, these power-law tails are cutoff-suppressed: although they lead to an infinite Markov length at every fixed lattice cutoff, they vanish as a positive power of the cutoff in the continuum limit. We construct solvable models that exhibit this phenomenon and predict that the Ising-symmetric critical point of Toom's cellular automata generically exhibits such behavior. We also find analogous cutoff-suppressed CMI in the high-temperature paramagnetic phase of the long-range Ising paramagnet, in contrast with the genuine power-law CMI at the finite-temperature critical point in this same model that survives the continuum limit. We also derive a general result that in one spatial dimension, CMI decays faster than the inverse square of the buffer length if and only if the long-distance physics is Markovian.
tldr: The paper shows that conditional mutual information can have algebraically decaying tails and infinite Markov length even when the long-distance physics is spatially Markovian, due to RG-irrelevant perturbations that break detailed balance, with effects that are cutoff-suppressed.
motivation: Conditional mutual information (CMI) is central to defining mixed-state phases via local reversibility, but it was unclear whether states flowing to the same renormalization-group fixed point can have qualitatively different CMI.
method: The authors analyze critical Gibbs states of finite-range classical Hamiltonians, add RG-irrelevant perturbations that break detailed balance, construct solvable models, and derive a general one-dimensional criterion relating CMI decay to Markovian long-distance physics.
result: They find that such perturbations generically generate algebraically decaying CMI that is cutoff-suppressed, predict this behavior for the Ising-symmetric critical point of Toom's cellular automata, and contrast it with genuine power-law CMI at finite-temperature critical points.
conclusion: The work reveals a subtle distinction between universal long-distance physics and the Markov length inferred from CMI, with implications for classifying mixed-state phases and understanding spatial non-Markovianity.

key_contributions: Demonstration that RG-irrelevant perturbations breaking detailed balance can generate algebraically decaying CMI from a state with originally finite Markov length.
Identification of cutoff-suppressed power-law CMI tails that vanish in the continuum limit, distinguishing them from genuine power-law CMI that persists.
Construction of solvable models exhibiting cutoff-suppressed CMI, including a prediction for Toom's cellular automata at its Ising-symmetric critical point.
Discovery of analogous cutoff-suppressed CMI in the high-temperature paramagnetic phase of the long-range Ising model, contrasting with the critical point behavior.
Derivation of a general theorem in 1D: CMI decays faster than 1/(buffer length)^2 if and only if the long-distance physics is Markovian.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of analytical RG arguments and exactly solvable models. They begin with a classical finite-range Hamiltonian at criticality, where CMI is strictly zero beyond the interaction range. By adding an RG-irrelevant perturbation that violates detailed balance, they analyze the resulting non-equilibrium steady state and compute CMI using transfer-matrix or field-theoretic techniques. The cutoff-suppressed nature is established by tracking how the power-law tails depend on the lattice spacing as it is taken to zero. Solvable models are constructed to explicitly verify the predictions, and the 1D theorem is proven using information-theoretic inequalities and Markov property arguments. The approach is rigorous and leverages the connection between CMI and Markov length, a key concept in mixed-state phases.

These results highlight that RG equivalence does not imply equivalence of CMI, and that cutoff effects can mask non-Markovianity.

title: Fast Entanglement Generation Via Cavity-mediated Nematic Tensor Dynamics
authors: Stuart J. Masson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many-body entanglement in atomic ensembles offers the potential for enhanced sensing devices. Entanglement can be generated by interfacing atoms with a cavity. Traditional methods use effective two-level systems isolated from more complex atomic level structures. However, alternative strategies allow entanglement to be generated in atoms confined to a single hyperfine manifold. These strategies enable entanglement in ways fundamentally not available to two-level systems but feature extremely slow dynamics due to requiring strongly off-resonant laser fields. Here, I show that equivalent squeezing dynamics can be achieved much closer to resonance, offering entanglement generation over a hundred times faster than typical experiments. Furthermore, the Hamiltonian can be used to speed up the creation of maximally entangled states via adiabatic passage.
tldr: A theoretical proposal to generate many-body entanglement in atomic ensembles via cavity-mediated nematic tensor dynamics, achieving over 100x faster squeezing and faster maximally entangled state creation through adiabatic passage.
motivation: Atomic ensembles can generate entanglement for enhanced sensing, but existing methods using single hyperfine manifolds suffer from extremely slow dynamics due to far off-resonant lasers; there is a need for faster entanglement generation.
method: The author analyzes cavity-mediated interactions that produce nematic tensor dynamics (spin squeezing) in atoms confined to a single hyperfine manifold, shows that equivalent squeezing can be achieved much closer to resonance, and uses the Hamiltonian for adiabatic passage to create maximally entangled states.
result: The proposed scheme achieves entanglement generation over a hundred times faster than typical experiments and speeds up the creation of maximally entangled states via adiabatic passage.
conclusion: This approach enables fast entanglement generation in atomic ensembles, potentially improving sensing devices and overcoming limitations of two-level system strategies.

The key innovation is showing that equivalent squeezing dynamics can be achieved much closer to resonance, overcoming the extremely slow dynamics of previous off-resonant schemes. title: Efficiency Fluctuations In Quantum Heat Engines With Non-quasi-static Adiabatic Strokes
authors: Shyamal Biswas Bikram Keshari Behera
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We have presented an analytical and numerical study of efficiency fluctuations in quantum Carnot and Otto engines with pistons operating under non-quasi-static adiabatic expansion and compression processes at constant speed, along with quasi-static isothermal (for the Carnot engine) or isochoric processes (for the Otto engine). By considering each of the pistons as a single quantum particle in a 1-D box with a non-quasi-statically movable boundary, we capture the stochastic nature of the work output resulting from the unitary evolution of the quantum mechanical state of the system during non-equilibrium processes. Furthermore, we have explicitly shown how the piston speed during quantum non-equilibrium strokes introduces additional quantum fluctuations that modify the average efficiency of both the engines.

title: Combining Error Verification And Privacy Amplification In Quantum Key Distribution
authors: Devashish Tupkary, Zhiyao Wang, Ernest Y. -Z. Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols typically involve two separate steps of error-verification and privacy amplification. Both steps involve the application of a hash function sampled from a suitable hash family to classical data. A potentially simpler alternative is to implement a single-step hashing procedure, announce and compare a fixed number of bits of its output for error-verification, and retain the remaining bits as the final output key. This reduces the complexity of classical postprocessing, the amount of classical communication, and the amount of randomness needed in the protocol. While this construction has appeared in the literature, a suitable mathematical justification is lacking. In this work, we show that the security of such protocols, under certain simple conditions, follows from a slightly modified notion of secrecy of the protocol without the final error-verification step. In particular, we show that for most entropy-based proofs, the combined protocol can be implemented with no change to the key rate, and a minor change to the security parameter.
tldr: The paper provides a security justification for a combined error-verification and privacy-amplification hashing step in QKD protocols, showing it preserves key rate while simplifying postprocessing.
motivation: QKD protocols typically perform error verification and privacy amplification as separate hashing steps, but a simpler single-step construction had lacked rigorous security proof.
method: The authors reduce the security of the combined protocol to a slightly modified secrecy notion for the protocol without final error verification, and analyze the impact within entropy-based security proofs.
result: For most entropy-based proofs, the combined protocol achieves the same key rate with only a minor change to the security parameter.
conclusion: The combined hashing procedure is rigorously justified, reducing classical postprocessing complexity, communication, and randomness requirements in QKD.

title: Exact Polariton-condensate States Via Nonlinear Stark Coupling
authors: Dakai He Abd Zhi Song
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a hybrid system of coupled cavities, with or without two-level atoms doped inside. By employing a building-block construction facilitated by nonlinear Stark coupling, we identify a manifold of exact many-body eigenstates that remain analytically tractable across arbitrary lattice geometries and atom distributions. We demonstrate that these exact states exhibit a dual physical nature depending on their spectral positioning: when embedded within the chaotic many-body spectrum, they manifest as quantum scars that violate the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis and undergo weak ergodicity breaking; conversely, as ground states within fixed-total-excitation sectors, they exhibit off-diagonal long-range order and form polariton condensates. Furthermore, numerical calculations of local excitation-number fluctuations suggest that negative Stark coupling shifts the Mott-insulator to superfluid transition toward weaker inter-cavity hopping. Our findings provide a versatile framework for engineering both coherent quantum phases and non-thermalizing states in diverse light-matter architectures.
tldr: Exact many-body eigenstates in coupled-cavity/atom hybrid systems via nonlinear Stark coupling manifest as either quantum scars violating ETH or polariton condensates with off-diagonal long-range order.

method: A building-block construction using nonlinear Stark coupling yields exact eigenstates across arbitrary lattice geometries and atom distributions; local excitation-number fluctuations are computed numerically to probe the Mott-insulator to superfluid transition.
result: The exact states exhibit a dual nature: embedded in the chaotic spectrum they are quantum scars with weak ergodicity breaking, while as ground states they form polariton condensates with off-diagonal long-range order; negative Stark coupling shifts the Mott-insulator to superfluid transition toward weaker hopping.

title: Attainable Boundaries Versus Operational Equivalence: Dual Benchmarks For The Hierarchical Assessment Of Quantum Resources
authors: Sunho Kim, Chunhe Xiong, Junde Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While conventional quantum resource theories quantify utility relative to an idealized set of free states, practical implementations are confined to a specific supply environment---a framework encompassing all states realizable or preparable via current experimental apparatus and design choices, not limited to free states. This work proposes a novel framework for evaluating the relative utility of arbitrary quantum states against the resource set made accessible by these current selections. We specifically focus our investigation on two canonical representations: the set of states reachable via free operations as the attainable boundary imposed by current experimental constraints, and the set defined through numerical optimization as the criterion for operational equivalence. Our framework establishes two core evaluation methodologies. First, we provide a strategy-dependent benchmark by assessing a state's performance relative to the reference set under its individually optimized strategy, thereby quantifying achievable performance. Second, we derive a computable lower bound on this superiority by considering optimal strategies for each state individually, enabling the quantification of strategy-independent relative performance independent of specific experimental setups. Beyond relative efficiency metrics, we demonstrate the practical utility of this approach for resource management scenarios, including the selective extraction of states advantageous for storage and distribution, and the concentration of residual resources. Using quantum entanglement as a paradigmatic example, we prove that distillable entanglement can be fully recovered via extraction and concentration when the reference set is restricted to pure states, thereby demonstrating the practical relevance of our framework.
tldr: The paper proposes a dual-benchmark framework for assessing the relative utility of quantum resources against experimentally accessible sets, with an entanglement example showing full recovery of distillable entanglement.
motivation: Conventional quantum resource theories evaluate utility relative to idealized free states, but practical implementations are constrained to specific experimentally accessible supply environments, requiring a more realistic benchmark.
method: It defines two reference sets—the attainable boundary reachable by free operations and the operational equivalence set from numerical optimization—then derives a strategy-dependent benchmark and a computable strategy-independent lower bound on relative performance.
result: The framework quantifies resource superiority and supports resource management tasks such as selective extraction and concentration; for entanglement, distillable entanglement is fully recoverable via extraction and concentration when the reference set is pure states.
conclusion: This work provides a practical, hierarchy-aware method for benchmarking quantum resources under experimental constraints, advancing operational resource theory and entanglement manipulation.

title: Quantum Jumps Of Sound
authors: Takuma Makihara, Erik Szakiel, Matthew P. Maksymowych, Oliver A. Hitchcock, Kaveh Pezeshki, Rachel G. Gruenke-Freudenstein, Mihir Pendharkar, Shannon P. Harvey, David I. Schuster, Amir H. Safavi-Naeini
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum mechanics predicts that a vibrating object's energy comes in discrete packets, yet no measurement of its position reveals this discreteness. Resolving individual energy levels requires a qualitatively different measurement, one coupling to the resonator's energy rather than its displacement. We use a superconducting qubit dispersively coupled to a nanomechanical resonator to perform repeated quantum nondemolition measurements of the phonon number. An aligned transfer-print technique integrating the qubit and resonator yields a mechanical lifetime of [MATH] milliseconds and a dispersive shift of [MATH] kilohertz per phonon. We heralded single-phonon states with 85% fidelity and observed quantum jumps between the resonator's first excited state and ground state. These discontinuous transitions are a striking manifestation of quantum mechanics in a massive, vibrating object.

Using an aligned transfer-print fabrication technique, they achieve a mechanical energy lifetime of T1 = 2.1 ms and a dispersive shift of 2χ/2π = 328 kHz per phonon. By repeatedly measuring the qubit's phase, they herald single-phonon Fock states with 85% fidelity and track the resonator's energy in real time, directly observing discontinuous transitions between the first excited state and the ground state. These jumps are a direct manifestation of energy quantization and quantum measurement backaction in a mechanical object containing billions of atoms.

title: Single-shot Magic State Factories For Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Varun Menon, Rohan Mehta, Andi Gu, Andrei C. Diaconu, Daniel Bochen Tan, Xiao Xiao, Michael J. Gullans, Qian Xu, Hengyun Zhou, Mikhail D. Lukin, J. Pablo Bonilla Ataides
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can substantially reduce the qubit overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but any useful architecture based on such codes also requires an efficient mechanism to implement non-Clifford gates in a fault-tolerant manner. The key ingredient is an efficient "escape" mechanism that teleports postselected logical magic states from tricycle codes to larger distance quadcycle codes. title: Geometry-optimized Hyperbolic Codes For Modular Fault-tolerant Quantum Architectures
authors: Steven Rayan Ahmed Adel Mahmoud
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum fault tolerance is a prerequisite to harness the full potential of quantum computers. However, achieving fault tolerance remains a major challenge since it requires optimizing tradeoffs between several intertwined theoretical and experimental parameters, including the encoding rate, code distance, parity-check weights, code planarity, and routing. Surface codes remain strong candidates for fault tolerance due to their simple geometric structure, established decoding methods, locality, and experimental attainability. In this work, we present finite families of hyperbolic surface codes that leverage the optimal efficiency scaling [MATH] attainable by surface codes with bounded local geometry. We show that optimizing the periodic identifications can double the code distance and thereby increase the code's efficiency by a factor of four, at fixed qubit count, encoding rate, and parity-check weight. We also address the routing problem of hyperbolic surface codes by introducing a topology-aware algorithm that partitions a hyperbolic code into bounded planar modules while reducing long-range communications demand. Circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations yield finite-size threshold estimates for both modular and monolithic layouts, showing that tripling the long-range gate error probability mildly lowers, but does not eliminate, the estimated error-correction thresholds. Together, these results strengthen the case for hyperbolic surface codes as structured and highly efficient large-scale quantum error correction codes for future fault-tolerant architectures.
tldr: The paper introduces geometry-optimized hyperbolic surface codes that improve code distance and efficiency while enabling modular, routing-aware fault-tolerant quantum architectures.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires optimizing tradeoffs among encoding rate, code distance, parity-check weight, planarity, and routing; surface codes are promising but need better geometric efficiency.
method: The authors construct finite families of hyperbolic surface codes with optimized periodic identifications and develop a topology-aware partitioning algorithm to map them into bounded planar modules, estimating thresholds via circuit-level Monte Carlo simulations.
result: Optimizing periodic identifications doubles code distance and quadruples efficiency at fixed qubit count, encoding rate, and parity-check weight; modular layouts maintain error-correction thresholds even with tripled long-range gate error.
conclusion: Hyperbolic surface codes offer a structured, highly efficient route toward large-scale fault-tolerant quantum architectures, with practical modular routing and favorable threshold estimates.

title: Helicity Decoupling Ultrastrong Rabi Splitting From Quantum Vacuum Dressing
authors: Ayoub El-Amrani, Nasir Boubekraoui, Zakaria Mzaouali, Houssam Sabri, Herschel Rabitz, Abdelouahed El Fatimy, Dukhyung Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polaritons and quantum vacuum dressing are usually regarded as intertwined consequences of ultrastrong light-matter coupling. Here we show that they can be controlled independently through helicity. We consider cyclotron resonance coupled to a chiral cavity supporting a single circular mode. When the helicity of the cavity field matches the cyclotron motion, energy is exchanged resonantly between light and matter, producing a large Rabi splitting and conventional polaritons, while the ground state remains the bare vacuum. Reversing the magnetic field reverses the cyclotron motion without changing the cavity. The same mode then couples through anomalous processes that create and annihilate light and matter excitations in pairs: the conventional polaritonic anticrossing disappears, while the ground state acquires squeezing and virtual excitations. These two regimes show that spectral hybridization and quantum vacuum dressing are distinct manifestations of ultrastrong coupling, and that a large Rabi splitting alone does not imply a dressed quantum vacuum. Helicity therefore provides a route to controlling polariton formation and quantum correlations as distinct resources in cavity quantum materials.

title: High-Rate Concatenated Quantum Error-Correcting Codes For Qudits
authors: Hayato Goto Takanori Nishi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Qudits provide a larger local Hilbert space than qubits and have recently attracted interest as building blocks for efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). In this work, we extend many-hypercube (MHC) codes, high-rate concatenated quantum codes, from qubits to qudits of prime dimension [MATH]. We construct the level-2 and level-3 MHC codes with parameters [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, and generalize the level-by-level minimum-distance (LLMD) decoder originally proposed for the qubit MHC codes. In a qudit [MATH]-error model, we evaluate the code-capacity performance of the qudit MHC codes for dimensions up to [MATH]. We find that the error threshold increases monotonically with the local dimension [MATH], reaching [MATH] for [MATH], nearly double the value of [MATH] for qubits. Furthermore, for sufficiently large local dimensions, we observe a pronounced waterfall regime in which the logical error rate decreases substantially faster than expected from conventional distance-based estimates. To understand the origin of the observed qudit advantage, we analyze the decoding performance in terms of the entropy of the underlying [MATH]-ary noise channel. This analysis reveals a competition between the increased syndrome information available at larger [MATH] and the simultaneous growth of the typical physical error weight at fixed entropy. These results demonstrate that higher-dimensional quantum systems can substantially improve the performance of high-rate concatenated quantum codes and motivate further development of qudit-based FTQC architectures.

title: Quantum non-Markovian Response Spectra
authors: Aaron Sander, John F. Kam, Gauthameshwar S., Robert Wille, Kavan Modi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum systems are rarely isolated from their surroundings. These hidden environments can retain information and return it later, producing correlated errors in quantum computers and complicating the interpretation of experiments.On a quantum processor, for example, one job can therefore leave an environmental trace that affects the next, even after the qubits themselves have been reset. Learning how this hidden influence persists and affects later behavior is therefore important, but the environment is often impossible to measure directly, and fully reconstructing its effects through tomography rapidly becomes impractical. Here, we introduce a response matrix that uses controlled interventions and observations of the system alone to reveal the temporal structure of environmental memory. The matrix records how future observations change across different controlled histories. Its spectrum characterizes how memory is structured and how it persists under specified system resets, while suitable linear combinations of its entries can rule out specified classical models of that memory. Because its history-future queries can be evaluated independently, numerical response matrices can be assembled in parallel. We establish the framework theoretically, characterize response spectra in an interacting spin process, and certify quantum memory in a two-qubit benchmark. This approach turns system observations into a probe of inaccessible environments and could support the diagnosis of correlated noise, tests of open system models, and memory-aware control design.
tldr: The paper introduces a response matrix built from controlled interventions and measurements of the system alone, whose spectrum reveals the temporal structure and persistence of hidden environmental memory in non-Markovian quantum processes.
motivation: Quantum devices are never truly isolated, and hidden environments can retain and later return information, causing correlated errors across reset operations that are hard to diagnose since the environment cannot be measured directly and full tomography is impractical.
method: The authors define a response matrix recording how future observations change across different controlled histories, characterize its spectrum theoretically, evaluate its entries via independently computable history-future queries (enabling parallelism), and use linear combinations to rule out specified classical memory models.
result: They establish the framework theoretically, characterize the response spectra for an interacting spin process, and certify genuine quantum memory in a two-qubit benchmark experiment.
conclusion: The approach turns accessible system observations into a probe of inaccessible environments, supporting correlated-noise diagnosis, open-system model testing, and memory-aware control design.

title: A Lower Bound On The Overhead Of Surgery On Sparse Stabiliser Codes
authors: Nou\'edyn Baspin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that performing lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes with sparse ancillas requires [MATH] ancillary qubits in the worst case. As a result, for codes with large [MATH], constant overhead ancillas can only realise a small fraction of possible measurements.
tldr: The paper establishes a lower bound on the number of ancillary qubits required for lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes, showing that constant-overhead ancillas can only implement a limited set of measurements.
motivation: Lattice surgery is a leading approach for implementing logical gates in quantum error correction, but the resource overhead of ancillary qubits is a critical practical concern.
method: The author derives an information-theoretic lower bound on the ancillary qubit count needed for general measurements via lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes with sparse ancillas.
result: For codes with large parameters, the worst-case ancillary overhead scales with the code size, implying that constant-overhead ancillas can only realise a small fraction of possible measurements.
conclusion: This work highlights fundamental limitations on the efficiency of lattice surgery and has implications for designing fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

Lattice surgery is a technique for implementing logical operations by measuring joint logical operators between code patches, and it is a cornerstone of many fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures. The authors focus on the scenario where the ancilla used to mediate the measurement is itself a sparse stabiliser code, meaning it has low-weight stabiliser generators and limited connectivity. They prove a lower bound: in the worst case, such a measurement requires $\tilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ ancillary qubits, where $k$ is the number of logical qubits encoded in the code. This result implies that for codes with large $k$, using a constant number of ancilla qubits (constant overhead) can only realise a vanishingly small fraction of all possible logical measurements. The paper likely employs combinatorial arguments and information-theoretic techniques to establish this bound, considering the constraints imposed by sparsity on the stabiliser generators and the need to preserve error-correcting properties. The findings highlight a fundamental trade-off between the sparsity of ancilla resources and the ability to perform arbitrary logical operations, with significant implications for the design of scalable quantum computing architectures based on sparse codes.

title: Sub-MHz Swap Spectroscopy Of Two-level Systems In Superconducting Qubits
authors: Joaquin Minguzzi, John Clai Owens, Oskar Painter, Matthew H. Matheny, Loren J. Swenson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An outstanding challenge in superconducting quantum circuits is mitigating loss from two-level system (TLS) defects. SWAP spectroscopy with flux-tunable qubits can detect individual TLSs, but the Rabi chevrons that signal coherent exchange have been observed only for the most strongly coupled defects. Here, we introduce a sequence with fast flux pulses only at state preparation and readout, switched off during the energy-relaxation delay for finer frequency resolution and longer interaction times. We detect Rabi chevrons at swap rates as low as 0.1 MHz, an order of magnitude lower than previously reported. In the dressed-state picture, we fit the coherent swap oscillations to extract the TLS energy-relaxation time. These Rabi chevrons reveal coherent TLSs with a median energy-relaxation time of 10 microseconds, at coupling strengths previously associated with incoherent TLSs. The swap coherence times exceed the qubit T2* limited by flux noise, indicating that the dressed gap protects them from low-frequency 1/f noise.
tldr: The paper introduces a fast-flux-pulse SWAP spectroscopy technique that detects coherent two-level system (TLS) defects in superconducting qubits at swap rates an order of magnitude lower than previously possible, revealing TLS energy-relaxation times around 10 microseconds.
motivation: Mitigating loss from TLS defects is a major challenge in superconducting quantum circuits, and existing SWAP spectroscopy has only observed Rabi chevrons for the most strongly coupled defects, limiting the study of weakly coupled coherent TLSs.
method: They use a sequence with fast flux pulses only at state preparation and readout, turning off flux modulation during the energy-relaxation delay to achieve finer frequency resolution and longer interaction times, and fit coherent swap oscillations in the dressed-state picture.
result: They detect Rabi chevrons at swap rates as low as 0.1 MHz, extract a median TLS energy-relaxation time of 10 microseconds, and find that swap coherence times exceed the qubit T2* limited by flux noise, indicating protection from low-frequency 1/f noise.
conclusion: The technique enables spectroscopy of weakly coupled coherent TLSs, providing insights into TLS coherence and decoherence mechanisms in superconducting qubits.

title: Photoluminescence Study Of Vanadium In 4h- And 6h- Silicon Carbide
authors: Ibrahim Boulares, Anne R. Evans, Jeremy L. Smith, Brenda Vanmil
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Point defects with optically addressable spin states are a key building block for quantum networks, but few solid-state emitters combine a spin-photon interface with emission in the low-loss telecommunications band. Vanadium (V4+) defects in silicon carbide (SiC) meet this requirement, emitting zero-phonon lines (ZPLs) throughout the telecom O-band in both the 4H- and 6H-SiC polytypes while retaining an addressable electron and nuclear spin system [1,2]. Although the orbital and spin structure of these defects has been characterized in detail, the polarization selection rules have not been fully mapped experimentally. Here we present polarization-dependent photoluminescence (PL) measurements of vanadium ZPLs in 4H- and 6H-SiC at cryogenic temperature, of two scattering geometries: edge and face-on (emission wavevector perpendicular and parallel to the crystal c-axis, respectively). Emission from two of the four {\alpha} sites, ({\alpha}2 and {\alpha}3) and the 6H-SiC {\gamma} sites, are polarized parallel to the c-axis ({\sigma}-polarized), whereas emission from {\alpha}1 and {\alpha}4 are polarized perpendicular to the c-axis ({\pi}-polarized). Additionally, we report preliminary, lower signal measurements of the sites.
tldr: Cryogenic polarization-dependent photoluminescence measurements map the zero-phonon-line polarization selection rules of vanadium (V4+) defects in 4H- and 6H-SiC for telecom-band spin-photon interfaces.
motivation: Vanadium defects in silicon carbide are promising solid-state emitters with addressable spins and telecom-band emission, but their polarization selection rules had not been fully mapped experimentally.
method: Polarization-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopy of vanadium ZPLs in 4H- and 6H-SiC at cryogenic temperature using edge and face-on scattering geometries.
result: The α2 and α3 sites in 4H-SiC and the γ sites in 6H-SiC emit σ-polarized light parallel to the c-axis, while α1 and α4 emit π-polarized light perpendicular to the c-axis; preliminary lower-signal measurements for additional sites are also reported.
conclusion: The work establishes polarization selection rules for V4+ in SiC, which is useful for designing quantum photonic devices based on telecom-emitting colour centres.

title: Engineering Quantum Interactions: From Effective Models To Validated Physical Predictions
authors: Sinara S. Dourado, Ciro Micheletti Diniz, Gabriel P. L. M. Fernandes, Rog\'erio J. de Assis, G. D. de Moraes Neto, Celso J. Villas-Boas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective models make complex quantum dynamics tractable by retaining only the states, processes, and timescales relevant to a given physical question. Their predictive power, however, depends on treating the retained manifold, initial state, observables, micromotion, dissipative channels, and eliminated degrees of freedom consistently. We develop a unified framework for constructing and validating effective descriptions using projection methods, Schrieffer--Wolff transformations, Magnus expansions, adiabatic elimination, small rotations, time coarse graining, and Floquet theory. The quantum Rabi model and its dispersive limits serve as recurring benchmarks for identifying control parameters, virtual processes, spectral corrections, observable dressing, and breakdown. Higher-order resonances and applications to collective light--matter coupling, Raman processes, spin-chain buses, lossy mediators, and driven lattices illustrate how effective interactions can be interpreted and designed. A physical prediction is organized into three order-consistent steps: encoding into the retained description, evolution under the effective dynamics, and reconstruction of the physical observable. This viewpoint exposes failures caused by leakage, small denominators, neglected micromotion, inconsistent observables, memory effects, or incorrectly transformed dissipation, while linking derivation, physical interpretation, and mechanism-guided discovery. Companion notebooks provide QuTiP implementations, convergence tests, and microscopic-to-effective comparisons.
tldr: A unified framework for constructing, validating, and interpreting effective quantum models, benchmarked on the quantum Rabi model and applied to light-matter, Raman, spin-chain, and driven-lattice settings.
motivation: Effective models are essential for tractable quantum dynamics, but their predictive power requires consistent treatment of the retained manifold, initial state, observables, micromotion, dissipation, and eliminated degrees of freedom.
method: The authors combine projection methods, Schrieffer-Wolff transformations, Magnus expansions, adiabatic elimination, time coarse graining, and Floquet theory, using the quantum Rabi model and its dispersive limits as recurring benchmarks.
result: The framework identifies control parameters, virtual processes, spectral corrections, observable dressing, and breakdown conditions, and exposes failures from leakage, small denominators, neglected micromotion, inconsistent observables, memory effects, and incorrectly transformed dissipation.
conclusion: The paper organizes physical predictions into encoding, effective evolution, and observable reconstruction, linking derivation, physical interpretation, and mechanism-guided discovery, with companion QuTiP notebooks provided.

title: Structured Leakage In OAM-encoded Qubits Revealed By Distributed Quantum Feature Extraction
authors: Yayu Mo, Nazifa Rumman, Sanjeev Shapkota, Thomas A. Searles, Sanjaya Lohani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes have emerged as an important platform for high-dimensional quantum communication but remain vulnerable to environmental noise and channel imperfections. Here we introduce a logical-qubit representation of OAM propagation in which modes evolve as qubits through noisy quantum channels. In this representation, turbulence manifests as leakage from the logical OAM subspace into turbulence-induced leakage components, providing a unified description of degradation in both single-photon and coherent-beam regimes. We show that turbulence-induced leakage exhibits systematic dependence on turbulence strength and OAM order, revealing structured signatures of information redistribution beyond the logical subspace. Leveraging this insight, we develop a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme that encodes high-dimensional OAM states into quantum representations and employs quantum convolutional operations to extract turbulence-robust features. Simulations and experimental measurements demonstrate robust extraction of these features across a broad range of turbulence strengths, OAM orders, and propagation conditions. Our results establish a direct link between OAM-channel dynamics, structured leakage, and quantum learning, providing a physics-informed framework for characterizing turbulence-degraded high-dimensional optical states and extracting robust signatures of turbulence-induced information redistribution.
tldr: The paper introduces a logical-qubit representation of OAM propagation through noisy channels and a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme to characterize turbulence-induced leakage and extract robust features from high-dimensional OAM states.
motivation: OAM modes are promising for high-dimensional quantum communication but are vulnerable to environmental noise and channel imperfections such as turbulence, requiring a unified description of degradation and robust methods for characterizing information redistribution.
method: The authors model OAM modes as qubits evolving through noisy quantum channels, interpret turbulence as leakage from the logical OAM subspace, and develop a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme using quantum convolutional operations on encoded high-dimensional OAM states.
result: Turbulence-induced leakage exhibits systematic dependence on turbulence strength and OAM order, and the quantum feature-extraction scheme robustly extracts turbulence-robust features across a broad range of turbulence strengths, OAM orders, and propagation conditions in simulations and experiments.
conclusion: The work establishes a direct link between OAM-channel dynamics, structured leakage, and quantum learning, offering a physics-informed framework for characterizing turbulence-degraded high-dimensional optical states and extracting signatures of information redistribution.

title: Certifying Hidden Paths: Scalable Topology Assurance For Qkd Networks
authors: Alessandro Colombo, Margherita Cozzolino, Stephan Krenn, Thomas Lor\"unser
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks rely on trusted repeaters, making the security properties of the selected communication path an essential part of end-to-end assurance. At the same time, network operators may be unwilling to disclose their internal topology. We present a topology-certification mechanism that lets a provider prove in zero knowledge that policy-compliant routes between two endpoints exist, without disclosing the routes in an individual presentation. Our main idea is to certify nodes and edges independently using multi-message signatures, rather than signing the complete graph as one object. For a route chosen in advance, proof size and cryptographic proving and verification work depend on its positions and attributes, independently of the overall network size, whereas route discovery and certification have separate graph-dependent costs. The construction hides the actual route length up to a public bound and sketches extensions to node-disjoint routes and monotonic additions within a graph epoch. We give a formal security model and conditional proofs of unforgeability and graph hiding for a generic construction. For a BBS-based construction, presentation-size estimates remain below [MATH]\,KiB at [MATH], and measured generation and verification times remain below [MATH]\,ms at [MATH] and [MATH].
tldr: The paper proposes a zero-knowledge topology-certification mechanism for QKD networks that proves policy-compliant routes exist without revealing the network topology.
motivation: Large-scale QKD networks depend on trusted repeaters, so end-to-end assurance requires verifying route security while operators may be unwilling to disclose their internal topology.
method: It certifies nodes and edges independently using multi-message signatures rather than signing the whole graph, with proofs for a pre-chosen route whose size scales independently of the overall network.
result: The construction hides route length up to a public bound, has a formal security model with conditional unforgeability and graph-hiding proofs, and a BBS-based instantiation keeps proof sizes below KiBs and generation/verification times below milliseconds.
conclusion: This enables scalable topology assurance for QKD networks while preserving route privacy, with possible extensions to node-disjoint routes and monotonic additions within a graph epoch.

title: Analog Quantum Simulation Of $\phi^4$ Field Theory With A Superconducting Transmission Line
authors: Ilan T. Rosen, Neill C. Warrington, Max Hays, Christopher Mcnally, Joshua Lin, Stephen Sorokanich III, Julian Bender
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum fields remains a fundamental challenge. We propose a superconducting transmission line for analog quantum simulation of [MATH]-dimensional [MATH] field theory. The transmission line comprises fluxonium-like circuit elements whose continuous and unbounded phase variables encode a scalar field without Hilbert-space truncation. Their anharmonic potentials provide strong interactions. Tuning the circuit parameters provides access to two distinct regimes. In the first, the transmission line emulates [MATH] field theory with a single-well potential. We confirm this correspondence through lattice Monte Carlo calculations of the low-energy spectra of both the circuit and lattice [MATH] theory. This regime enables scattering experiments between counter-propagating particle wave packets. The second parameter set yields a double-well potential that emulates [MATH] theory in the symmetry-broken phase and hosts degenerate vacua. Interfaces between the two vacua form topological kinks, and the transmission line can simulate kink-antikink collisions. We present state preparation and measurement protocols for both collision experiments, enabling spatially resolved, real-time studies of particle and soliton scattering in an interacting quantum field theory.
tldr: The paper proposes a superconducting transmission line with fluxonium-like elements for analog quantum simulation of φ⁴ field theory, including scattering and kink-antikink collision protocols.
motivation: Understanding interacting quantum field dynamics remains challenging, and analog quantum simulators can provide real-time, spatially resolved studies beyond classical computation.
method: They design a transmission line of fluxonium-like circuits whose continuous phase variables encode a scalar field, with tunable anharmonic potentials yielding single-well and double-well regimes, and validate low-energy spectra via lattice Monte Carlo.
result: The single-well regime emulates φ⁴ theory and enables counter-propagating particle scattering, while the double-well regime realizes symmetry-broken φ⁴ theory with degenerate vacua and topological kinks, including kink-antikink collisions.
conclusion: The platform offers state preparation and measurement protocols for real-time studies of particle and soliton scattering in an interacting quantum field theory using superconducting circuits.

title: Classification Of Bipartite Observables I: Stable And Uniformly Stable Observables
authors: Jos\'e Iovino Eduardo Due\~nez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When two quantum systems are prepared independently and each is driven to an idealized limit, the expectation of a bipartite observable may depend on which system is idealized first. We call an observable stable when it does not. We show that an observable is stable if and only if every idealized preparation of one system can be simulated to arbitrary accuracy, uniformly over all probes, by finite mixtures of actual preparations, provided that the probing system is idealized first; on stable observables, two idealized preparations have a unique, symmetric independent product. Under a uniform form of stability, the number of preparations that [MATH] adaptive probes can tell apart at a fixed margin is bounded by a polynomial in [MATH], and responses can be learned with a bounded number of mistakes; otherwise, at some margin, [MATH] probes tell apart [MATH] preparations. The swap test, Hong--Ou--Mandel coincidences and discrete equality tests are uniformly stable, with bounds independent of the dimension, while order comparisons of discrete spectra unbounded above are unstable. The proofs rest on the classical fact that a single double limit condition appears, under different names, in topology (Grothendieck), functional analysis (Krivine--Maurey), algebra (Arens), probability (Simons) and combinatorics (Pt\'ak), and in model theory as Shelah's stability; the independent product corresponds to Harrington's lemma. Model theory supplies a common language for these conditions; we use it as a Rosetta stone, pairing each physical question with its mathematical formulation.
tldr: The paper classifies bipartite observables as stable or uniformly stable using model theory, linking stability to the structure of the observable algebra.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a notion of stability for bipartite observables in quantum theory, addressing the ambiguity that arises when two independently prepared quantum systems are each driven to an idealized limit. The order in which the systems are idealized can affect the expectation value of a bipartite observable. An observable is called stable if this order does not matter. The authors prove that stability is equivalent to the condition that every idealized preparation of one system can be simulated to arbitrary accuracy, uniformly over all probes, by finite mixtures of actual preparations, provided the probing system is idealized first. On stable observables, two idealized preparations have a unique, symmetric independent product. Under a uniform form of stability, the number of preparations that n adaptive probes can distinguish at a fixed margin is bounded by a polynomial in n, and responses can be learned with a bounded number of mistakes; otherwise, at some margin, n probes can distinguish 2^n preparations. The swap test, Hong-Ou-Mandel coincidences, and discrete equality tests are shown to be uniformly stable with dimension-independent bounds, while order comparisons of discrete spectra unbounded above are unstable. The proofs rely on a classical double limit condition that appears in multiple mathematical fields, including topology (Grothendieck), functional analysis (Krivine-Maurey), algebra (Arens), probability (Simons), combinatorics (Pták), and model theory (Shelah's stability). The independent product corresponds to Harrington's lemma. Model theory provides a unifying language, acting as a Rosetta stone to pair physical questions with their mathematical formulations.

Proves an equivalence between stability and the uniform simulability of idealized preparations by finite mixtures of actual preparations, with a unique symmetric independent product on stable observables.

Establishes a dichotomy for learning and discrimination: uniform stability implies polynomial bounds on the number of preparations distinguishable by n adaptive probes and bounded mistake learning, while instability allows exponential discrimination (2^n preparations).

Demonstrates that the swap test, Hong-Ou-Mandel coincidences, and discrete equality tests are uniformly stable with dimension-independent bounds, whereas order comparisons of discrete spectra unbounded above are unstable.
Uncovers a deep connection between quantum stability and a classical double limit condition appearing across multiple mathematical disciplines, using model theory as a unifying framework.

title: On Linearity Or Non-linearity In Machine Learning For Quantum Chaotic Dynamics
authors: Francesco Perciavalle, Agostino Gallo, Francesco Plastina, Gianluigi Greco, Nicola Lo Gullo, Carlo Adornetto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurately simulating chaotic quantum many-body dynamics remains a major computational challenge for classical methods, due to the rapid buildup and spatial spreading of entanglement during the evolution. This raises the question of whether machine learning can provide an effective alternative for predicting quantum dynamics. We address this question by formulating quantum dynamics as a time-series forecasting problem, using a few-qubit PXP chain, realizable with Rydberg-atom arrays, as a benchmark. By varying the initial state, the system spans dynamical regimes ranging from ergodic behavior to quantum many-body scarring, providing a controlled setting for testing forecasting models across qualitatively different dynamics. We compare two contrasting architectures: an expressive nonlinear Transformer and DLinear, a simple linear forecasting model. The Transformer accurately predicts dynamics in the more ergodic regime, but its performance progressively deteriorates as the initial state approaches the scarred limit. In contrast, DLinear remains accurate across the entire family of initial states, with its main deviations consisting of small high-frequency oscillations that have little effect on the overall prediction error. Remarkably, these results show that observables generated by complex quantum many-body dynamics can be forecast with high accuracy through a simple linear mapping from past to future observations. This reveals that the complexity of the underlying quantum evolution need not translate into an equally complex forecasting problem.
tldr: Machine learning forecasting of quantum chaotic many-body dynamics shows that a simple linear model (DLinear) outperforms a nonlinear Transformer across ergodic to scarred initial states, indicating that complex quantum evolution need not require equally complex forecasting.
motivation: Classically simulating chaotic quantum many-body dynamics is challenging due to rapid entanglement buildup, so the authors ask whether machine learning can effectively predict such dynamics.
method: They formulate quantum dynamics as a time-series forecasting problem using a few-qubit PXP chain (realizable with Rydberg-atom arrays), and compare a nonlinear Transformer with a simple linear DLinear model across initial states ranging from ergodic to quantum many-body scarring.
result: The Transformer accurately predicts dynamics in the ergodic regime but deteriorates toward the scarred limit, whereas DLinear remains accurate across all initial states with only small high-frequency deviations that barely affect overall prediction error.
conclusion: Observables from complex quantum many-body dynamics can be forecast with high accuracy via a simple linear mapping, revealing that the complexity of the underlying quantum evolution does not necessarily translate into a complex forecasting problem.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates whether machine learning can efficiently forecast the dynamics of chaotic quantum many-body systems, which are notoriously difficult to simulate classically due to entanglement growth. The Transformer performs well in the ergodic regime but degrades as the initial state approaches the scarred limit. In contrast, DLinear maintains high accuracy across all initial states, with only minor high-frequency oscillations that negligibly affect prediction error. The key finding is that observables from complex quantum many-body dynamics can be forecast accurately via a simple linear mapping from past to future observations, suggesting that the complexity of the underlying quantum evolution does not necessarily imply a complex forecasting problem.
key_contributions: Demonstrates that a simple linear model (DLinear) can accurately forecast quantum many-body dynamics across ergodic and scarred regimes, outperforming a more expressive Transformer in the scarred limit.
Formulates quantum dynamics forecasting as a time-series problem and benchmarks it on a PXP chain, a experimentally relevant model for Rydberg-atom arrays.
Shows that the complexity of quantum evolution does not translate to complexity in forecasting, as linear mappings suffice for accurate predictions.
Provides a controlled comparison of nonlinear (Transformer) and linear (DLinear) architectures across qualitatively different dynamical regimes (ergodic vs. scarred).
Highlights the potential of simple machine learning models for predicting quantum dynamics, challenging the assumption that expressive models are always necessary.

The forecasting task is to predict future values of observables given a window of past observations. Two architectures are compared: a Transformer, which is a nonlinear attention-based model capable of capturing long-range dependencies, and DLinear, a simple linear layer that decomposes the time series into trend and seasonal components. The models are trained on data from some initial states and tested on others, or trained and tested on the same state but with different time windows. The performance is evaluated using prediction error metrics, likely mean squared error or similar. The choice of DLinear is motivated by its simplicity and recent success in time-series forecasting, while the Transformer serves as a strong nonlinear baseline. The experimental setup ensures a fair comparison by using the same input/output format and training procedure.
deep_read.results_analysis: The Transformer accurately predicts dynamics in the ergodic regime but its performance deteriorates as the initial state approaches the scarred limit. In contrast, DLinear remains accurate across the entire family of initial states, with its main deviations consisting of small high-frequency oscillations that have little effect on the overall prediction error. The paper likely reports quantitative metrics such as mean squared error (MSE) or R^2 scores, showing that DLinear achieves lower error than the Transformer in the scarred regime, while both perform similarly in the ergodic regime. title: Uncertainty Quantification For Quantum Fidelity Estimation
authors: Stephen Becker Kuchibhotla Aditi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum fidelity estimation is a fundamental task in quantum information and computing to benchmark the quality of quantum states, and hence of quantum processes, on noisy quantum hardware. Point estimates of fidelity by existing methods generally lack the rigorous uncertainty quantification required for reliable preparation and verification of these tasks. While Bayesian and bootstrap frameworks are widely used for uncertainty quantification, they are sensitive to model misspecification or lack formal coverage guarantees in non-asymptotic regimes. This paper introduces a hybrid "Bayesian-informed" conformal prediction-based framework to provide distribution-free, rigorous prediction intervals for quantum state fidelity estimation which can be used, with care, to approximate confidence intervals with respect to the quantum randomness of Born's rule. The framework requires a point estimator, and we consider both classical point estimators as well as data-driven neural net estimators. We evaluate the robustness of the methodology across a diverse range of experimental challenges, including finite-sample noise, tomographic incompleteness, physical model error, and out-of-distribution data. Our results demonstrate that conformalized estimators maintain statistical validity where traditional methods fail, offering a scalable and reliable approach for the verification of modern quantum systems. The best performing variant of our methodology is based on a class-conditional conformal prediction, as this most closely approximates the conditional coverage desired for a true confidence interval.
tldr: Introduces a conformal prediction-based framework for distribution-free uncertainty quantification in quantum state fidelity estimation.
motivation: Fidelity estimation is essential for benchmarking noisy quantum hardware, but existing point estimates lack rigorous uncertainty quantification in non-asymptotic regimes.
method: A hybrid Bayesian-informed conformal prediction framework using classical and neural net point estimators, tested under finite-sample noise, tomographic incompleteness, model error, and out-of-distribution data.
result: Conformalized estimators maintain statistical validity where traditional Bayesian and bootstrap methods fail, with class-conditional conformal prediction best approximating conditional coverage.
conclusion: The approach offers scalable and reliable uncertainty quantification for verifying quantum systems, though it is primarily a statistical methodology rather than a core quantum information theory contribution.

title: Demonstration Of Subspace-search Variational Quantum Eigensolver Using Photonic Orbital Angular Momentum Qudits
authors: Kang-Min Hu, Myung-Hyun Sohn, Yong-Su Kim, Kwang Jo Lee, Hyun Woo Kim, Hyang-Tag Lim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate excited state energies are essential for interpreting fluorescence and photochemical processes, yet variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware have largely been confined to ground states. Subspace-search VQE (SSVQE) offers a NISQ-friendly route to excited states without ancilla-based overlap measurements, however it has lacked an experimental demonstration since it requires the coherent preparation and manipulation of multiple orthogonal basis states under a shared variational unitary. Here we realize SSVQE on a photonic platform by encoding orthogonal qudit states in the orbital angular momentum of single photons and optimizing a shared variational circuit. We estimate excited state energies for a four-dimensional [MATH] molecule and an eight-dimensional Heisenberg chain, thereby demonstrating scalable excited state eigensolving in a high-dimensional Hilbert space. Our results establish photonic qudits as a resource-efficient pathway to excited state quantum simulation.
tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a subspace-search variational quantum eigensolver for excited states using photonic orbital angular momentum qudits.
motivation: Accurate excited state energies are important for photochemistry and fluorescence, but VQE on NISQ hardware has mostly targeted ground states; SSVQE avoids ancilla-based overlap measurements but had not been experimentally realized.
method: The authors encode orthogonal qudit states in the orbital angular momentum of single photons and optimize a shared variational circuit to estimate excited state energies of a four-dimensional molecule model and an eight-dimensional Heisenberg chain.
result: They achieve excited state eigensolving in a high-dimensional Hilbert space, showing that photonic qudits can serve as a resource-efficient platform for quantum simulation.
conclusion: Photonic orbital angular momentum qudits provide a viable path toward scalable excited state quantum simulation with a NISQ-friendly variational algorithm.

title: Q-Capsule: A Localized Capsule-Based Quantum Neural Architecture For Barren Plateau Mitigation
authors: Awal Ahmed Fime, Tasfia Zaman Samiha, Saika Zaman, Dimitris Pados, George Sklivanitis, Abdur R. Shahid, Ahmed Imteaj
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational quantum algorithms are often limited by barren plateaus: gradients vanish as circuit size and depth increase, making quantum neural networks difficult to train. We propose Q-Capsule, a localized capsule-based quantum neural architecture that mitigates this problem through register partitioning, local readout, sparse inter-capsule coupling, trainable data re-uploading, and Quantum Fisher Information Matrix (QFIM)-guided adaptive depth growth. By restricting the dominant support of each observable to a small capsule and controlling inter-capsule entanglement, Q-Capsule preserves useful gradient signals while retaining communication between local quantum representations. As the register width increases, Q-Capsule consistently maintains stable gradient variance, whereas globally entangling baselines exhibit exponential suppression with a log-gradient-variance slope near -ln 2 per qubit. Q-Capsule also produces more structured optimization landscapes, higher parameter efficiency, improved robustness to depolarizing noise, and lower measurement requirements. Its adaptive policy achieves 98.1% accuracy on binary classification and 97.7% on four-class classification, while using approximately 73% fewer two-qubit gates than the fixed-deep model on the multiclass task.
tldr: Q-Capsule is a localized capsule-based quantum neural architecture that mitigates barren plateaus through register partitioning, local readout, sparse inter-capsule coupling, and QFIM-guided adaptive depth growth.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms often suffer from barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with circuit size and depth, making quantum neural networks difficult to train.
method: The architecture partitions the quantum register into local capsules with restricted observable support and controlled inter-capsule entanglement, augmented by trainable data re-uploading and Quantum Fisher Information Matrix (QFIM)-guided adaptive depth growth.
result: Q-Capsule maintains stable gradient variance as register width increases, whereas globally entangling baselines show exponential suppression with a log-gradient-variance slope near -ln 2 per qubit; it also achieves 98.1% binary and 97.7% four-class accuracy with about 73% fewer two-qubit gates and improved noise robustness.
conclusion: Q-Capsule offers a promising approach to mitigate barren plateaus in quantum neural networks, though its contribution is primarily an architectural and machine-learning advance rather than an information-theoretic result.

title: From An Entropic Inequality For Sums In Abelian Groups To The Theorems Of Ruzsa And Pl\"unnecke
authors: Chandra Nair, Aref Namayandeh, Zhaobang Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a direct information-theoretic proof of the Pl\"unnecke--Ruzsa inequalities for finite subsets of abelian groups. The argument rests on an elementary coupling inequality proved by maximizing joint entropy, without tensor powers or asymptotic constructions. It also yields Ruzsa's sumset triangle inequality and an extension to non-abelian groups.
tldr: The paper gives a direct, elementary information-theoretic proof of the Plünnecke–Ruzsa sumset inequalities for finite subsets of (mostly abelian) groups using a coupling inequality derived from maximizing joint entropy.
motivation: The Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequalities are central results in additive combinatorics, but existing proofs are often involved; the authors aim to give a transparent entropy-based derivation that avoids tensor-power or asymptotic arguments.
method: They prove an elementary coupling inequality by maximizing joint entropy of a suitable pair of random variables, then apply it directly to obtain Ruzsa's sumset triangle inequality, the Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequalities, and an extension to non-abelian groups.
result: The approach reproduces the standard sumset growth inequalities without asymptotic constructions and extends them to non-abelian groups, all from a single entropic inequality.
conclusion: The work illustrates the power of elementary entropy inequalities as a tool in additive combinatorics, providing short and unified proofs of classical sumset results.

title: The Hint Weight Of Ml-dsa Signatures Is Key-Dependent: An Empirical Study Across The Three Fips 204 Parameter Sets
authors: Dominik Blain
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every ML-DSA (FIPS 204) signature carries a public hint vector h. We find that the Hamming weight of each hint polynomial h_k depends on the signing key: to first order it measures the Euclidean norm of (t0)_k, the low-order part of t that key generation leaves out of the public key. A closed-form model predicts the per-key mean weight with Pearson r between 0.95 and 0.98; once the norm is accounted for, we detect no key-dependent signal above sampling noise. We measure the effect on the reference C implementation, with 200 keys and 2,000 signatures per key for each parameter set. A one-way ANOVA rejects key-independence of the total hint weight for ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 (F = 30.1, 10.3, 11.1). The effect is weak: the key explains 0.5% to 1.5% of the variance of the total weight. A single signature identifies its key among 200 with 1.1 to 1.3 times chance accuracy from the total weight, and 1.5 to 1.8 times from the per-polynomial weight vector. A one-sided test at significance 0.001 separates two typical keys with probability one half after about 1,300 to 3,700 signatures per key. The hint weight does not endanger the signing key. The Dilithium designers do not treat t0 as secret, and t0 is known to be recoverable from signatures. The hint weight is, however, a weak statistical fingerprint: with enough signatures, it can be used to test whether they come from a common key, without the public key. Bounded-weight signing, a backward-compatible filter whose effect on the security argument we did not analyze, removes 86-91% of the between-key spread of the total weight but leaves the per-polynomial channel largely intact.
tldr: The Hamming weight of ML-DSA signature hint polynomials depends on the signing key, acting as a weak statistical fingerprint despite not endangering the key.
motivation: To investigate whether the public hint vector in ML-DSA signatures leaks key-dependent information that could be exploited for key identification or linkage.
method: Empirical study on the reference C implementation with 200 keys and 2,000 signatures per key across ML-DSA-44, -65, and -87, using a closed-form model, one-way ANOVA, and one-sided tests.
result: Key explains only 0.5–1.5% of variance in total hint weight; a single signature identifies its key 1.1–1.3× above chance from total weight and 1.5–1.8× from per-polynomial weights; separating two keys at significance 0.001 requires about 1,300–3,700 signatures per key.
conclusion: The hint weight is a weak statistical fingerprint that does not compromise signing security, and bounded-weight signing removes most between-key spread in total weight but leaves the per-polynomial channel largely intact.

title: Axiomatic Incompatibility Between Thermal Equilibrium And Volume-Dependent Entropy In Ideal Gas Theory
authors: Andrea Paglietti
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A rigorous macroscopic analysis of classical thermodynamics reveals an overlooked contradiction at the foundations of ideal gas theory: the traditional volume dependent formula for entropy violates the fundamental axiom of thermal equilibrium during reversible isothermal processes. This paper resolves this inconsistency by establishing a strict operational distinction between strictly isothermal and quasi isothermal processes. We show that in order for the perfect gas to be strictly consistent with the laws of classical thermodynamics, the thermodynamic entropy of a perfect gas must be a function of temperature only. This independence of volume is also confirmed by a new analysis of the adiabatic free expansion of an ideal gas, which is found to be intrinsically reversible. To reconcile these results with standard thermodynamic practice, we introduce the concept of a pseudo isothermal process (a finite sequence of small adiabatic and isochoric steps) and show that the classical equations for work and heat apply rigorously to these real processes, as opposed to strictly isothermal ones.
