We conclude by discussing the profound implications of these findings for statistical mechanics, showing that while the corrected thermodynamic entropy is in perfect agreement with Maxwell's kinetic theory, it is essentially different from the Planck Boltzmann formula. Thus, thermodynamic entropy and statistical microstate counting are two different physical quantities, and the present analysis provides a simple way to free classical thermodynamics from the paradoxes of microscopic disorder.
tldr: The paper argues that the volume-dependent entropy formula for an ideal gas violates the axiom of thermal equilibrium and should be replaced by a temperature-only entropy, with a distinction between strictly and quasi isothermal processes.
motivation: There is an overlooked foundational contradiction in classical ideal gas thermodynamics between the traditional volume-dependent entropy and the requirement of thermal equilibrium during reversible isothermal processes.
method: A macroscopic axiomatic analysis of classical thermodynamics, introducing a strict operational distinction between strictly isothermal and quasi isothermal processes, and re-examining adiabatic free expansion and pseudo isothermal processes.
result: Thermodynamic entropy of a perfect gas must depend only on temperature, the adiabatic free expansion is intrinsically reversible, and classical work/heat equations apply rigorously to pseudo isothermal rather than strictly isothermal processes.
conclusion: Thermodynamic entropy is fundamentally different from statistical microstate counting via the Planck-Boltzmann formula, and the corrected classical thermodynamics avoids the paradoxes of microscopic disorder.

title: Integer Programming On Polytopes Of Chv\'atal Rank One Is As Hard As Lattice Problems
authors: Alberto Del Pia
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A rational polyhedron has Chv\'atal rank at most one if a single round of Chv\'atal-Gomory cuts yields its integer hull. For such polyhedra, integer feasibility is in NP [MATH] coNP by a result of Boyd and Pulleyblank from the early 1980s, so it is unlikely to be NP-hard. Whether it is polynomial has remained open since then. We answer this question negatively, under either of two standard assumptions from lattice-based cryptography. First, a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem would solve bounded distance decoding with polynomial factors in deterministic polynomial time, contradicting a widely believed conjecture. Second, assuming the hardness of learning with errors, an average-case analogue of bounded distance decoding, the problem is also hard on average, for an efficiently samplable distribution of polytopes. Both results rest on an elementary sufficient condition: a polyhedron has Chv\'atal rank at most one if its width is less than one along every row of some unimodular matrix. For our polytopes, such a matrix exists but is hard to find.
tldr: The paper proves that integer feasibility on polyhedra of Chvátal rank one is computationally hard under lattice-based cryptographic assumptions, resolving a long-standing open question negatively.
motivation: Despite being in NP ∩ coNP and thus unlikely NP-hard, whether integer programming on Chvátal rank-one polyhedra is polynomial-time solvable has been open since the 1980s.
method: The author establishes an elementary sufficient condition—width less than one along every row of a unimodular matrix—for Chvátal rank at most one, and reduces bounded distance decoding and learning with errors to integer feasibility on such polytopes.
result: A polynomial-time algorithm for the problem would solve bounded distance decoding with polynomial factors in deterministic polynomial time, and under the LWE assumption the problem is also average-case hard for an efficiently samplable distribution of polytopes.
conclusion: The work shows that integer programming on Chvátal rank-one polytopes is as hard as lattice problems, providing strong evidence against polynomial-time solvability.

title: Provable Subexponential Algorithms For Nist Third-Round Lattice Families
authors: Yiming Gao, Xuyuan Han, Honggang Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give provable classical subexponential algorithms for secret recovery in growing parameter families associated with NIST third-round lattice candidates. For the Kyber/ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, SABER, NTRU LPRime, and Dilithium/ML-DSA families studied here, polynomial moduli and polylogarithmic coefficient scales yield recovery of the short secret component in expected time and space [MATH]. For noisy or rounded linear relations, we exploit an exact gap in the squared Euclidean norm of a comparison vector defined by each coordinate guess. One Gaussian list suffices to identify every secret coordinate by binary search, without enumerating the others. We establish the required sampling guarantees through new geometric bounds for structured public operators over prime and power of two moduli. The construction builds on the Wagner-style Gaussian sampling framework of Ducas, Engelberts, and Loyer (CRYPTO 2025) and the low-error decision-LWE algorithm of Han, Gao, and Hu (2026). For quotient relations of NTRU type, we develop an affine slice search: fixing coordinates restricts candidate pairs to slices of the public lattice, and their estimated Gaussian masses guide the choice of each next coordinate. In the stated modulus window, Falcon's key generation quality condition supplies the required mass bound. The algorithm then recovers an equivalent signing key with high probability in time and space [MATH]. The same search recovers the short key core for cyclic NTRU-HPS/HRSS. Together, these results give subexponential algorithms for problem families associated with all seven NIST third-round lattice candidates. Despite the subexponential complexity, our results do not establish a reduction in the concrete security of the currently specified parameter sets.
tldr: The paper presents provable classical subexponential-time algorithms for secret recovery in lattice problem families underlying all seven NIST third-round post-quantum cryptographic candidates.
motivation: Lattice-based schemes such as Kyber, Dilithium, and Falcon form the backbone of post-quantum standardization, so understanding the asymptotic hardness of their underlying structured lattice problems is of central cryptographic interest.
method: The authors extend the Wagner-style Gaussian sampling framework of Ducas, Engelberts and Loyer with a one-list binary-search coordinate recovery technique exploiting an exact squared-norm gap, plus an affine slice search for NTRU-type quotient relations, supported by new geometric bounds on structured public operators over prime and power-of-two moduli.
result: For polynomial moduli and polylogarithmic coefficient scales, they achieve subexponential classical time and space for recovering short secrets in Kyber/ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, SABER, NTRU LPRime, Dilithium/ML-DSA, Falcon and NTRU-HPS/HRSS families; notably the results do not translate into concrete security reductions for deployed parameter sets.
conclusion: The work gives asymptotic subexponential cryptanalytic algorithms across all NIST third-round lattice families but leaves the concrete security of currently specified parameters essentially untouched.

title: Three Improved Lower Bounds For Binary Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Kazuki Ota, Takayuki Osa, Tatsuya Harada
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Error-correcting codes are a foundational technology for representing information robustly against noise in communication and data storage. The binary code packing problem, which seeks to maximize the number of codewords at a fixed code length and minimum distance, is a fundamental problem in coding theory that remains open for many parameter choices. We give explicit binary codes with parameters [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], where [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] denote the code length, number of codewords, and minimum distance, respectively. These establish the lower bounds [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], where [MATH] denotes the maximum possible number of codewords, improving the respective lower bounds 80, 192, and 64 in the public table of general binary codes. Most notably, the third result improves the lower bound supplied by a lexicographic construction for the first time in 66 years, while the first two improve bounds that have stood for 21 years. The new codes represent more messages without changing the code length or error-correction guarantees, with gains compounding multiplicatively across blocks. We release all codewords and an exhaustive verifier to enable independent verification.
tldr: The paper constructs explicit binary error-correcting codes that improve three lower bounds on the maximum number of codewords for fixed length and minimum distance.
motivation: The binary code packing problem is a fundamental open problem in coding theory, and improving lower bounds helps understand achievable code sizes for specific parameters.
method: The authors provide explicit constructions of binary codes with specified parameters and release all codewords plus an exhaustive verifier for independent verification.
result: The new codes improve the respective lower bounds 80, 192, and 64 in the public table of general binary codes, with one bound improving for the first time in 66 years and two for the first time in 21 years.
conclusion: These codes allow more messages to be represented without changing code length or error-correction guarantees, and the gains compound multiplicatively across blocks.

title: Accelerating Hqc For Post-Quantum Tls 1.3 On X86 IoT Gateways
authors: Jihoon Jang, Hyunju Park, Jebin Kim, Seokhie Hong, Suhri Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-quantum TLS at an IoT gateway must protect many device connections without large increases in handshake delay, CPU cost, or network traffic. HQC provides code-based diversity beyond ML-KEM, but its computation and ciphertext sizes can increase these costs. We optimize HQC for x86 processors with AVX2, AVX-512, and the Galois Field New Instructions (GFNI), and integrate the resulting implementations into TLS 1.3. We extend branch-free Toom-Cook/Karatsuba multiplication to AVX-512, accelerate Reed-Solomon decoding with GFNI, improve Reed-Muller decoding, accelerate SHA3-512 and fixed-weight sampling, and port Frobenius additive FFT (FAFFT) multiplication to AVX-512 + GFNI for HQC-5. On an Intel Core i5-1135G7 processor, our AVX2 implementation reduces decapsulation by 11.1-21.5% over the fastest prior AVX2 results. Our AVX-512 implementation reduces key generation by 24.9-29.5%, encapsulation by 10.4-11.1%, and decapsulation by 20.6-26.1% relative to Cabral et al. across the three HQC parameter sets. We evaluate the effects of these implementations on TLS 1.3 handshake latency and server and client CPU costs, as well as the effects of round-trip time (RTT) and bandwidth. In local loopback TLS measurements, our AVX-512 HQC-5 implementation reduces handshake latency from 3.22 ms to 2.92 ms compared with Cabral et al. On a constrained path with 1 Mbit/s bandwidth and an added RTT of 50 ms, the HQC-5 handshake takes 243 ms, compared with 87 ms for ML-KEM-1024. This indicates that HQC public-key and ciphertext sizes, rather than implementation speed, determine the remaining handshake cost on constrained links.
tldr: The paper optimizes the code-based post-quantum KEM HQC for x86 processors using AVX2, AVX-512, and GFNI, and integrates it into TLS 1.3 to measure handshake latency and CPU costs on IoT gateways.
motivation: Post-quantum TLS at IoT gateways must protect many device connections without prohibitive increases in handshake delay, CPU cost, or traffic, and HQC offers code-based diversity beyond ML-KEM at the price of larger computations and ciphertexts.
method: The authors extend branch-free Toom-Cook/Karatsuba multiplication to AVX-512, accelerate Reed-Solomon decoding with GFNI, improve Reed-Muller decoding and SHA3-512/fixed-weight sampling, and port Frobenius additive FFT multiplication to AVX-512+GFNI for HQC-5, then benchmark the resulting TLS 1.3 integration.
result: AVX2 reduces decapsulation by 11.1–21.5%, while AVX-512 cuts key generation by 24.9–29.5%, encapsulation by 10.4–11.1%, and decapsulation by 20.6–26.1% versus prior work; on a 1 Mbit/s link with 50 ms RTT the HQC-5 handshake takes 243 ms versus 87 ms for ML-KEM-1024.
conclusion: HQC public-key and ciphertext sizes, rather than implementation speed, dominate the remaining handshake cost on constrained links, so further gains require protocol or size-level improvements rather than micro-optimization alone.

title: A Zero-Knowledge Signature Framework For Efficient Post-Quantum Message Authentication In Cooperative Automated Driving
authors: Takahito Yoshizawa, Aysajan Abidin, Edoardo Pena-Gonzalez, Bart Preneel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAV) rely on authenticated Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications to exchange safety-critical information among vehicles and roadside infrastructure. As the automotive industry transitions toward post-quantum cryptography (PQC), the significantly larger public keys and signatures of standardized PQC digital signature algorithms introduce substantial communication overhead, which challenges the scalability of certificate-based V2X authentication, particularly for high-frequency cooperative awareness messages (CAM). This paper presents ZKS-PQC, a zero-knowledge signature framework that enables communication-efficient post-quantum message authentication for cooperative V2X systems. Instead of transmitting complete post-quantum public keys and signatures, the proposed framework replaces this authentication material with a compact Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) while preserving compatibility with existing certificate-based trust architectures. This approach supports incremental migration and backward compatibility with the legacy ECDSA. The framework is implemented using the Open Quantum Safe (liboqs) and ZKP (Bulletproofs) libraries, and we evaluated the performance of standardized NIST PQC signature algorithms and additional candidate algorithms. Experimental validation on both a Linux platform and a commercial On-Board Unit (OBU) demonstrates substantial reductions in message size exceeding 95% for all algorithms, while limiting additional processing overhead by staying within the order of milliseconds at both sender and receiver in many algorithms, consistent with the latency requirements of real-time V2X operation. By decoupling communication overhead from the size characteristics of post-quantum signature algorithms, ZKS-PQC offers a practical migration strategy for scalable, quantum-resilient message authentication in future CAV systems.
tldr: ZKS-PQC replaces bulky post-quantum public keys and signatures in V2X cooperative driving messages with compact Bulletproofs zero-knowledge proofs, cutting message size by over 95% while retaining certificate-based trust.
motivation: Post-quantum signature schemes have large keys and signatures, creating excessive communication overhead for high-frequency cooperative awareness messages in connected and automated vehicles, threatening the scalability of certificate-based V2X authentication.
method: The authors design a zero-knowledge signature framework that substitutes standard PQC public-key/signature authentication material with a compact ZKP, implemented with liboqs and Bulletproofs and evaluated against NIST standardized and candidate PQC signature algorithms.
result: Experimental validation on Linux and a commercial On-Board Unit shows message-size reductions exceeding 95% across all algorithms, with added processing overhead remaining on the order of milliseconds at both sender and receiver, compatible with real-time V2X latency requirements.
conclusion: ZKS-PQC decouples V2X communication overhead from PQC signature sizes, offering a practical, backward-compatible migration path to quantum-resilient message authentication in future CAV systems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Inference Of Conditional Future Probabilities With Reduced Memory Cost
authors: Jianjun Chen, Akshat Gupta, Chengran Yang, Ariel Neufeld, Jayne Thompson, Thomas J. Elliott, Mile Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many potential future events have devastating consequences, from the onset of earthquakes to financial black swan events. Accurate predictions of their probability of occurrence are vital. Yet as the stochastic systems underlying such events become increasingly complex, these probabilities can depend on ever-growing amounts of past data, which require ever more memory to track. The accuracy of our estimates is ultimately limited by both computational and memory constraints; the former to reduce sampling error, the latter to avoid sampling bias. Traditional quantum algorithms -- such as amplitude estimation -- address only the former, and become untenable especially in near-future quantum devices where quantum memory is a premium. Here, we offer quantum-algorithmic means to reduce systematic bias while maintaining a quadratic speed-up. Our results thus advance the timeline for the practical deployment of quantum technologies, and illustrate their additional benefits when simulating processes of growing complexity.
tldr: The paper proposes quantum-algorithmic methods to estimate conditional future probabilities with reduced memory cost while retaining a quadratic speed-up over classical sampling.
motivation: Accurate prediction of rare future events is limited by computational sampling error and by the memory needed to track ever-growing past data; existing quantum algorithms such as amplitude estimation address only the former.
method: The authors develop quantum algorithms that reduce systematic bias in estimating conditional future probabilities, maintaining a quadratic speed-up and lowering quantum memory requirements.
result: The approach achieves reduced memory cost and systematic bias while preserving quadratic quantum speed-up, making it more suitable for near-term quantum devices with limited quantum memory.
conclusion: The work advances the practical deployment of quantum technologies for simulating complex stochastic processes, illustrating benefits beyond raw computational speed-up.

title: Scaling Quantum Optimization To The Thousand-Qubit Scale With Distributed Quantum Sampling
authors: Amana Liaqat, Ahmed Darwish, Stephen Diadamo, Dan Holme, Kieran Mcdowall, Emre Sahin, Naeimeh Mohseni, Giorgio Cortiana, Corey O'meara
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition (MBD) seeks a sparse weighted sum of matchings and is a challenging optimization problem with applications in network scheduling and energy trading. We scale a quantum-assisted decomposition method by combining single-layer QAOA sampling with Extended Fully-Corrective Frank-Wolfe (E-FCFW) optimization, spectral graph partitioning, and greedy feasibility repair. We demonstrate the pipeline on the 1,354-node PEGASE bus test case (representing a 1,354-bus transmission grid with 1,710 transmission lines), whose 1,710 edges define a native 1,710-variable matching optimization problem requiring 1,710 qubits in the unpartitioned encoding. Partitioning enables distributed execution on IBM superconducting quantum processors. The best reported hardware result uses a 50-qubit partition bound, while reducing partitions to 20 qubits degrades convergence in the partition-size comparison. Larger partitions are more demanding for matrix product state (MPS) simulation, and bond-dimension tests show that truncating quantum correlations reduces candidate quality. The results therefore motivate retaining a substantive quantum sampling task within each partition as the overall problem scales. On the PEGASE-1354 benchmark, repaired QAOA samples achieve lower residual decomposition error than both simulated annealing and uniform random sampling baselines, while spatial circuit packing reduces hardware execution time by approximately a factor of three. These results demonstrate that combining spectral partitioning, spatial circuit packing, and classical feasibility repair provides an executable path for deploying gate-based quantum sampling on thousand-variable constrained optimization problems on current hardware.
tldr: The paper scales a quantum-assisted Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition pipeline using QAOA sampling, spectral graph partitioning, spatial circuit packing, and classical repair, demonstrating on a 1,354-node grid benchmark with up to 50-qubit partitions on IBM superconducting hardware.
motivation: Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition is a challenging optimization problem for network scheduling and energy trading, and scaling quantum sampling to thousand-variable constrained problems on near-term hardware remains difficult.
method: The approach combines single-layer QAOA sampling with Extended Fully-Corrective Frank-Wolfe optimization, spectral graph partitioning, spatial circuit packing, and greedy feasibility repair, evaluated via MPS simulation and IBM superconducting processors.
result: Repaired QAOA samples achieve lower residual decomposition error than simulated annealing and uniform random sampling baselines, and spatial circuit packing reduces hardware execution time by roughly a factor of three, with 50-qubit partitions outperforming 20-qubit partitions.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical path for deploying gate-based quantum sampling on thousand-variable constrained optimization problems using current hardware, motivating retention of substantive quantum sampling tasks within each partition as problems scale.

title: Quantum Simulation Of A Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System With Superconducting Circuits
authors: Han-Xin Che, Yangyang Yu, Tao Zhang, Wen Zheng, Hai-Feng Yu, Xinsheng Tan, Yang Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperbolic geometry hosts a plethora of exotic quantum phenomena ranging from holographic duality to novel topological phases. However, investigating these effects experimentally remains challenging due to the Euclidean constraints of natural crystalline materials. While recent synthetic lattices have achieved static realizations, they often lack the dynamical tunability required to explore the full geometric landscape. Here, we overcome these limitations by implementing a quantum simulation of hyperbolic geometry within the parameter space of a superconducting quantum circuit. We construct a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System (HDQS) by mapping the hyperbolic properties onto the dynamically controllable Hamiltonian parameters. By probing the systems' response under geometric quantum driving, we elucidate how the intrinsic geometry of the parameter space dictates observable physical quantities. Furthermore, we extend the theoretical framework to realize ensemble simulation. This generalization enables us to harness the fast coherent control of superconducting qubits to capture essential geometric characteristics, establishing a versatile platform for exploring quantum dynamics on hyperbolic manifolds.
tldr: The paper implements a quantum simulation of hyperbolic geometry using the parameter space of a superconducting quantum circuit.
motivation: Hyperbolic geometry hosts exotic quantum phenomena, but experimental exploration is difficult because natural materials are Euclidean.
method: The authors map hyperbolic properties onto dynamically controllable Hamiltonian parameters of a superconducting circuit to create a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System, and probe its response under geometric quantum driving.
result: They observe how the intrinsic geometry of the parameter space dictates physical quantities and extend the framework to ensemble simulation.
conclusion: Superconducting qubits provide a versatile platform for exploring quantum dynamics on hyperbolic manifolds, establishing a new route for quantum simulation of non-Euclidean geometries.

title: Disorder-induced Nuclear-transition Doublet At Nominally Cubic $^{229}$Th Sites
authors: Andrei Derevianko
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The [MATH]Th nuclear clock transition is inhomogeneously broadened even at sites of nominally cubic symmetry, where the electric-field gradient of the ideal lattice vanishes. We show that dilute static point-defect disorder produces a doublet with a zero at the quadrupole-free frequency. The doublet is symmetric in the isotropic approximation; size misfit point defects introduce a small lobe asymmetry without removing the zero. Charged and size-misfit defects share inverse-cube scaling and an approximately common normalized profile, whose width separates into a host-controlled background and a term linear in the [MATH]Th density. In a heavily doped [MATH]Th:CaF[MATH] crystal [Nature 657, 626 (2026)], the thorium-linked contribution is comparable to the measured 1.1 MHz width; in a lightly doped crystal [arXiv:2606.08870], the 0.9 MHz width bounds the host background. Neither spectrum shows the predicted dip, which points to the presence of extended defects in both crystals. If the predicted dip is resolved, it can provide a nuclear-clock discriminator referenced to the quadrupole-free nuclear transition frequency.
tldr: Dilute static point-defect disorder is predicted to produce a doublet in the inhomogeneously broadened 229Th nuclear clock transition at nominally cubic sites.
motivation: The 229Th nuclear clock transition is inhomogeneously broadened even at cubic sites where the ideal electric-field gradient vanishes, motivating a microscopic understanding of disorder effects.
method: A theoretical model of charged and size-misfit point-defect disorder is developed and compared with measured spectra in heavily and lightly doped Th:CaF2 crystals.
result: The model predicts a doublet with a zero at the quadrupole-free frequency, inverse-cube scaling, and a width separating host background from a thorium-density-linear term; the absence of the predicted dip suggests extended defects.
conclusion: Resolving the predicted dip could provide a nuclear-clock discriminator referenced to the quadrupole-free nuclear transition frequency.

title: Finite- And Long-range Spin-wave Free-energy Asymptotics For The Two-dimensional Quantum Heisenberg Ferromagnet
authors: Andreas Klippel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the two-dimensional quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet with asymptotically radial power-law exchange, we prove the leading low-temperature free energy at every fixed spin, uniformly on the weak-field scale. We obtain fractional and logarithmically corrected laws associated with the dispersions predicted in [16, 17]. Quantum Monte Carlo simulations support the associated anomalous magnon dispersions for spin one-half [20]. For kernels with finite second moment, we also extend the nearest-neighbour theorem [14], generalizing Takahashi's quadratic law [21] and its weak-field dependence [11].
tldr: The paper rigorously derives leading low-temperature free-energy asymptotics for the two-dimensional quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet with power-law exchange, revealing fractional and logarithmic corrections tied to anomalous magnon dispersions.
motivation: Understanding low-temperature thermodynamics and spin-wave excitations in low-dimensional quantum magnets with long-range or finite-range interactions is a fundamental problem in quantum statistical mechanics.
method: The author uses mathematical analysis of spin-wave free-energy asymptotics, including rigorous proofs for radial power-law kernels, and supports the predicted magnon dispersions with quantum Monte Carlo simulations.
result: The main results are fractional and logarithmically corrected free-energy laws associated with anomalous magnon dispersions, and an extension of the nearest-neighbour theorem for kernels with finite second moment that generalizes Takahashi's quadratic law and its weak-field dependence.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous low-temperature free-energy asymptotics for 2D quantum Heisenberg ferromagnets, unifying and extending earlier spin-wave results, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Flash-Based Relativistic Collapse Model For Quantum Fields
authors: Nicol\`{o} Piccione
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spontaneous collapse models provide a possible, testable solution to the quantum measurement problem, but constructing a relativistic version applicable to quantum field theory remains an important open challenge. Challenges in constructing relativistic collapse models include avoiding superluminal signaling and foliation dependence, controlling energy production, and ensuring vacuum stability. Here, we present a relativistic collapse framework that addresses these problems at the cost of introducing a new space of physical states, whose complete characterization is left open. A modified, history-dependent Aharonov--Albert prescription describes instantaneous nonlocal state updates on arbitrary spacelike foliations while preserving foliation independence. To ensure vacuum stability, we modify the standard unitary evolution through a prescription that we name dynamical vacuum subtraction. The resulting dynamical map is linear and trace-preserving but not positive on the full set of standard density operators. We establish no-signaling by proving microscopic parameter independence, and identify conditions under which standard nonrelativistic collapse dynamics are recovered. Finally, we apply our framework to a free massive scalar field, obtaining finite particle-number and energy-increase rates at leading order in the long-time regime, together with further promising evidence for the consistency of the framework.
tldr: The paper proposes a flash-based relativistic collapse model for quantum fields that addresses no-signaling, foliation dependence, and vacuum stability using a modified Aharonov-Albert prescription and dynamical vacuum subtraction.
motivation: Constructing a relativistic version of spontaneous collapse models applicable to quantum field theory remains an open challenge, with key issues including superluminal signaling, foliation dependence, energy production, and vacuum stability.
method: The framework uses a history-dependent Aharonov-Albert prescription for instantaneous nonlocal state updates on arbitrary spacelike foliations, and introduces dynamical vacuum subtraction to modify standard unitary evolution, yielding a linear trace-preserving but non-positive dynamical map.
result: No-signaling is established via microscopic parameter independence, and application to a free massive scalar field gives finite particle-number and energy-increase rates at leading order in the long-time regime.
conclusion: The framework addresses major obstacles for relativistic collapse models at the cost of introducing a new space of physical states, with further evidence for consistency and recovery of nonrelativistic dynamics under certain conditions.

title: Nonlinear Feedback In Josephson Circuit Optimization: Application To A Kerr-Reversal Jtwpa
authors: Emanuele Palumbo, Alessandro Alocco, Andrea Celotto, Luca Fasolo, Bernardo Galvano, Patrizia Livreri, Emanuele Enrico
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimizing Josephson-based nonlinear microwave devices is computationally demanding because the straightforward approach requires exploring broad circuit parameter spaces through expensive nonlinear simulations. Josephson Circuits Optimizer addresses this problem by using harmonic balance simulations in two stages: fast linear simulations to select promising circuit configurations according to properties such as impedance and phase matching, followed by nonlinear simulations to optimize their operating conditions. However, pump-induced effects such as impedance renormalization and Kerr-induced modifications of phase matching are not captured during the initial linear stage. We therefore introduce a nonlinear feedback extension that transfers information from the pumped response back to the linear optimization. The approach is investigated using a Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifier with a reversed-Kerr architecture, whose model is validated against experimental gain measurements. We then evaluate the difference between the linear and pumped response values of a metric based on the input reflection coefficient, while excluding configurations with insufficient third-harmonic suppression. This discrepancy is considered a candidate feedback observable, as it exhibits features similar to the gain landscape, supporting its use in subsequent optimization cycles.
tldr: The paper introduces a nonlinear feedback extension to a Josephson circuit optimizer and applies it to a reversed-Kerr JTWPA, using pump-induced discrepancies between linear and nonlinear response metrics as a candidate feedback observable.
motivation: Optimizing Josephson nonlinear microwave devices is computationally demanding because pump-induced effects such as impedance renormalization and Kerr-induced phase-matching modifications are not captured by the initial fast linear optimization stage.
method: The authors extend the Josephson Circuits Optimizer with a nonlinear feedback loop that transfers pumped-response information back to the linear optimization, validate the JTWPA model against experimental gain measurements, and evaluate the difference between linear and pumped values of an input-reflection-coefficient-based metric while excluding configurations with insufficient third-harmonic suppression.
result: The linear-versus-pumped discrepancy exhibits features similar to the gain landscape, supporting its use as a feedback observable in subsequent optimization cycles.
conclusion: Nonlinear feedback can improve Josephson circuit optimization by incorporating pump-induced effects, potentially enhancing the design of JTWPA and similar superconducting microwave devices.

title: Optical Signals Synthesized From An Optical Lattice Clock With Uncertainty Of 1.3e-17
authors: Yuan Yao, Jinpeng Zou, Haosen Shi, Hongfu Yu, Longsheng Ma, Yanyi Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report an accurate optical frequency synthesizer, which can generate single-frequency laser light with high frequency stability and accuracy at desired frequencies over a wide optical region. The frequency of the output signal is divided from an 171Yb optical lattice clock via an accurate optical frequency divider based on an optical frequency comb. Therefore, the output of the optical frequency synthesizer inherits the frequency accuracy from the Yb optical clock. The frequency uncertainty of the 171Yb optical lattice clock is evaluated to be 6.8 mHz, corresponding to a fractional frequency uncertainty of 1.3E-17, mainly limited by the blackbody radiation shift and the lattice-induced light shift.
tldr: The paper reports an optical frequency synthesizer that inherits the accuracy of a 171Yb optical lattice clock via an optical frequency comb, achieving fractional frequency uncertainty of 1.3e-17.
motivation: Accurate optical frequency synthesis is needed to transfer the stability and accuracy of optical clocks to other optical frequencies for applications in precision metrology and spectroscopy.
method: An optical frequency divider based on an optical frequency comb is used to divide the frequency of a 171Yb optical lattice clock and generate single-frequency laser light at desired optical frequencies.
result: The output signals inherit the clock's accuracy, with the 171Yb optical lattice clock evaluated to have a fractional frequency uncertainty of 1.3e-17, mainly limited by blackbody radiation and lattice-induced light shifts.
conclusion: The demonstrated synthesizer provides highly stable and accurate optical signals over a wide optical region, useful for optical clock comparisons and precision measurements.

title: A General Framework For Crystallization In Maximal Hard-core Models
authors: Alexander Barg, Qidong He, Geyang Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study general maximal hard-core models on periodic lattice-type graphs. While for standard models, phase coexistence may arise for high activity, for maximal models this behavior may occur also for sufficiently low activity values. Relying on the concept of volume allocation, we develop a {\em unified set of assumptions} that imply the Peierls condition, a convergent cluster expansion for the partition function, and hence the conclusions of Pirogov-Sinai theory for this class of models. We further check these assumptions for a number of examples including standard lattice-type periodic graphs, proving crystallization for both high and low activity. We also derive estimates for the values of activity that bound the phase coexistence regions in the phase diagram, rewriting for this purpose the proof of a technical result in the derivation of Pirogov-Sinai theory.
tldr: The paper develops a unified framework for proving crystallization in general maximal hard-core models on periodic lattice-type graphs using Pirogov-Sinai theory.
motivation: Maximal hard-core models can exhibit phase coexistence at both high and low activity, unlike standard models, motivating a general theory for their phase behavior.
method: The authors introduce volume allocation assumptions that imply the Peierls condition and a convergent cluster expansion, then verify these assumptions for several examples and derive bounds on activity for phase coexistence.
result: They establish crystallization for both high and low activity in standard lattice-type periodic graphs and provide estimates for the activity values bounding phase coexistence regions.
conclusion: The framework extends Pirogov-Sinai theory to maximal hard-core models, offering a systematic approach to analyzing crystallization and phase diagrams in this class.

title: Retromorphic Testing Of Quantum Compiler Passes
authors: Olivia Di Matteo Mushahid Khan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum compilers play a critical role in transforming high-level quantum programs into optimized, hardware-compatible circuits. However, verifying the correctness of compiler passes remains challenging, as determining the expected output of large, deeply entangled quantum circuits is computationally intractable. This challenge is further amplified when compiler passes modify already complex circuit structures, making manual validation of transformed circuits impractical. In this work, we perform a systematic analysis of unit tests for quantum compiler passes in four quantum programming frameworks (PennyLane, Qiskit, Cirq, and pytket). Our findings indicate validation is dominated by program-content and program-metric assertions, and test circuits are generally small and shallow. Motivated by these observations, we introduce a testing methodology for automated validation of quantum compiler passes based on retromorphic testing and principles from the Hadamard test. This methodology analyzes a compiler pass, test circuit, and expected pass behavior to verify semantic preservation and intended structural modifications. We implement our methods in a framework, RetroQ, and apply it to compiler passes in PennyLane and Qiskit. Experimental evaluation reproduced several existing bugs as well as uncovered previously undetected defects, such as flawed symbolic parameter handling, incorrect commutation logic, failure to recognize self-adjointness of gates, and runtime crashes. These findings highlight the need for compiler-pass-specific testing methodologies to improve the reliability of the evolving quantum software stack.
tldr: The paper introduces retromorphic testing, based on the Hadamard test, to automatically validate quantum compiler passes and detects bugs in PennyLane and Qiskit.
motivation: Verifying the correctness of quantum compiler passes is challenging because expected outputs of large entangled circuits are intractable to compute, and current unit tests are dominated by shallow, content-based assertions.
method: The authors systematically analyze unit tests across PennyLane, Qiskit, Cirq, and pytket, then propose a retromorphic testing methodology using Hadamard-test principles to check semantic preservation and intended structural modifications, implemented in a framework called RetroQ.
result: RetroQ reproduced several existing bugs and uncovered previously undetected defects in PennyLane and Qiskit, including flawed symbolic parameter handling, incorrect commutation logic, failure to recognize self-adjointness, and runtime crashes.
conclusion: Compiler-pass-specific testing methodologies are needed to improve the reliability of the quantum software stack.

title: Omnisolver: An Extensible Interface To Ising Spin-glass And Qubo Solvers: Adding A Distributed Gpu Brute-force Plugin
authors: Konrad Ja{\l}owiecki, Jakub Paw{\l}owski, Bart{\l}omiej Gardas, {\l}ukasz Pawela
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This software update extends Omnisolver with , a first-class plugin for exact exhaustive search of QUBO and Ising instances on CUDA-enabled GPUs. The update contributes three components: packaging of the single-GPU brute-force kernel of [Computer Physics Communications 260, 107728, 2021] as a first-class Omnisolver plugin with a uniform Python and CLI interface, a Ray-based distributed framework that splits the search into [MATH] fixed-variable subproblems and dispatches them across multiple GPUs and hosts, with a controller that gathers and merges partial results, and numerical stabilization of the fast ground-state path through compensated incremental updates, periodic exact energy re-anchoring, and best-buffer refresh. Stabilization activates automatically for [MATH] leaving the public sampler API is unchanged. On dense random Ising instances we measure exhaustive solve times up to [MATH] on [MATH] NVIDIA H100 (96 GB) GPUs, reaching [MATH] days at [MATH] in close agreement with the empirical [MATH] doubling rule, with the distributed sampler reaching the full [MATH] speedup over a single H100 from [MATH] onwards. The plugin thereby serves as a practical ground-truth oracle for state-of-the-art classical heuristics such as the Simulated Bifurcation Machine.
tldr: Omnisolver is extended with a distributed GPU brute-force plugin for exact exhaustive search of QUBO and Ising spin-glass instances.
motivation: Exact solvers for QUBO and Ising problems are needed as ground-truth oracles to benchmark classical heuristics such as simulated bifurcation machines.
method: The authors package a single-GPU brute-force kernel as an Omnisolver plugin and add a Ray-based distributed framework that splits the search into fixed-variable subproblems across multiple GPUs and hosts, with numerical stabilization for large instances.
result: On dense random Ising instances the plugin achieves exhaustive solve times up to very large scales, reaching days at certain sizes on 96 GB H100 GPUs and showing full distributed speedup over a single H100 from a threshold problem size onward.
conclusion: The plugin provides a practical extensible ground-truth oracle for state-of-the-art classical heuristics in QUBO and Ising optimization.

title: A Sign In Space Part 2, A New Simulated First Contact Scenario Engaging The Global Scientific Seti Network, And Integrating Deep Space Technologies Into Seti Search
authors: Daniela de Paulis, Andrea Melis, Daniel Estevez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence programme aims to find evidence of extraterrestrial intelligence. SETI scientists pursue this objective by searching for technosignatures primarily in the radio or optical spectrum. The IAA SETI Committee has been developing protocols to offer guidelines in case of an actual extraterrestrial signal reception. These protocols establish procedures to confirm the authenticity of the signal and its actual extraterrestrial nature, as well as the committee's role in managing the discovery in relation to the scientific community and the general public, targeting scientific queries in relation to the management and development of equipment and methodologies employed in current SETI search. The project A Sign in Space part 2 aims to actively engage the global SETI community and the global telescope network, with scientific facilities responding and coordinating themselves to confirm the extraterrestrial nature of the received signal. The project develops some of the societal, scientific and technological methodologies already employed in the interdisciplinary work A Sign in Space. Here, we established a global collaboration between SETI scientists, radio observatories and the European Space Agency to test the communication and technological pipeline and protocols leading to the reception of a simulated extraterrestrial signal by a network of radio telescopes across the globe. We also employed an ESA spacecraft for system validation. A Sign in Space part 2 aims to further implement deep space technologies in SETI search through a structured and sustained programme, in collaboration with ESA, the SETI Institute and the Italian Institute for Astrophysics. The project will aim to stage and test the entire Post Detection procedure, implementing the protocol as envisioned by the IAA SETI committee.
tldr: The paper describes 'A Sign in Space Part 2', a simulated first-contact scenario that engages a global network of radio telescopes and ESA spacecraft to test SETI post-detection protocols.
motivation: SETI scientists need validated procedures for confirming and responsibly managing the reception of a putative extraterrestrial technosignature, but end-to-end communication and coordination protocols remain largely untested.
method: The authors orchestrated a global collaboration between SETI researchers, radio observatories, the SETI Institute, INAF, and ESA, transmitting a simulated extraterrestrial signal and using an ESA spacecraft for system validation to exercise the detection pipeline across multiple facilities.
result: The project demonstrated the feasibility of coordinating a worldwide telescope network to receive and authenticate a simulated signal, while surfacing practical and procedural gaps in the IAA SETI post-detection protocol.
conclusion: The work establishes a framework for a sustained programme integrating deep-space technologies into SETI search and for rehearsing the full post-detection procedure with international partners.

title: The Hellinger Conjecture For Antipodal Boolean Functions
authors: Vu Khac Ky
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The balanced Hellinger conjecture compares the overlap of two output laws induced by a Boolean decision under binary symmetric noise. We prove that a single input coordinate minimizes this overlap among antipodal decisions, whose values reverse when all input signs are reversed, throughout the noise interval. The proof uses a normalized nuclear norm of the cross-class block of the Gram matrix of square-root channel densities. Multiplication by an antipodal decision exchanges the even and odd Fourier spaces preserved by the Gram matrix. A coordinate exchange attains the minimum cost of matching their spectra. A matrix contraction extends the sharp bound to arbitrary independent binary-input channels. Fixed coordinate flips and randomized decisions follow from the same argument and concavity. These extensions give bounds for information and testing, including linear Gaussian observations, and a weighted edge-boundary inequality.
tldr: The paper proves the balanced Hellinger conjecture for antipodal Boolean functions under binary symmetric noise, with extensions to general binary-input channels and applications to information bounds and Gaussian observations.
motivation: The Hellinger conjecture concerns minimizing the overlap of output distributions from Boolean decisions corrupted by noise, a problem in classical information theory and Boolean Fourier analysis.
method: The proof uses a normalized nuclear norm of the cross-class block of the Gram matrix of square-root channel densities, exploiting exchange between even and odd Fourier spaces under antipodal decisions and a matrix contraction argument.
result: A single input coordinate minimizes the overlap throughout the noise interval, and the sharp bound extends to arbitrary independent binary-input channels, fixed coordinate flips, randomized decisions, and linear Gaussian observations.
conclusion: These extensions yield bounds for information and testing, including a weighted edge-boundary inequality, but the work is purely classical and does not engage quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: On The Impossibility Of Estimating The Average Mixing Time
authors: Amedeo Roberto Esposito Nathan A. Judd
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish nearly-matching converse bounds on the sample complexity of estimating the average mixing time of a Markov chain from a single stationary trajectory. Unlike the worst-case mixing time, which maximises the total-variation distance to stationarity over all initial states, the average mixing time averages this distance under the stationary distribution and can therefore be substantially smaller. Our converse bounds establish when estimation is impossible, and match the key dependencies in existing achievability bounds, up to logarithmic factors. Together, these bounds provide nearly-tight PAC guarantees for estimating the average mixing time.
tldr: The paper establishes nearly-tight converse bounds on the sample complexity of estimating the average mixing time of a Markov chain from a single stationary trajectory.
motivation: Average mixing time can be much smaller than worst-case mixing time, so understanding whether it can be estimated from limited stationary data is important for PAC-style guarantees.
method: The authors derive information-theoretic converse bounds for estimating average mixing time, comparing them with existing achievability bounds up to logarithmic factors.
result: They obtain nearly-matching upper and lower bounds, characterizing when estimation is impossible and providing nearly-tight PAC guarantees.
conclusion: The bounds show that estimating average mixing time from a single stationary trajectory has sample complexity governed by key dependencies matching existing achievable rates.

title: Noise-Induced Navigation In Non-convex Domains And Compact Manifolds
authors: Karthik Elamvazhuthi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this note, we study the problem of designing a feedback law that globally steers a system to a prescribed target configuration. Even if the system is fully actuated, topological obstructions generally prevent the existence of globally asymptotically stabilizing continuous feedback laws. We revisit this problem in a stochastic setting by allowing noise to enter through the control channels. Using a criterion for asymptotic stability in the large that combines local Lyapunov stability with positive recurrence, we constructively show that one can construct elementary feedback laws that achieve global asymptotic stability in the large, of the target equilibrium point in connected Euclidean domains with obstacles and manifolds without boundary. For Euclidean domains with obstacles, we also show that the method extends naturally to the problem of finding the minimizer of a strongly convex function with non-convex constraints. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of the approach for Euclidean domains with circular obstacles and the two dimensional sphere. Additionally, we study the role noise strength when there is a non-convex obstacle, in which case the system might show metastability.
tldr: The paper constructs noise-enabled feedback laws that achieve global asymptotic stability for systems constrained by topological obstructions, with applications to non-convex domains and compact manifolds.
motivation: Topological obstructions can prevent globally stabilizing continuous feedback laws for fully actuated systems, even when local control is possible.
method: The authors combine local Lyapunov stability with positive recurrence to design elementary stochastic feedback laws, and extend the approach to minimizing strongly convex functions under non-convex constraints.
result: They demonstrate global asymptotic stability in the large for target equilibria in Euclidean domains with obstacles and on manifolds without boundary, including numerical experiments on circular obstacles and the 2D sphere, and they discuss metastability for non-convex obstacles.
conclusion: Noise in control channels can overcome topological obstructions to global stabilization, providing a constructive stochastic control framework, though it is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Decision-Sufficient Posterior Approximation
authors: Sean Plummer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the consequences of requiring a posterior approximation to preserve a specified downstream decision problem. A target posterior [MATH] and loss determine a regret geometry on actions, a baseline approximation [MATH] determines the forward-Kullback-Leibler information required to induce action changes, and a restricted approximation family [MATH] determines which such changes are available. Contracting KL divergence over Bayes-action fibers gives exact distances to decision adequacy and decision failure together with the least-informative posterior deformations that reach either side of the decision boundary. In regular finite-dimensional problems, the target and baseline constructions have quadratic local limits: a target regret Hessian [MATH] and a baseline information metric [MATH] . Their generalized eigenproblem [MATH] orders local decision directions by regret consequence per unit information cost and induces a tolerance-dependent effective dimension. For restricted approximation families, the tangent image separates decision coverage from information efficiency: a family may miss consequential decision directions, or it may realize reachable directions only at excess Fisher cost. The resulting framework provides decision-relative criteria for comparing and designing posterior approximation families.
tldr: The paper develops a decision-theoretic geometry for posterior approximations, characterizing when an approximate posterior suffices for a specified downstream decision problem via regret Hessians and KL/Fisher information metrics.
motivation: Posterior approximations (e.g., variational inference) are usually evaluated by divergence to the target posterior, but what actually matters is preserving downstream decisions; the paper asks what it means for an approximation to be decision-sufficient.
method: It defines regret geometry on actions, measures forward-KL information needed to change actions, and contracts KL divergence over Bayes-action fibers to obtain exact distances to decision adequacy/failure; local quadratic limits yield a generalized eigenproblem relating regret Hessian to a baseline information metric.
result: The framework yields decision-relative distances to the decision boundary, ordered local decision directions by regret-per-information-cost, an induced effective dimension, and a tangent-image decomposition separating decision coverage from information efficiency in restricted approximation families.
conclusion: The paper offers decision-relative criteria for comparing and designing posterior approximation families, grounded in information geometry rather than pure distributional fidelity.

title: Where Do The Tokens Go? Understanding And Reducing Costs In Llm Agents For Vulnerability Discovery
authors: Li Lu, Yanjie Zhao, Hongjie Chen, Haoyu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents can spend millions of tokens during vulnerability discovery without producing a working proof of concept (PoC). What consumes that budget, and why does it fail to produce results? We diagnose these costs and failures through a multi-axis open-coding study of 200 CyberGym traces, spanning four agents (i.e., Codex, OpenCode, Cybench, and EnIGMA) under an unaided baseline and four existing efficiency methods. The study reveals three key findings. First, different agents vary substantially in success and cost, and higher spending does not consistently yield better outcomes. Second, code localization and understanding, together with vulnerability reasoning and trigger design, account for 60.4% of tokens and represent the two leading bottlenecks in failed runs. Third, only 24.4% of matched comparisons preserve success at lower total cost; unsuitable signals and auxiliary overhead limit the benefits of existing methods. Motivated by these findings, we present AVRI, an Agent-centric Vulnerability Reasoning Interface built around a persistent Bidirectional Evidence Trace (BET). BET connects how the harness consumes input with the conditions required to make a selected operation unsafe, retaining source-supported correspondences alongside the agent's hypotheses and open questions. Reading, analysis, and persistence commands help agents build and reuse this evidence rather than repeatedly retrieve and reconstruct it. On 20 evaluation tasks, AVRI reduces total cost by 18.0% for Codex and 23.7% for OpenCode while preserving success rates and improving or maintaining recall.
tldr: This paper diagnoses token costs and failures in LLM agents for vulnerability discovery and proposes an agent-centric interface called AVRI to reduce costs while preserving success.
motivation: LLM agents can consume millions of tokens during vulnerability discovery without producing a working proof of concept, so the authors aim to understand where the budget goes and why existing efficiency methods often fail.
method: They conduct a multi-axis open-coding study of 200 CyberGym traces across four agents and four efficiency methods, then design AVRI around a persistent Bidirectional Evidence Trace (BET) that links harness inputs to unsafe operation conditions and maintains source-supported correspondences, hypotheses, and open questions.
result: The study finds that code localization/understanding and vulnerability reasoning/trigger design account for 60.4% of tokens and are leading bottlenecks in failed runs, while only 24.4% of matched comparisons preserve success at lower total cost; AVRI reduces total cost by 18.0% for Codex and 23.7% for OpenCode on 20 evaluation tasks while preserving success and improving or maintaining recall.
conclusion: The work provides a diagnostic account of token expenditure in LLM-driven vulnerability discovery and shows that an evidence-centric interface can lower costs without sacrificing success, though it is outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Propagation-Invariant Transmission Eigenmodes In Weakly Scattering Media
authors: P. A. Quinto-Su J. C Osorio-Tascon
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Propagation-invariant beams (PIBs) with annular angular spectra preserve their transverse intensity structure over extended propagation distances. Here, we investigate whether scattering invariant modes (SIMs) can simultaneously exhibit scattering and propagation invariance. We measure free-space and sample transmission matrices (TMs) in an orthonormal annular basis for weak, moderate, and strong scattering media and identify localized SIMs (LSIMs) whose angular spectra remain predominantly confined to one or a few neighboring rings. Under weak scattering, 75 of the 128 SIMs considered for annular localization satisfy this criterion, with LSIMs exhibiting Bessel-like propagation. Under moderate scattering, 25 LSIMs are recovered after filtering low-intensity spectral components, whereas none are found under strong scattering. Although increasing modal crosstalk progressively suppresses annular localization and nondiffracting behavior, SIMs retain higher transverse-intensity correlation over propagation than the Gaussian-like and Bessel beams in the moderate and strong regimes. These results show that annular localization enables SIMs to acquire propagation invariance when scattering is weak, whereas the enhanced propagation robustness of SIMs can persist even after this localization is lost.
tldr: The paper studies whether scattering-invariant modes in weakly scattering media can simultaneously exhibit propagation invariance, finding annular localization enables nondiffracting behavior only for weak scattering.
motivation: Propagation-invariant beams preserve transverse intensity over distance, while scattering-invariant modes resist disorder; the authors ask whether both properties can coexist in the same optical mode.
method: They measure free-space and sample transmission matrices in an orthonormal annular basis for weak, moderate, and strong scattering media, identifying localized scattering-invariant modes whose angular spectra remain confined to a few rings.
result: Under weak scattering, 75 of 128 modes show annular localization and Bessel-like propagation; moderate scattering yields 25 after filtering, and strong scattering yields none, though scattering-invariant modes retain higher transverse correlation than Gaussian-like or Bessel beams.
conclusion: Annular localization enables propagation invariance only when scattering is weak, but enhanced propagation robustness of scattering-invariant modes can persist even after localization is lost.

title: High-resolution Mapping Of The Phase Boundary Of The Honeycomb-lattice Blume--Capel Ferromagnet
authors: Claudio J. Dasilva Eluiz C. M. Filho
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a high-resolution numerical study of the spin-1 Blume--Capel ferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice ([MATH]). Wang--Landau estimates of the joint density of states [MATH], combined with field mixing, are used to map the first-order transition line and locate the tricritical point at [MATH]. Histogram reweighting of Metropolis simulations for [MATH] and [MATH] provides an independent consistency check, with a crossing temperature near [MATH], compatible with the Wang--Landau extrapolation. From the field-mixing analysis we obtain [MATH], while the slope of the multicanonical coexistence line yields the consistent and more precise estimate [MATH]. Normalizing by the zero-temperature field [MATH], the available honeycomb, square, triangular, and simple-cubic estimates cluster near [MATH], corresponding to a magnitude about [MATH] larger than the mean-field value [MATH]; no systematic dependence on coordination number or dimensionality is resolved over the range examined. Finite-size scaling of [MATH] gives [MATH], consistent with the tricritical Ising value [MATH], while the fourth-order cumulant scaling is compatible with [MATH]. Deep in the first-order regime, the cumulant approaches the expected two-phase limit [MATH]. Multicanonical simulations up to [MATH], using weights constructed directly from the Wang--Landau density of states for [MATH] and rescaled and refined for larger systems, yield an interface-tension exponent [MATH], consistent with the tricritical prediction [MATH]. Finally, we map the continuous branch of the phase boundary from the same density-of-states data, obtaining [MATH]; estimates sufficiently close to the tricritical point are affected by crossover from Ising to tricritical scaling.
tldr: A high-resolution numerical study maps the phase boundary and tricritical point of the spin-1 Blume-Capel ferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice using Wang-Landau and multicanonical methods.
motivation: The Blume-Capel model exhibits rich phase behavior including first-order transitions and tricritical points, but precise characterization on the honeycomb lattice remains incomplete.
method: Wang-Landau estimates of the joint density of states combined with field mixing and histogram reweighting of Metropolis simulations are used to locate the phase boundary, tricritical point, and interface-tension exponent.
result: The tricritical point and critical exponents are determined, with finite-size scaling consistent with tricritical Ising values; normalized tricritical field estimates cluster near a universal value across lattice geometries.
conclusion: The findings provide precise numerical estimates for the honeycomb Blume-Capel ferromagnet and suggest no systematic dependence of the normalized tricritical field on coordination number or dimensionality over the examined range.

title: Energy-barrier Characterization Of Secured Basins In Coupled Oscillators With Inertia
authors: Jaiyong Lee, Daekyung Lee, Seung-Woo Son, Sang Hoon Lee, Mi Jin Lee, Heetae Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The second-order Kuramoto model captures rotor dynamics relevant to synchronization in power grids. In actual power grids, violation of angle-stability limits can trigger protective actions that are not included in the model, restricting its validity to trajectories that remain within these limits. We therefore define the secured basin as the region of disturbance space comprising disturbances whose trajectories remain within the angle-stability limits throughout the transient. We then characterize the secured basin through energy barriers, quantifying their characteristic energy scale and heterogeneity across perturbation directions. Across seven power-grid models, this characterization revealed angle-stability vulnerabilities overlooked when stability is assessed solely by the final synchronization state. It also showed that the two energy-barrier measures characterizing the secured basin exhibit distinct associations with structural connectivity and dynamical parameters. This characterization further offers practical advantages, as energy thresholds derived from state-space perturbations remain effective in distinguishing secured and unsecured outcomes under short-duration power disturbances and can be estimated efficiently by concentrating simulations near the secured-basin boundary. Overall, the secured-basin framework provides a useful basis for distinguishing node-level structural and dynamical influences on transient stability in oscillator networks with synchronization constraints.
tldr: This paper characterizes the secured basin of the second-order Kuramoto model for power grids using energy barriers to quantify transient stability under angle-stability limits.
motivation: The second-order Kuramoto model is widely used for power-grid synchronization, but it ignores protective actions triggered by angle-stability violations, limiting its validity to trajectories that remain within stability limits.
method: The authors define the secured basin as the set of disturbances whose trajectories stay within angle-stability limits throughout the transient, and characterize it via energy-barrier measures across seven power-grid models.
result: Energy barriers reveal angle-stability vulnerabilities that are missed when only final synchronization is considered, and the two barrier measures show distinct relationships with structural connectivity and dynamical parameters.
conclusion: The secured-basin framework provides a practical basis for distinguishing structural and dynamical influences on transient stability in oscillator networks with synchronization constraints.

title: The Markov Accessibility Topology And Its Probabilistic Structure
authors: Jorge Vielma Lourival Lima
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we associate a canonical topology with the transition operator of a discrete-time Markov chain. We prove that this construction defines an Alexandroff topology, called the Markov Accessibility Topology, and subsequently establish that it coincides with the Alexandroff topology induced by the accessibility relation. This establishes a direct connection between probabilistic accessibility and order-theoretic topology, allowing several classical notions from Markov chain theory to be interpreted in topological terms. Among other results, we characterize absorbing subsets as closed sets, relate irreducibility to topological connectedness and the triviality of the topology, describe minimal open neighborhoods through accessibility and hitting probabilities, and investigate the communication quotient together with its relationship to lumpability.
tldr: The paper introduces the Markov Accessibility Topology, an Alexandroff topology canonically associated with the transition operator of a discrete-time Markov chain, linking probabilistic accessibility to order-theoretic topology.
motivation: The authors aim to connect Markov chain theory with topology by showing that probabilistic accessibility relations induce a natural Alexandroff topology.
method: They define a topology from the transition operator, prove it coincides with the Alexandroff topology of the accessibility relation, and interpret classical Markov chain concepts (absorbing sets, irreducibility, communication) topologically.
result: Absorbing subsets are characterized as closed sets, irreducibility corresponds to topological connectedness and triviality, minimal open neighborhoods are described via accessibility and hitting probabilities, and the communication quotient is related to lumpability.
conclusion: The Markov Accessibility Topology provides a topological framework for Markov chains, but the work is purely classical and falls outside the quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems directions.

title: Analysis And Detection Of Stagnation In Floating-Point Summation
authors: William Woolfenden Mantas Mikaitis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stagnation in the summation of floating-point numbers occurs when the running sum, or the accumulator, does not change its value despite addends being greater than zero. Here we define different types of stagnation - commonly referred to as swamping or absorption, where one operand in an addition is nearly or completely rounded off---in floating-point summation, and propose algorithms for detecting it in numerical code that uses floating-point arithmetic. Whilst cancellation in floating-point arithmetic has been studied, for example by Lam et al. in `Dynamic floating point cancellation detection', stagnation has not been exploited as a property for detecting and reporting accuracy loss in floating-point operations. We have built prototype dynamic stagnation detection tools in two languages, MATLAB and Julia, and applied them to applications ranging from basic summation of a vector, to matrix multiplication, to a fluid flow simulation model. With this tool, users are able to identify areas of their floating-point code where stagnation occurs - in those areas of the code one may need to switch to a higher precision number format, apply stochastic rounding, or use different summation algorithms such as compensated summation. To the best of our knowledge we provide a first rigorous definition of stagnation in floating-point summation.
tldr: The paper defines stagnation in floating-point summation (swamping/absorption) and proposes dynamic detection tools in MATLAB and Julia for numerical code.
motivation: Stagnation causes loss of accuracy in floating-point summation, but unlike cancellation it has not been exploited as a detectable property for reporting accuracy loss.
method: The authors give a rigorous definition of different stagnation types and build prototype dynamic stagnation detection tools in MATLAB and Julia, applying them to vector summation, matrix multiplication, and a fluid flow simulation.
result: The tools identify regions in floating-point code where stagnation occurs, pointing to places where higher precision, stochastic rounding, or compensated summation may be needed.
conclusion: This work provides a first rigorous definition and practical detection method for stagnation in floating-point summation, helping users locate and mitigate accuracy loss.

title: When Does Inexact Matching Ensure Balance And Inference Without Adjustment?
authors: Ying Jin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One-to-one matching without replacement is a classical approach to constructing comparable treated and control samples in the design of observational studies. It pairs each treated unit with a distinct control while minimizing a covariate distance objective. With continuous covariates, the matched pairs generally remain inexact, which contributes to bias in downstream analysis. Its key theoretical properties, such as the resulting imbalance between matched pairs and when it is negligible to support valid inference, remain unclear. In this paper, we analyze one-to-one matching based on [MATH]-dimensional, continuous covariates with a quadratic covariate-distance objective. First, we find that when [MATH], under standard conditions on the propensity score ensuring abundant control samples near each treated sample, the imbalance (difference between within-group averages) is root-[MATH] negligible uniformly over the family of smooth functions with a common first- and second-order derivative bound. However, such balance is subject to a dimension restriction, as we construct examples in which the imbalance is root-[MATH] non-negligible when [MATH] and dominates root-[MATH] rate when [MATH]. Second, we show that when [MATH], the matched design allows valid Wald-type and bootstrap inference for the average treatment effect on the treated, distributional treatment effects, and quantile treatment effects. Thus, the same outcome-blind matched design supports various downstream inferences without having to tailor the design to the targets. Finally, paired randomization inference based on the matched design is asymptotically valid in the super-population sense for [MATH] but can fail when [MATH]. We corroborate the theoretical results with numerical experiments.
tldr: Analyzes when one-to-one matching with continuous covariates yields negligible imbalance and supports valid causal inference without outcome adjustment, focusing on dimension restrictions.
motivation: Matching without replacement is widely used in observational studies, but its theoretical guarantees for balance and downstream inference under continuous covariates are unclear.
method: The paper studies one-to-one matching with a quadratic covariate-distance objective in d dimensions, deriving imbalance bounds under smoothness assumptions and constructing counterexamples for high dimensions.
result: For d <= 3, imbalance is root-n negligible and Wald-type, bootstrap, and randomization inference are asymptotically valid; for d >= 4, imbalance can dominate and inference may fail.
conclusion: The matched design's validity for causal inference depends critically on covariate dimension, with a sharp transition at d=3 for the considered settings.

title: Language Modeling Is Monotone Compression
authors: Noam Mazor, Andrew Morgan, Rafael Pass
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A long-standing hypothesis in artificial intelligence and neuroscience posits that intelligence is closely related to compression: the ability to compress information efficiently intuitively reflects capacities associated with intelligence and learning. Indeed, recent experimental works verify this intuition by showing connections between the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and their ability as compressors: for instance, Deletang et al. (ICLR'24) demonstrate that LLMs can be used as powerful compressors, and Huang et al. (COLM'24) show that the compression ability of LLMs is highly correlated with their performance on benchmarks for knowledge and reasoning. In this work, we initiate a theoretical study of this connection. Our main result is that LLMs (formally modeled as next-token predictors) are equivalent to monotone (a.k.a. order-preserving) compression algorithms---namely, compression algorithms where the encoding process preserves the ordering of the inputs---in the sense that the one can be constructed from the other while preserving the same error up to an additive gap of 2. We next show that the monotonicity is required for this equivalence to hold if and only if cryptographic (infinitely-often) one-way functions exist. As a direct corollary, we get a cryptographic result of independent interest: the notion of next-bit pseudoentropy (a computational analogue of entropy) of a distribution is equivalent to monotone incompressibility of the distribution. (Previously, it was only known (Haitner et al., ITCS'23) that incompressibility implies next-bit pseudoentropy.).
tldr: This paper theoretically proves that large language models, modeled as next-token predictors, are equivalent to monotone compression algorithms up to an additive error of 2.
motivation: The work aims to formalize and study the long-standing hypothesis that intelligence is closely related to compression, motivated by recent experimental links between LLM performance and compression ability.
method: The authors model LLMs as next-token predictors and analyze their equivalence to monotone (order-preserving) compression algorithms using cryptographic reductions and the existence of one-way functions.
result: They show that LLMs and monotone compression are equivalent up to an additive gap of 2, that monotonicity is necessary if and only if infinitely-often one-way functions exist, and that next-bit pseudoentropy is equivalent to monotone incompressibility.
conclusion: The paper establishes a theoretical foundation for the intelligence-compression connection and derives a cryptographic result about next-bit pseudoentropy, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Exact Convex Reformulations Of Binary Quadratic Programs From Facially Reduced Semidefinite Relaxations
authors: Mingming Xu Hao Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop MIQCR-FR, a framework for exact convex reformulation from facially reduced semidefinite relaxations of equality-constrained binary quadratic problems. Standard mixed-integer quadratic convex reformulation (MIQCR) uses dual multipliers of the original relaxation. Facial reduction (FR) reduces the semidefinite matrix order, but recovery of the original dual multipliers is not guaranteed in general. For this class of problems, we identify how retaining the linear equalities and their products with each binary variable enables this recovery. An established dual recovery formula gives an explicit extension of every feasible solution of the reduced dual to the original dual, preserving its bound. For approximate multiplier estimates, we give a spectral shift restoring dual feasibility and two constructions optimizing different bounds within a restricted multiplier family. Maximizing the dual bound yields a trust-region subproblem; maximizing the continuous MIQCR bound requires only a reduced eigenvalue calculation.
