result: Quadratic hindrance yields no positive GOE in any dimension; one dimension gives a sharp convexity-based classification, and higher dimensions yield exact Riccati criteria and dimension-induced positive GOE examples.
conclusion: The results reveal a dimension-induced gain mechanism absent from the classical ribosome flow model, but the topic does not align with quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: From Investigation Failures To Reliable Soc Agents: Understanding And Improving LLM-Based Alert Triage
authors: Saimon Amanuel Tsegai (daphne), Alex Kantchelian (daphne), Danfeng (daphne), Yao, Peng Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security operations centers (SOCs) must triage large volumes of alerts, most of which are benign, while missed attacks can remain uninvestigated. Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents can retrieve evidence during triage, but it remains unclear how reasoning strategies determine what to gather and when an investigation is sufficient to close an alert. We study five representative approaches spanning single-pass tool use, iterative retrieval, sampled investigations, self-review, and explicit verification. To support this study, we build ALERT-BENCH, an interactive benchmark that replays enterprise telemetry through a live SIEM and requires each system to retrieve evidence. Across 1,247 alerts from a multi-stage attack scenario, every approach missed at least 40.4% of attack-related alerts. Trace analysis shows that attack alerts are more likely to be dismissed when searches return no records, same-context review has negative net correction, and dismissal receives no consistently stronger investigation than escalation. Based on these findings, we further design AIDA (Adversarial Investigation and Dialectical Analysis), a multi-agent framework that requires an explicit proposed decision before independent challenge and stronger evidentiary requirements before dismissal. AIDA preserves investigation history in an append-only Investigation Ledger and keeps the challenge in a separate reasoning context. A separate Judge adjudicates the proposed decision and challenge against evidence, resolving the alert or requesting another round when evidence is missing. On the same alerts, AIDA achieves an F1 score of 0.958, compared with 0.371-0.744 for the studied approaches, and reduces the false-negative rate from 40.4% to 3.1% while escalating 18.4% of alerts to analysts. These results show that structuring evidence retrieval and decision review can substantially improve agentic SOC triage.
tldr: This paper studies LLM-based tool-using agents for SOC alert triage and proposes AIDA, a multi-agent framework that improves F1 and reduces false negatives.
motivation: Security operations centers struggle with high alert volumes, and while LLM agents can retrieve evidence during triage, it is unclear how reasoning strategies affect evidence gathering and closure decisions.
method: The authors build ALERT-BENCH, an interactive benchmark replaying enterprise telemetry through a live SIEM, evaluate five representative triage approaches, and design AIDA with an append-only investigation ledger, independent challenge, and a separate judge.
result: All baseline approaches missed at least 40.4% of attack-related alerts, while AIDA achieved F1 0.958, reduced false negatives to 3.1%, and escalated 18.4% of alerts.
conclusion: Structuring evidence retrieval and decision review substantially improves agentic SOC triage, though the work is outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networking, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: An Explicit Shuffle Construction Of The Homotopy Span Model Of Differential Linear Logic
authors: Paul-Andr\'e Melli\`es, Federico Olimpieri, Lionel Vaux Auclair
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a direct and explicit construction of the homotopy span model of linear logic originally formulated by Melli\`es using abstract homotopy theory in the Quillen category Cat of small categories equipped with its natural model structure. Following the principles of homotopy theory, the formulas and proofs of linear logic are interpreted in the model as small categories up to categorical equivalence, the notion of weak homotopy equivalence underlying the natural Quillen model structure on Cat. Here, we explain how the original interpretation of proofs as fibrant spans can be replaced by a more liberal interpretation of proofs as separately fibrant spans. This relaxation from fibrant spans to separately fibrant spans enables us to give a simple and intuitive description of the homotopy span model, where the axiom and cut links are interpreted as identity spans, and where the symmetries of the exponential modality are captured by a shuffle structure on the interpretation of proofs.
tldr: The paper gives an explicit construction of the homotopy span model of differential linear logic using separately fibrant spans and a shuffle structure on categorical interpretations.
motivation: The homotopy span model was originally formulated abstractly via homotopy theory, and the authors aim to provide a more direct and intuitive construction.
method: They work in the Quillen category Cat of small categories and relax the interpretation of proofs from fibrant spans to separately fibrant spans, capturing exponential modality symmetries by a shuffle structure.
result: The construction interprets linear logic proofs as small categories up to categorical equivalence, with axiom and cut links as identity spans and symmetries handled by shuffles.
conclusion: This provides a simplified explicit description of the homotopy span model, bridging abstract homotopy-theoretic semantics and proof-theoretic interpretations of differential linear logic.

title: When Flaws Cascade: Understanding Vulnerabilities And Exploitation Chains In JavaScript Engines
authors: Yuhan Ma, Jiongchi Yu, Xiaofei Xie, Qiang Hu, Zhiyi Zhang, Junjie Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: JavaScript engines are pivotal to modern web browsers, enabling the execution of dynamic and interactive web applications. However, their complexity and widespread adoption make them prime targets for attackers exploiting vulnerabilities. While existing research has focused on detecting vulnerabilities of JavaScript engines, a significant gap remains in systematically understanding the characteristics of these vulnerabilities, including their symptoms, root causes, and exploitability. This paper bridges this gap by presenting the first comprehensive empirical study on vulnerabilities in JavaScript engines, investigating their characteristics and potential exploitation strategies. We construct a dataset comprising 241 vulnerabilities across four mainstream JavaScript engines from 2017 to 2024. Through in-depth analysis, we first develop taxonomies for symptoms and root causes. Building on this understanding, we investigate the exploitability of these vulnerabilities, identifying key prerequisites and extracting vulnerability trigger chains that demonstrate how logical errors propagate into memory safety violations. Additionally, we analyze the mitigation strategies to counter these exploits. Finally, we summarize key implications for various stakeholders, including developers and researchers, offering actionable insights to improve the security and resilience of JavaScript engines.
tldr: This paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study of vulnerabilities in JavaScript engines, analyzing their symptoms, root causes, exploitability, and mitigation strategies.
motivation: JavaScript engines are critical to web browsers and are frequent targets of attacks, yet prior research has focused on detection rather than systematically understanding the characteristics and exploitation of their vulnerabilities.
method: The authors construct a dataset of 241 vulnerabilities across four mainstream JavaScript engines from 2017 to 2024, develop taxonomies for symptoms and root causes, and extract vulnerability trigger chains showing how logical errors propagate into memory safety violations.
result: The study identifies key prerequisites for exploitation, characterizes cascading failure chains, and analyzes mitigation strategies used to counter these exploits.
conclusion: The paper provides actionable implications for developers and researchers to improve the security and resilience of JavaScript engines.

title: Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks On Speculative Decoding
authors: Adam Y. J. Jones, Yu Yuan, Sergio Maffeis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular technique for increasing the speed and reducing the costs of large language model (LLM) inference by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model forward pass. The resulting benefit depends on the ability of the drafter to approximate the target model's distribution. In this work, we study Speculative Rejection Attacks (SRAs), a novel class of attacks that cause draft and target models to disagree more often, resulting in fewer draft tokens being accepted per draft cycle. This leads to more target model forward passes needed per generated token, slowing down inference and increasing costs for the victim. We introduce two attacks which append an adversarial suffix to attacker-controlled content to degrade speculative decoding on a victim's prompts. Both attacks optimise the expected length of the accepted speculative prefix, estimating per-depth acceptance from the target's probability of the drafted proposals (Speedbump-P) or from the overlap between the draft and target distributions (Speedbump-D). In some cases, attacks degrade speculative decoding to the point of being slower than autoregressive decoding. The degradation reduces the output quality - regularisation restores output quality but gives up most of the degradation, trading effectiveness for stealthiness. Additionally, the suffixes remain effective under sampling, and transfer across drafters (Speedbump-P) or across target models sharing a drafter (Speedbump-D). These findings identify the draft-target interaction of speculative decoding as a realistic attack surface through which adversarial inputs can inflate inference costs.
tldr: The paper introduces Speculative Rejection Attacks (SRAs), adversarial suffixes that increase draft-target disagreement in speculative decoding, thereby slowing LLM inference and inflating serving costs.
motivation: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference by having a drafter propose tokens that a target model verifies in bulk, but this efficiency relies on strong draft-target distributional alignment, which the authors hypothesize is exploitable.
method: Two suffix-optimization attacks (Speedbump-P and Speedbump-D) are proposed that minimize the expected accepted speculative prefix length, estimated either from the target model's probability of drafted proposals or from draft-target distribution overlap.
result: The attacks can degrade speculative decoding below autoregressive baseline speed, remain effective under sampling, and transfer across drafters (Speedbump-P) or across target models sharing a drafter (Speedbump-D), with regularization trading degradation for stealth.
conclusion: The draft-target interaction in speculative decoding constitutes a realistic adversarial attack surface that an attacker can exploit to inflate victim inference costs, motivating robustness considerations in speculative decoding deployments.

title: The First Type Of Power Mean Bounds For The Gaussian Hypergeometric Function
authors: Zhen-Hang, Yang, Jing-Feng Tian
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, by using a signs rule for a class of special power series and a recurrence relation of coefficients involving hypergeometric series, we find the necessary and sufficient conditions for the sharp (at the left endpoint) inequalities between the hypergeometric function and power mean (Hm-Pm inequality) to hold in all possible cases, which greatly extends those known results and solve the rest of problem on the sharp (at the left endpoint) power mean bounds for the hypergeometric mean.
tldr: The paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for sharp power mean bounds on the Gaussian hypergeometric function.
motivation: To extend known results and solve the remaining cases of sharp power mean bounds for the hypergeometric mean.
method: It uses a signs rule for a class of special power series and a recurrence relation of coefficients involving hypergeometric series.
result: Necessary and sufficient conditions are found for the sharp inequalities between the hypergeometric function and power mean to hold in all possible cases at the left endpoint.
conclusion: The work greatly extends known Hm-Pm inequalities and completes the problem of sharp power mean bounds for the hypergeometric function.

title: A Counterexample To Two Compactness Conjectures Of Brudnyi
authors: Ran Xu Jinghao Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a quasi-Banach function lattice [MATH] on [MATH] whose quasi-norm is order continuous and invariant under every translation. Nevertheless, [MATH] contains a bounded sequence with common compact support which is equicontinuous in [MATH] and has no norm-convergent subsequence. This provides a counterexample to Conjectures 2.5 and 2.11 proposed by Brudnyi in .
tldr: The paper constructs a quasi-Banach function lattice that provides a counterexample to two compactness conjectures of Brudnyi.
motivation: Brudnyi proposed compactness conjectures for quasi-Banach function lattices, and resolving them is of interest in functional analysis.
method: The authors explicitly construct a translation-invariant quasi-Banach function lattice with order-continuous quasi-norm and exhibit a bounded equicontinuous sequence with common compact support lacking a norm-convergent subsequence.
result: The constructed lattice satisfies the conditions of Brudnyi's Conjectures 2.5 and 2.11 yet violates their conclusions, thus disproving both conjectures.
conclusion: These counterexamples show that the proposed compactness criteria for quasi-Banach function lattices do not hold in general, refining the understanding of compactness in this setting.

title: Strategic Governance Of Ai Models In Earth Science
authors: Makoto Kelp, Amirhossein Arzani, Patricia Castellanos, Paul Griffiths, Ivan Higuera-Mendieta, Manuel Perez-Carrasco, Viral Shah, Patrick Obin Sturm, James Weber
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI foundation models pretrained on weather and climate data are increasingly fine-tuned to Earth science tasks well beyond weather forecasting. Their development and adoption are outpacing the scientific community's ability to evaluate them. These models are judged almost entirely by benchmark skill metrics, which measure how closely a forecast reproduces a reference product but not whether a model represents the physical processes governing the system it predicts. Forecast skill and physical reliability are therefore distinct properties. The distinction is most consequential under the nonstationary conditions of a changing climate for which these models were never trained. We identify five priorities for the physical evaluation of AI models in Earth science from task-specific emulators to foundation models, spanning training data, fine-tuning, behavioral testing, mechanistic interpretability, and output validation. We recommend three activities for the coming decade: 1) open AI-ready evaluation datasets, 2) a shared reporting standard for physics-based evaluation, and 3) a dedicated research program on the safety of these models.
tldr: This perspective argues that AI foundation models in Earth science must be evaluated for physical reliability, not just benchmark skill, and proposes governance priorities for their development and use.
motivation: AI models pretrained on weather and climate data are being fine-tuned for diverse Earth science tasks faster than the community can evaluate them, and current evaluation relies almost entirely on benchmark skill metrics that do not assess whether models capture governing physical processes.
method: The authors synthesize concerns from Earth science and AI evaluation to identify five priorities for physical evaluation—spanning training data, fine-tuning, behavioral testing, mechanistic interpretability, and output validation—and recommend three governance activities for the coming decade.
result: They propose open AI-ready evaluation datasets, a shared reporting standard for physics-based evaluation, and a dedicated research program on the safety of Earth science AI models.
conclusion: Ensuring the reliability of AI models in Earth science requires shifting from purely skill-based benchmarks to physics-aware evaluation and coordinated governance, especially under nonstationary climate conditions.

title: Localized, Unstable, And Entangled: Exploring `Us Vs. Them' Bias In Large Language Models
authors: Tabia Tanzin Prama, Julia Witte Zimmerman, Christopher M. Danforth, Peter Sheridan Dodds
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit us-vs.-them bias: A behavioral asymmetry in which prompts framed around an ingroup (``we''/``us'') receive systematically more positive continuations than matched prompts framed around an outgroup (``they''/``them''). Using Edge Attribution Patching (EAP), we localize this behavior to directed circuits in GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Large, Llama-2 7B, and Llama-3 8B. Across models, high-attribution edges are sparse and concentrated primarily in middle-to-late layers, while ingroup- and outgroup-related pathways are only partially overlapping and reorganize under fine-tuning. Behavioral comparisons and 30-token generations show that the measured asymmetry extends beyond next-token evaluation. Targeted patching of EAP-ranked edges reduces the bias score more than equal-cardinality random-edge controls, but also substantially degrades performance on CoLA, HellaSwag, and WikiText-2, suggesting that bias-relevant pathways are functionally entangled with broader language capabilities. Overall, our findings characterize us-vs.-them bias as a sparse, context-dependent, and functionally entangled computational phenomenon whose internal organization varies across the models examined.
tldr: The paper localizes us-vs.-them bias in large language models to sparse, partially overlapping circuits using Edge Attribution Patching, showing that bias-relevant pathways are functionally entangled with broader language capabilities.
motivation: Large language models exhibit systematic ingroup/outgroup behavioral asymmetry, and understanding its internal computational basis may inform bias mitigation.
method: Applied Edge Attribution Patching to GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Large, Llama-2 7B, and Llama-3 8B to identify high-attribution edges underlying us-vs.-them bias, then compared ingroup and outgroup pathways and performed targeted edge patching.
result: Bias-relevant circuits are sparse and concentrated in middle-to-late layers, only partially overlap between ingroup and outgroup, reorganize under fine-tuning, and targeted patching reduces bias but substantially degrades CoLA, HellaSwag, and WikiText-2 performance.
conclusion: Us-vs.-them bias is a context-dependent, functionally entangled computational phenomenon whose internal organization varies across models, complicating simple circuit-level debiasing.

title: An Ecology Of Participation For Fusion Energy Development
authors: Aditi Verma, Katie Snyder, Andrea Morales Coto, Nathan Kawamoto, Daniel Hoover, Ana Kova, Sara Eskandari, Stephanie O'malley, Jared Owens, Mahmud Farooque, Gabrielle Hoelzle, Stephanie Diem, Kevin Daley
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decisions that will shape future fusion facilities, including the production of waste, the management of tritium, the achievement of safety, and impacts on land, water, and local communities, are increasingly becoming sociotechnical in nature. For prior energy technologies, fission among them, such decisions were made top-down and met sustained public opposition. Research shows such opposition is rarely a deficit of public understanding and is instead rooted in place-specific environmental, health, sociocultural, and economic concerns and in distrust of how technologies are selected and sited. We argue that fusion developers have an opportunity to design differently, and we propose an ecology of participation: multiple, complementary modalities of engagement sustained over time, replacing the one-off public consultations now typical of large infrastructure projects. We synthesize human- and environment-centered design frameworks and introduce a framework that reinterprets opposition as a divergence between communities and technology developers in values, norms, or design characteristics. We present six case studies from our work: participatory technology assessment focus groups, participatory design workshops, immersive virtual-reality models of a fusion facility, the Global Fusion Forum platform, the Imaginary Energies speculative design platform, and Heartbeat, an arts-based sound installation. Mapping these onto the values-norms-design framework shows how each interrogates or closes a different part of the expert-public gap, and exposes two limitations of fusion public engagement efforts writ large: developers are seldom asked to articulate their own values and norms, and the environment is represented only indirectly. We close with five guiding questions for fusion researchers building their own participatory engagements.
tldr: The paper proposes an 'ecology of participation' framework to make fusion energy development more inclusive, drawing on six participatory engagement case studies to reinterpret public opposition as a values-norms-design divergence.
motivation: Decisions shaping future fusion facilities are increasingly sociotechnical, and past energy technologies such as fission suffered sustained public opposition rooted in place-specific concerns and distrust rather than a deficit of public understanding.
method: The authors synthesize human- and environment-centered design frameworks into a values-norms-design framework and map six of their own engagement cases (participatory technology assessment, design workshops, VR facility models, forums, speculative design, arts-based installation) onto it.
result: The mapping shows how each modality interrogates a different part of the expert-public gap, while exposing two broad limitations of fusion engagement: developers rarely articulate their own values and norms, and the environment is only indirectly represented.
conclusion: The paper closes with five guiding questions for fusion researchers designing participatory engagements, arguing that sustained, complementary modes of engagement should replace one-off public consultations.

title: Why Llm Agents Favor Their Group: Stakes, Observed Norms, And Reputation
authors: Yujiao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents favor their own group because they have watched their members favor each other. The group label alone does little once the decision has a cost; what drives favoritism is observed behavior, and an individual's own record can override it. We test this in small societies with arbitrary group labels, ten rounds of point sharing, and matched one-shot decisions across fifteen OpenAI models and three Claude models, about 4,400 societies and 3.3 million audited model calls. First, the large effect of a bare group label reported in earlier work appears only when giving others points costs the agent nothing; once the agent can keep points for itself, that effect collapses on every model that shows it. Second, under a stake, interaction history becomes the main source of favoritism: the history effect is statistically positive on 13 of 15 models, reaches about 3.5-8 points out of 10 on 11, grows with the number of rounds played, and extends to labeled strangers the agent has never met. Third, with scripted histories, favoritism falls to near zero under an egalitarian norm and reverses when the agent's own group is seen favoring the other side; stronger models side with an individual's record when it conflicts with the group. Group favoritism is thus conformity to observed group behavior, carried to strangers by the label and overridden by individual reputation. The same account predicts responses to betrayal, scandal, and a free offer to change group: public reprimand repairs betrayal better than apology or restitution, allocation punishment remains confined to the offending member, and a formed group cannot be bought but can, on weaker models, be invited away.
tldr: LLM agents favor their own group primarily due to observed group behavior rather than bare group labels, and individual reputation can override this favoritism.
motivation: To understand why language-model agents exhibit in-group favoritism, testing whether group labels alone or observed norms and personal history drive the effect.
method: Controlled experiments with 4,400 small societies, 10 rounds of point sharing, and matched one-shot decisions across 18 LLM models, analyzing 3.3 million audited calls.
result: Group label effect collapses when favoring others is costly; interaction history drives favoritism (3.5-8 points on 11 models, extending to labeled strangers), and scripted egalitarian norms reduce it to near zero.
conclusion: Favoritism is conformity to observed group behavior, carried by labels to strangers and overridden by individual reputation, with implications for betrayal repair and group change.

title: Octonionic Kittaneh Numerical Radius Inequalities
authors: K. Mahesh Krishna
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that for certain classes of matrices over octonions, a weak version of breakthrough numerical radius inequalities obtained by Kittaneh [, 2005}] hold.
tldr: The paper proves weak octonionic analogues of Kittaneh's numerical radius inequalities for certain matrix classes.
motivation: Kittaneh's numerical radius inequalities are important in matrix analysis, and the author aims to extend them to matrices over octonions.
method: The work likely uses algebraic properties of octonions and operator inequalities to establish weak versions of the classical bounds.
result: For certain octonionic matrix classes, a weak form of Kittaneh's numerical radius inequalities is shown to hold.
conclusion: The results broaden the scope of numerical radius inequalities to the non-associative octonionic setting.

title: On A New Class Of $q$-fractional Integral Operators Involving Multivariate $q$-Mittag-Leffler Functions
authors: Min-Jie Luo, Qing-Hui Peng, Ravinder Krishna Raina
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractional integral operators involving special functions as kernels have long been one of the main subjects of fractional calculus. As a discrete version of classical fractional calculus, [MATH]-fractional calculus not only brings often new phenomena and new perspectives but also provides new useful areas for describing and studying new problems of applied nature. Recently, Luo and Zhou (see below) developed a methodology for formulating well-behaved [MATH]-fractional integral operators steming from a basic general theory. Our aim in this paper is to define and introduce a new class of [MATH]-fractional integral operators whose kernel involves a new multivariate [MATH]-Mittag-Leffler function. We shall also define the corresponding [MATH]-fractional derivatives (as the inverses of [MATH]-fractional integral operators) and define also the [MATH]-Caputo fractional derivative operators. We discuss in detail the similarities and variations between the [MATH]-operators and their counterparts in classical theory, particularly in Prabakar fractional calculus. Further, applications of the defined operators in solving certain [MATH]-fractional differential equations are also considered. We also mention throughout this paper some useful relevances of our established results with certain known important cases. In the concluding remarks, we point out briefly few possible proposals (or directions) for further work on the present subject matter of [MATH]-calculus.
tldr: Introduces a new class of q-fractional integral and derivative operators whose kernels involve multivariate q-Mittag-Leffler functions.
motivation: q-fractional calculus is a discrete version of classical fractional calculus that can reveal new phenomena and provide tools for applied problems.
method: Defines q-fractional integral operators with multivariate q-Mittag-Leffler kernels, along with inverse q-fractional derivatives and q-Caputo derivatives, and compares them with classical and Prabhakar fractional calculus.
result: Establishes a new operator class, discusses similarities and variations with existing fractional calculus, and applies the operators to certain q-fractional differential equations.
conclusion: The work lays a foundation for further study in q-calculus and suggests possible directions for future research.

title: A Local Proof Of Langlands's First Main Lemma For Local Epsilon Factors Over Nonarchimedean Local Fields
authors: Fukuhiro Ueda
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a complete local proof of Langlands's First Main Lemma for local epsilon factors over nonarchimedean local fields. The proof builds on Dwork's [MATH]-adic calculations and Langlands's formulation of the local method. The present paper reformulates these calculations in a common normalization and extends the argument to equal characteristic. A more systematic treatment of stationary parameters and conductor cases is intended to make the calculations easier to follow. Norm--trace correction formulas yield the equal-characteristic extension. The author is also completing a local proof of Langlands's Second Main Lemma and will verify it in Lean. Together with the present result and Langlands's remaining reductions, that work will give a complete proof of the local construction of local epsilon factors envisioned by Langlands. OpenAI ChatGPT assisted with drafting and wording revisions of this manuscript; the author audited the manuscript, checked the proof, and assumes full responsibility.
tldr: The paper provides a local proof of Langlands's First Main Lemma for local epsilon factors over nonarchimedean local fields, extending prior p-adic calculations to equal characteristic.
motivation: Langlands's local construction of epsilon factors relies on two main lemmas; a fully local proof of the First Main Lemma was missing, especially in equal characteristic.
method: The author reformulates Dwork's p-adic calculations in a common normalization, treats stationary parameters and conductor cases systematically, and uses norm-trace correction formulas for equal characteristic.
result: A complete local proof of the First Main Lemma is obtained, with an extension to equal characteristic and a normalization that unifies earlier arguments.
conclusion: Together with the author's ongoing local proof of the Second Main Lemma and Langlands's reductions, this work moves toward a complete local construction of local epsilon factors.

title: On The Rank Condition For Perfect Cuboids
authors: Valery Asiryan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Paulsen and West associate perfect cuboids with triples of rational points on a congruent-number elliptic curve and assert that the corresponding curve has rank at least two. The proof of their Theorem 4.2 contains a gap: translation of a generator by a point of order two interchanges only the odd-indexed terms of two coordinate sequences, rather than the entire sequences. We exhibit two explicit counterexamples to that intermediate assertion and give a complete proof of the rank obstruction. The division-polynomial argument reduces a hypothetical rank-one configuration to one remaining parity pattern. Ingram's primitive-divisor theorem then forces an additive relation among its indices, which is incompatible with a positivity lemma on the elliptic curve. More precisely, the three points of every positive cuboid configuration generate a subgroup of rank at least two, even when the ambient curve has larger rank. The proof is unconditional.
tldr: The paper identifies and fixes a gap in a proof about rank conditions for perfect cuboids using elliptic curves and division polynomials.
motivation: Paulsen and West associated perfect cuboids with rational points on a congruent-number elliptic curve and claimed the curve has rank at least two, but their proof contained an error in handling translations by a point of order two.
method: The author exhibits explicit counterexamples to the intermediate assertion, provides a complete division-polynomial argument that reduces a hypothetical rank-one configuration to one parity pattern, and applies Ingram's primitive-divisor theorem to derive an incompatible additive relation.
result: The proof establishes that the three points of every positive cuboid configuration generate a subgroup of rank at least two, even when the ambient elliptic curve has larger rank, unconditionally.
conclusion: The rank obstruction for perfect cuboids is rigorously confirmed, correcting the flawed argument in prior work and strengthening the connection between perfect cuboids and elliptic curve ranks.

title: Existence And Uniqueness Of Viscosity Solutions For Stochastic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman Equations
authors: Jinniao Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study stochastic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equations arising from stochastic optimal control problems with random coefficients and possible degenerateness. The viscosity solution is reformulated by using adapted smooth random test fields that touch on stopped space--time neighborhoods almost surely. The state coefficients are predictable, with no continuity assumption on their dependence on the underlying Brownian path. Under linear growth of locally Lipschitz drift and diffusion coefficients, polynomial growth of the running and terminal cost coefficients, and a nonempty separable metric space-valued control set, we show that the value function is the unique viscosity solution in this formulation among adapted continuous fields with square-integrable random polynomial growth bounds. The comparison proof constructs adapted fields from controlled trajectories and spatially shaken conditional values, using a weak semimartingale decomposition and regularization of its positive finite-variation part. In particular, the uniqueness allows for diffusion coefficients being random, degenerate, and depending on time, state, and control, whereas earlier uniqueness results of Qiu [SIAM J. Control Optim. 56 (2018), pp. 3708--3730] and Qiu and Zhang [Ann. Appl. Probab. 33 (2023), pp. 889--930] were obtained under additional structural restrictions on the diffusion coefficient, such as determinism combined with either superparabolicity or independence of the state and controls.
tldr: This paper proves existence and uniqueness of viscosity solutions for stochastic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations arising in stochastic optimal control with random, possibly degenerate coefficients.
motivation: Stochastic HJB equations with random coefficients and degenerate diffusion are important for optimal control under model uncertainty, but previous uniqueness results require restrictive structural assumptions on the diffusion coefficient.
method: The authors reformulate viscosity solutions using adapted smooth random test fields on stopped space-time neighborhoods, and prove a comparison theorem via adapted fields constructed from controlled trajectories and spatially shaken conditional values, using weak semimartingale decomposition and regularization.
result: They show that the value function is the unique viscosity solution among adapted continuous fields with square-integrable random polynomial growth bounds, allowing diffusion coefficients that are random, degenerate, and depend on time, state, and control.
conclusion: The work extends uniqueness results for stochastic HJB equations by removing previous structural restrictions on the diffusion coefficient, broadening the applicability of viscosity solution theory in stochastic optimal control.

title: When Surjectivity Demands Pathology
authors: Piotr Ma\'ckowiak Piotr Kasprzak
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we characterize surjective nonlinear composition operators acting between the space of sequences of bounded variation and the space of bounded sequences. We show that their generators exhibit highly pathological behavior. To complement this, we construct explicit examples, confirming that such exotic objects do in fact exist.
tldr: The paper characterizes surjective nonlinear composition operators between the space of sequences of bounded variation and the space of bounded sequences, showing pathological generator behavior and constructing explicit examples.
motivation: Composition operators on sequence spaces are of interest in functional analysis, and the surjective nonlinear case is less understood. The authors aim to characterize such operators and understand their generators.
method: They analyze surjective nonlinear composition operators from the space of sequences of bounded variation to the space of bounded sequences, proving structural results about their generators and providing explicit constructions.
result: The generators of these operators exhibit highly pathological behavior, and the authors construct concrete examples confirming the existence of such exotic objects.
conclusion: Surjectivity imposes restrictive and pathological conditions on nonlinear composition operators between these sequence spaces, with explicit examples demonstrating that such operators exist.

title: Modeling And Performance Evaluation Of Distributed Satellite Antennas: Space Is Much Closer Than One Might Think
authors: Giacomo Bacci, Riccardo de Gaudenzi, Marco Luise, Luca Sanguinetti
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed satellites can deliver broadband connectivity directly to commercial handsets. In the formation of arrays (FoA) architecture, cooperating satellites synthesize a large aperture whoseextent depends on their number, arrangement, and spacing, with intersatellite distances ranging from tens of meters to hundreds of kilometers. For representative S-band geostationary and low-Earth-orbit configurations, the Fraunhofer distance may exceed the nadir link range at spacings on the order of a hundred meters. Therefore, accurate assessment of FoA performance across satellite populations and spacings requires spherical-wave modeling for users in the radiative near field, below the formation's Fraunhofer distance. Planar models of satellite positions, array orientations, and user locations must also be assessed against spherical geometries accounting for orbital and Earth curvature. This paper combines these models to quantify how simplifying assumptions affect throughput and outage probability. Numerical results show that multi-antenna precoding based on a local plane-wave approximation within each satellite array closely matches the spherical-wave reference. A global plane-wave approximation can instead cause severe losses, including full outage. In the investigated scenarios, formation curvature has little impact, whereas neglecting Earth curvature overestimates low-Earth-orbit throughput. These findings clarify when geometric and propagation approximations remain reliable and demonstrate that, for large distributed antenna apertures, space is much closer than one might think.
tldr: The paper models and evaluates distributed satellite antenna arrays for broadband handset connectivity, comparing spherical-wave near-field effects and planar approximations on throughput and outage probability.
motivation: Distributed satellite formations can synthesize large apertures for direct-to-handset broadband, but simplifying planar wave and geometry assumptions may misestimate performance, especially when the Fraunhofer distance exceeds the link range.
method: The authors combine spherical-wave propagation modeling for users in the radiative near field with assessments of planar versus spherical satellite positions, array orientations, and Earth curvature for S-band GEO and LEO configurations.
result: Local plane-wave approximation per satellite array closely matches the spherical-wave reference, while a global plane-wave approximation can cause severe losses including full outage; formation curvature has little impact, but neglecting Earth curvature overestimates LEO throughput.
conclusion: Accurate evaluation of distributed satellite arrays requires spherical-wave modeling over relevant spacings and Earth curvature for LEO, clarifying when geometric and propagation approximations remain reliable.

title: Projection Schemes And The Fixed Point Property In Nonreflexive Banach Spaces
authors: T. Dom\'{\i}nguez Benavides, M. Jap\'on, P. K. Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the notion of a projection scheme on a Banach space and develop an abstract framework for studying the fixed point property (FPP) for nonexpansive mappings. Within this framework, we obtain a general criterion ensuring the FPP for a broad class of nonreflexive Banach spaces. In particular, every uniformly convex Banach space admits an isometric embedding into a nonreflexive Banach space having the FPP. This criterion unifies and extends several previously known fixed point results for nonreflexive Banach spaces with Schauder bases. As an application of our general result, we characterize the FPP for variable Lebesgue spaces. More precisely, we prove that if [MATH] is a [MATH]-finite measure space and [MATH] is a measurable function, then [MATH] has the FPP if and only if it does not contain an isometric copy of [MATH]. Consequently, as in the classical Lebesgue space framework, the presence of an isometric copy of [MATH] completely characterizes the failure of the FPP in variable Lebesgue spaces. This result yields a class of nonreflexive Banach spaces with the fixed point property that contains isometric copies of infinitely many [MATH]-spaces, [MATH]. Although nonreflexive sequence spaces with the FPP are known, to the best of our knowledge, these variable Lebesgue spaces provide the first examples of nonreflexive Banach function lattices with the FPP.
tldr: This paper develops an abstract projection-scheme framework for the fixed point property of nonexpansive mappings in nonreflexive Banach spaces and applies it to variable Lebesgue spaces.
motivation: The authors aim to unify and extend fixed point results for nonreflexive Banach spaces and characterize the fixed point property in variable Lebesgue spaces.
method: They introduce projection schemes on Banach spaces and derive a general criterion for the fixed point property, then apply it to analyze variable Lebesgue spaces.
result: The criterion yields nonreflexive Banach spaces with the fixed point property, and for variable Lebesgue spaces the FPP is characterized by the absence of an isometric copy of c0.
conclusion: This provides the first examples of nonreflexive Banach function lattices with the fixed point property and extends classical fixed point theory.

title: Optimal Control Of Dynamic Gas Networks Using Gaussian Processes With Chance-Constraint Reformulation
authors: Taiwo A. Adebiyi, Robert Ferrando, Manuel Garcia, Ruda Zhang, Saif R. Kazi, Kaarthik Sundar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural gas networks must accommodate variable demand and supply while maintaining pressure across pipelines whose stored gas couples operating decisions through time. Probabilistic surrogates can simplify compressor scheduling, but their predictive uncertainty must remain reliable where optimization uses it. We combine direct learning of the minimum pressure margin with assessment at optimizer-selected schedules. Using a warped Gaussian process, we express the posterior pressure requirement as one inequality in its predictive mean and standard deviation. We then parameterize block and Fourier schedules so scalar predictions and analytic derivatives replace trajectory states and time integration in whole-day optimization. In steady state, a surrogate that passes held-out accuracy and coverage checks nevertheless falls below the minimum pressure on 71% of its own dispatches at a nominal 1% tolerance, as the optimizer is drawn to schedules where the margin is overestimated. This diagnostic motivates an enrichment loop that audits selected dispatches against the physics and updates the surrogate by exact conditioning, with fitted quantities held fixed. The loop restores steady-state minimum-pressure risk control at every studied tolerance, with conditioning about four orders of magnitude faster than refitting. In transient operation, we complement this enrichment with empirical threshold calibration to address residual hourly optimism, bringing hourly violation rates closer to their declared tolerances with little compressor work overhead.
tldr: This paper develops a Gaussian process surrogate with chance-constraint reformulation and enrichment loops for optimal control of natural gas networks under uncertainty.
motivation: Natural gas networks must schedule compressors while maintaining pipeline pressure under variable demand, but probabilistic surrogates can misestimate pressure margins exactly where an optimizer exploits them.
method: The authors use a warped Gaussian process to learn the minimum pressure margin directly, reformulate the posterior pressure requirement as one inequality in predictive mean and standard deviation, and parameterize block and Fourier schedules for whole-day optimization with an enrichment loop that audits selected dispatches and updates the surrogate by exact conditioning.
result: A surrogate passing held-out accuracy and coverage checks still violates minimum pressure on 71% of its dispatches at 1% nominal tolerance, while enrichment restores steady-state risk control at every studied tolerance and is about four orders of magnitude faster than refitting; empirical calibration also improves transient hourly violation rates.
conclusion: The proposed diagnostic and enrichment approach improves reliability of chance-constrained optimization for gas network scheduling, but it is an applied engineering/optimization contribution unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: QoS-Aware Joint Concurrency And HARQ-Limit Design For HARQ-CC-Aided Slow Fluid Antenna Multiple Access
authors: Sixu Han, Kai-Kit Wong, Hanjiang Hong, Haoyu Liang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid automatic repeat request with Chase combining (HARQ-CC) improves the reliability of slow fluid antenna multiple access (sFAMA), but its transmission limit must be jointly optimized with user concurrency. This paper proposes a quality-of-service (QoS)-aware joint design of concurrency level U and HARQ limit C for downlink HARQ-CC-aided sFAMA. Based on the selected-port signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) distribution, we derive multi-round decoding failure probabilities and develop a two-stage optimization that maximizes feasible concurrency and then selects the minimum C satisfying outage and mean-service constraints. We prove that the first feasible C minimizes service duration for a given U, and that feasible U values form an initial segment, enabling optimal bisection search. Numerical results agree with Monte Carlo simulations under full Jakes spatial covariance. The proposed adaptive FAS design supports six concurrent users, compared with three to five for fixed-HARQ FAS and two for HARQ-adaptive fixed-position-antenna (FPA), demonstrating that joint concurrency and HARQ adaptation expands the QoS-feasible region of FAS.
tldr: The paper proposes a QoS-aware joint design of concurrency level and HARQ limit for downlink HARQ-CC-aided slow fluid antenna multiple access.
motivation: HARQ-CC improves reliability of slow fluid antenna multiple access (sFAMA), but its transmission limit must be jointly optimized with user concurrency to meet quality-of-service constraints.
method: Based on the selected-port signal-to-interference ratio distribution, the authors derive multi-round decoding failure probabilities and develop a two-stage optimization that maximizes feasible concurrency and then selects the minimum HARQ limit satisfying outage and mean-service constraints, proving properties that enable bisection search.
result: Numerical results agree with Monte Carlo simulations under full Jakes spatial covariance; the proposed adaptive design supports six concurrent users, compared with three to five for fixed-HARQ FAS and two for HARQ-adaptive fixed-position-antenna.
conclusion: Joint concurrency and HARQ adaptation expands the QoS-feasible region of fluid antenna systems.

title: Uniformly Convex Stalks And Kucher's $\ell_{\infty}(E)$ Problem
authors: Hui Li, Sijie Luo, Lian Wu, Dejian Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kucher asked whether [MATH] is a Grothendieck space for every super-reflexive Banach space [MATH]. We answer this question affirmatively by proving the stronger result that [MATH] has Pe{\l}czy\'nski's property [MATH]. Combined with the natural dual representation of [MATH], this yields that every non-weakly compact operator on [MATH] fixes a copy of [MATH]. The main ingredient is a general property-[MATH] theorem for function modules over zero-dimensional compact Hausdorff spaces with stalks admitting a common modulus of uniform convexity. The proof is based on Gierz's integral representation of functionals and the weak compactness of the associated canonical measures. In the case of [MATH], the relevant stalks are ultrapowers of [MATH], and super-reflexivity provides the uniform geometric control required by the theorem. We also derive several consequences for operators on [MATH], including weak compactness into separable spaces, reflexivity of separable quotients, and compactness of operators into Schur spaces.
tldr: This paper proves that certain Banach spaces of operators have Pelczynski's property (V), answering Kucher's problem about l_infty(E) and Grothendieck spaces.
motivation: Kucher asked whether l_infty(E) is a Grothendieck space for every super-reflexive Banach space E; this work resolves that question in the affirmative.
method: The authors establish a general property-(V) theorem for function modules over zero-dimensional compact Hausdorff spaces with stalks having a common modulus of uniform convexity, using Gierz's integral representation and weak compactness of canonical measures.
result: They prove that l_infty(E) has Pelczynski's property (V), hence is a Grothendieck space, and derive consequences such as non-weakly compact operators fixing a copy of l_infty and compactness results into Schur spaces.
conclusion: The paper solves a Banach space theory problem and provides operator-theoretic consequences, but it is purely mathematical and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Nonminimizing Attractors Of Stochastic Subgradient Methods On Semialgebraic Functions
authors: Jiajin Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We disprove a conjecture of Davis, Drusvyatskiy, and Jiang (2026) that subdifferential regularity can be removed from the generic guarantee of convergence to local minimizers for stochastic subgradient methods. We construct a globally Lipschitz, coercive, semialgebraic function in two dimensions for which the method converges to a nonminimizing Clarke critical point. For suitable power-law stepsizes, this convergence holds for open sets of initial points and linear tilts of the objective, uniformly over all perturbation sequences within a prescribed bound.
tldr: The paper disproves a conjecture by Davis, Drusvyatskiy, and Jiang by constructing a two-dimensional semialgebraic function on which stochastic subgradient methods converge to a nonminimizing Clarke critical point.
motivation: To test whether subdifferential regularity can be removed from generic convergence guarantees to local minimizers for stochastic subgradient methods.
method: The author constructs a globally Lipschitz, coercive, semialgebraic function in two dimensions and analyzes the convergence of stochastic subgradient methods with power-law stepsizes.
result: For suitable power-law stepsizes, convergence to a nonminimizing Clarke critical point occurs for open sets of initial points and linear tilts, uniformly over bounded perturbation sequences.
conclusion: The conjecture that subdifferential regularity is unnecessary for generic convergence to local minimizers is false; regularity remains essential in general.

title: Detection-Guided Adaptive Purification With Diffusion Models For Robust Audio Deepfake Detection
authors: Qiben Yan Muhammed Salih Kayhan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio deepfake detectors remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations that suppress the acoustic cues used for detection, allowing manipulated utterances to evade the detector. Although existing defenses can improve robustness, they require retraining the detector or introduce additional distortion. Diffusion-based purification instead leaves the pretrained detector unchanged, but existing methods use the same purification strength for all inputs, creating a trade-off between removing adversarial perturbations and preserving the subtle spoofing cues needed for detection. In this paper, we propose Detection-Guided Adaptive Purification (DGAP), a diffusion-based defense that adjusts purification strength per input. Building on the observation that a light purification perturbs the detector score of an adversarial input far more than that of a benign one, the framework uses the resulting score shift as a reference-free indicator of adversarial manipulation. Inputs with small shifts are passed unchanged, whereas flagged inputs undergo stronger purification before final detection. We evaluate the framework against three adversarial attack settings across three deepfake detectors, and compare it with nine existing defenses. Our results show that DGAP achieves the best defense performance across all detectors while leaving benign inputs nearly unaffected, and remains effective under the defense-aware adaptive attack.
tldr: The paper proposes a detection-guided adaptive diffusion purification defense to improve the robustness of audio deepfake detectors against adversarial perturbations.
motivation: Audio deepfake detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that suppress spoofing cues, and existing defenses either require retraining or distort benign inputs.
method: DGAP uses the detector score shift under light diffusion purification as a reference-free indicator of adversarial manipulation, applying stronger purification only to flagged inputs.
result: Across three detectors and multiple attack settings, DGAP achieves the best defense performance while leaving benign inputs nearly unaffected and remaining effective under adaptive attacks.
conclusion: Adaptive, detection-guided purification can improve adversarial robustness of audio deepfake detectors without retraining the pretrained detector.

title: CPU-Auth: Device Fingerprinting For Authentication Via Dvfs Side-Channel
authors: Ryan Swift
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lack of effective authentication has resulted in numerous security and privacy breaches, including unauthorized access to protected information, identity theft, and fraud. One approach to mitigating such attacks is Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), in which users must provide multiple pieces of information for authentication. Some secondary authentication factors include SMS text verification codes, biometrics, and tokens. Each contains at least one notable flaw: SMS is notoriously insecure; biometrics rely upon access to sensitive personal data; and tokens require dependence on third-party providers (e.g. OAuth providers). This work explores CPU-Auth, a novel authentication mechanism based on unique variations in the physical characteristics of the CPU of a computing device. By measuring the behavior of the Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) governor remotely from within a browser, unique properties of the CPU can be leveraged to establish a hardware-based device fingerprint for use in CPU-Auth. The performance of CPU-Auth is evaluated on over 50,000 data traces using distance-based and deep learning methods. CPU-Auth is part of a larger research project, and the results provided in this report reflect only the contributions made to the project by members of this group.
tldr: CPU-Auth uses DVFS side-channel measurements from a browser to build a CPU-based device fingerprint for authentication.
motivation: Existing multi-factor authentication methods such as SMS, biometrics, and tokens have security, privacy, or third-party dependency flaws.
method: The work remotely measures Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling governor behavior within a browser and evaluates over 50,000 traces using distance-based and deep learning methods.
result: The results indicate that CPU variations observable through DVFS side channels can serve as a hardware fingerprint for authentication.
conclusion: CPU-Auth is a novel authentication mechanism based on CPU physical characteristics, though this report only documents the group's partial contributions.

title: Nomos: Compiling Written Policies Into Statically Verified Tool-Call Gates For Llm Agents
authors: Min-Young Yu, Tony Kim, Jang Won Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents violate the policies they are deployed to enforce, often silently. Prior defenses hand-write rules, query an LLM verifier per action, or compile policies through heavyweight formal machinery. Naive compilation fails: extracted rules block the tool satisfying their own precondition, or read arguments their tool lacks. NOMOS, a four-pass compiler, turns a natural-language policy into a deterministic tool-call gate; static verification with tool-schema-level checks alone (no prover, solver, or LLM) repairs or rejects 37% (airline) and 13% (retail) of candidates, without which most shipped rules are inoperable. Replaying compiled rules over undefended transcripts flags bindings that refuse legitimate work (a development binding refused 95.9% of task-passing calls); no evaluation binding is flagged. On [MATH]-bench the gate cuts violations of reference-encoded clauses among state-changing calls from 66.3% to 2.6% (airline) and 30.8% to 6.9% (retail), raising airline task success significantly for [MATH]; a 26B on-premise compilation is not significantly worse than hand-written or frontier-compiled rules. Unlike AgentDojo's shipped defenses, it reaches a zero attack success rate (ASR) on banking, where nine attack families collapse onto three structural rules. On the other three suites its ASR is at most 3.6%, from goals with no tool call to govern and one write admitted by a binding weaker than its clause; a second agent model, Llama-3.3-70B, reproduces the effect on both benchmarks. Decisions take microseconds without an LLM call, at a domain-dependent benign-utility cost; compilation runs on-premise on open-weight gemma-4-26B.
tldr: NOMOS is a four-pass compiler that turns natural-language policies into deterministic, statically verified tool-call gates for LLM agents.
motivation: Tool-using LLM agents often violate their deployment policies silently, and prior defenses rely on hand-written rules, per-action LLM verification, or heavyweight formal methods.
method: The compiler extracts rules, statically verifies them against tool-schema-level checks without a prover, solver, or LLM, repairs or rejects invalid candidates, and replays rules over undefended transcripts.
result: Static verification repairs or rejects 37% (airline) and 13% (retail) of candidate rules; the gate cuts violations among state-changing calls from 66.3% to 2.6% on airline and 30.8% to 6.9% on retail, reaching zero ASR on banking and at most 3.6% on other suites, with microsecond decisions and a domain-dependent benign-utility cost.
conclusion: On-premise compilation with a 26B model is viable and not significantly worse than hand-written or frontier-compiled rules, showing that lightweight static verification can make tool-call policy enforcement practical.

title: Brace: Differential Privacy For Dense Associative Memory With Lsr Energy
authors: Zhaoyang Shi Chang Qu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dense associative memory (DAM) provides an energy-based framework for memory retrieval with close connections to attention mechanisms in modern artificial intelligence. Despite growing interest in differential privacy for AI, the privacy of DAM retrieval dynamics remains relatively unexplored. In this paper, we develop a differential privacy framework for log-sum-ReLU (LSR) dense associative memory, whose finite-support retrieval dynamics pose distinctive challenges for privacy-preserving computation. We propose the Boundary-Responsive Adaptive Correction Evolution (BRACE) algorithm, a differentially private retrieval mechanism for LSR-DAM that adaptively corrects boundary-sensitive perturbations to control their cumulative effect over the retrieval trajectory. In theory, we prove that our method is minimax optimal by deriving dimension-independent terminal and full-trajectory retrieval error rates, with optimal dependence on the inverse temperature and, in the growing-horizon regime, the retrieval horizon. We further establish central limit theorems that enable uncertainty quantification for private retrieval by characterizing its asymptotic distribution and the additional variability introduced by privacy. Numerical experiments compare our proposed method with baseline differential privacy approaches and evaluate its retrieval accuracy. Together, our results provide a theoretical foundation for optimal privacy-preserving retrieval and uncertainty quantification in energy-based associative memory systems.
tldr: The paper proposes BRACE, a differentially private retrieval algorithm for log-sum-ReLU dense associative memory, with minimax optimal error rates and central limit theorems for uncertainty quantification.
motivation: Dense associative memory (DAM) is an energy-based model related to attention, but privacy-preserving retrieval in DAM remains largely unexplored, especially for finite-support LSR dynamics.
method: The authors introduce Boundary-Responsive Adaptive Correction Evolution (BRACE), which adaptively corrects boundary-sensitive perturbations over retrieval trajectories to achieve differential privacy.
result: They prove minimax optimality via dimension-independent terminal and full-trajectory retrieval error rates, establish central limit theorems for private retrieval, and validate the approach numerically against baselines.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for optimal privacy-preserving retrieval and uncertainty quantification in energy-based associative memory systems.

title: ProxyEraseAgent: Blind Watermark Removal In The Wild
authors: Jun Yao, Chao Wang, Yupeng Qiu, Zehua Ma, Weiming Zhang, Bin Liu, Han Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Invisible image watermark removal has received growing attention. Despite substantial progress, existing attacks face a tension between practicality and specificity. Attacks exploiting detector outputs, decoder responses, or paired images can be tailored to the watermark decision boundary, but require information rarely available in realistic scenarios. Conversely, attacks based on compression, geometric distortion, or reconstruction are easily deployed from a single watermarked image, but remain largely open-loop: they apply generic transformations without knowing if the image is moving toward watermark failure. Thus, the key challenge in single-image blind watermark removal is not merely how to transform the image, but how to obtain a useful removal direction without accessing the hidden decoder. To bridge this gap, we propose ProxyEraseAgent, an agent-driven framework recovering attack specificity through proxy decoder responses. Publicly available watermarking schemes provide a natural knowledge base of candidate decoders, where some are informative for a given unknown image. Our insight is that a decoder producing a strong calibrated response to the query image likely shares a nearby decoding boundary with the hidden target mechanism. ProxyEraseAgent ranks these decoders by calibrated response strength and uses the top ones as proxy boundary estimators. Their responses then guide a progressive search over heterogeneous removal operations (e.g., geometric distortion, JPEG compression, image reconstruction, and gradient perturbation) under perceptual-quality constraints. Experiments across 11 watermarking systems show ProxyEraseAgent achieves a 94.8% attack success rate, demonstrating the effectiveness of response-guided proxy retrieval and feedback-driven sequential planning for blind watermark removal.
tldr: ProxyEraseAgent is an agent-driven framework for blind invisible image watermark removal that uses responses from publicly available proxy decoders to guide a progressive search over removal operations.
motivation: Existing watermark removal attacks face a trade-off: highly specific attacks require privileged information (detector outputs, decoder responses, paired images) rarely available in practice, while generic single-image attacks (compression, geometric distortion, reconstruction) are open-loop and cannot tell whether they are approaching watermark failure.
method: The framework treats public watermarking schemes as a knowledge base of candidate decoders, ranks them by calibrated response strength to the query image, and uses the top scorers as proxy estimators of the hidden decision boundary; their feedback then drives a sequential, perception-constrained search over heterogeneous removal operations including geometric distortion, JPEG compression, reconstruction, and gradient perturbation.
result: Experiments across 11 watermarking systems report a 94.8% attack success rate, demonstrating the effectiveness of response-guided proxy retrieval and feedback-driven planning.
conclusion: Recovering attack specificity through proxy decoder responses enables practical, single-image blind watermark removal, showing that agentic search with proxy feedback is a viable direction for watermark-erasure research.

title: DRL-Based AoI Minimization For Rsma In Finite-Blocklength Mu-miso
authors: Enes Kaya, Mehmet Alp Demircio\u{g}lu, Elif Tugce Ceran, Melda Yuksel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This letter investigates age-of-information (AoI) minimization in multi-user wireless networks operating in the finite-blocklength (FBL) regime, which is critical for low-latency transmission of short state-update packets. While rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) provides a powerful and flexible framework for interference management in multi-user FBL systems, the joint optimization of its parameters, such as precoding vectors, power allocation, and rate-splitting ratios, to guarantee information freshness results in analytically intractable complexity. To address this challenge, we propose an actor--critic deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework to learn dynamic resource-allocation policies in multi-user multiple-input single-output (MU-MISO) broadcast channels. Simulation results show that the proposed RSMA-RL framework achieves consistently lower AoI than the state-of-the-art benchmarks, with substantial gains observed at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and short blocklengths, while matching benchmark performance at high SNR with significantly lower online complexity via a single neural-network forward pass at execution.
tldr: This letter proposes a deep reinforcement learning framework to minimize age-of-information in finite-blocklength multi-user MISO systems using rate-splitting multiple access.
motivation: Low-latency transmission of short state-update packets requires optimizing information freshness, but joint optimization of RSMA parameters in finite-blocklength MU-MISO is analytically intractable.
method: An actor-critic deep reinforcement learning algorithm learns dynamic resource-allocation policies for precoding vectors, power allocation, and rate-splitting ratios in multi-user broadcast channels.
result: Simulations show the RSMA-RL framework achieves consistently lower AoI than state-of-the-art benchmarks, with substantial gains at low SNR and short blocklengths and lower online complexity via a single neural-network forward pass.
conclusion: DRL-based RSMA resource allocation effectively minimizes AoI in finite-blocklength MU-MISO networks, offering a practical low-complexity solution for timely status updates.

title: MORDOR:Mitigating Overheads Of Read Disturbance Preventive Operations Via Elastic Refresh Scheduling
authors: Maria Makeenkova, Ataberk Olgun, F. Nisa Bostanc{\i}, \.ismail Emir Y\"uksel, Spiros Galanopoulos, Onur Mutlu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern DRAM chips are susceptible to read disturbance phenomena such as RowHammer, where repeatedly accessing (hammering) a row of DRAM cells (i.e., a DRAM row) induces bitflips in other physically nearby (victim) DRAM rows. A common practice to avoid such bitflips is to preventively refresh victim rows that might otherwise experience bitflips. Unfortunately, preventive refreshes cause long latencies and need to be performed urgently before the aggressor row is activated again to ensure data integrity. This is done by prioritizing them over demand memory requests, thereby potentially imposing significant delays on those requests and causing performance and energy overheads. Our goal in this work is to alleviate these overheads by scheduling preventive refreshes off the critical path of demand memory requests. We propose MORDOR, a new preventive refresh scheduling policy that significantly reduces system performance degradation and energy consumption caused by preventive refresh operations. MORDOR is integrated into the memory controller and operates alongside memory-controller-based read disturbance mitigation techniques to intelligently delay preventive refresh operations, while maintaining their data integrity guarantees. MORDOR leverages the key observation that a preventive refresh operation targeting an aggressor row can be delayed to serve any other demand memory request, as long as that memory request does not access the aggressor row. By doing so, MORDOR executes latency-critical memory requests before long-latency preventive refresh operations, while mitigating read disturbance bitflips. We evaluate MORDOR by integrating it into six state-of-the-art read disturbance mitigation techniques. Our comprehensive evaluation shows that MORDOR significantly improves system performance and energy efficiency at low area cost.
tldr: MORDOR is a memory-controller refresh scheduling policy that delays preventive RowHammer refreshes off the critical path to reduce performance and energy overhead while preserving data integrity.
motivation: Preventive refreshes used to mitigate DRAM read disturbance are prioritized over demand memory requests, causing significant latency, performance, and energy overheads.
method: MORDOR schedules preventive refresh operations to be delayed and served after any demand request that does not access the same aggressor row, and is integrated into six state-of-the-art read disturbance mitigation techniques.
result: The policy improves system performance and energy efficiency at low area cost compared with baseline preventive refresh handling.
conclusion: Elastic refresh scheduling can alleviate the overheads of read disturbance mitigation without sacrificing the data integrity guarantees of preventive refreshes.

title: Epistemic Disturbance In The Graph Model For Conflict Resolution: State-Preserving Actions, Four-Valued Assessments, And The Distinction Between Capability And Intention
authors: Yukiko Kato
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the graph model for conflict resolution (GMCR), a decision maker (DM) either moves the conflict to another state or does nothing. The basic definitions leave inaction implicit, so every action that leaves the state unchanged is treated as doing nothing. Yet announcements, exercises, leaks and selective disclosures are neither moves nor inaction: they leave the state unchanged but change what other DMs believe about which moves are available and which moves others would want to make. We introduce such state-preserving actions by augmenting states with the DMs' epistemic states: a physical move changes the physical state, a state-preserving action changes only the epistemic state, and inaction is the absence of a transition. Actions generate evidence through observer-specific interpretation maps. Building on a four-valued extension of GMCR from the author's earlier work, which separates evidence for and against, we show that evidence for a move can only enable perceived moves and evidence against can only disable them, that two of the four reduction operators ignore one kind of evidence, and that contradictory assessments are absorbing under monotone accumulation. With the monotonicity of stability in move sets, this fixes the direction in which any action moves a DM's stability judgements and characterizes when actions can enable provocation or deterrence. Capability assessments affect all sanction-based stability concepts, and on the DM's own side also Nash stability, whereas intention assessments affect only sequential stability. Hedging between two candidate types weakly expands or shrinks an observer's sequentially stable set according to how it reads contradiction. In the 1995 DVD format negotiation, general metarationality cannot distinguish its phases, since the computer industry group could always sanction; sequential stability, which asks whether it would, can.
tldr: The paper introduces state-preserving actions into the graph model for conflict resolution (GMCR) by augmenting states with epistemic states, and develops a four-valued assessment framework to separate capability and intention in stability analysis.
motivation: GMCR traditionally treats any action that leaves the state unchanged as inaction, but real-world actions like announcements, exercises, and leaks alter other decision makers' beliefs without changing the physical state.
method: The author augments physical states with decision makers' epistemic states, defines observer-specific interpretation maps for evidence, and builds on a four-valued extension of GMCR that separates evidence for and against moves.
result: Evidence for a move can only enable perceived moves while evidence against can only disable them; two reduction operators ignore one kind of evidence; contradictory assessments are absorbing under monotone accumulation; capability assessments affect all sanction-based stability concepts and Nash stability, whereas intention assessments affect only sequential stability.
conclusion: The framework characterizes when actions enable provocation or deterrence and shows that sequential stability, unlike general metarationality, can distinguish phases in the 1995 DVD format negotiation by asking whether the computer industry group would sanction.

title: Fast Angular Sweep Monostatic Radar Cross Section Computation Via Model Order Reduction
authors: Valentin de la Rubia Noelia Naranjo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The radar cross section (RCS) is a fundamental parameter in radar engineering, as it determines the detectability of a given target by a radar system. Increasing interest in very low observability (VLO) targets has arisen recently. As a result, especial effort is put in developing numerical tools to accurately predict the electromagnetic scattering from perfect electric conductor objects. Integral equation methods are commonly used in this task. However, full-wave computation of the monostatic RCS at a single angle can be rather time-consuming, nevermind computing the RCS in a specific angular interval with a fine sampling. In fact, this is what is needed in industrial applications. A reduced-order model for fast full-wave monostatic RCS evaluation is proposed to easily achieve fine details in the desired angular domain. An open source integral equation solver, taken into account as a black box, is used to get the electromagnetic scattering in non-penetrable objects at some specific incident angles. Several radar targets will show the possibilities and capabilities of these model order reduction approaches.
tldr: A model-order-reduction approach is proposed to rapidly compute monostatic radar cross sections over a fine angular sweep using an existing integral-equation solver as a black box.
motivation: Computing monostatic RCS at fine angular resolution via full-wave integral equation methods is prohibitively time-consuming, yet industrial applications require such fine angular detail for low-observability targets.
method: A reduced-order model is built from full-wave electromagnetic scattering data computed at a few selected incident angles by an open-source integral equation solver for perfect electric conductor targets, then used to interpolate the RCS across the angular domain.
result: Several radar target examples demonstrate that the model-order-reduction framework captures fine angular details of the monostatic RCS while drastically reducing computation time compared to brute-force sampling.
conclusion: Model order reduction enables fast, accurate monostatic RCS evaluation over angular intervals, offering a practical numerical tool for radar engineering of very low observability targets.

title: Unilateral And Equitransitive Tilings By Squares Of Sizes 1, 2, 3, And 4
authors: Layan Arrabi, Casey Mann, Fatima Muniz, Harmony Vargas, Rachel Villafranca
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article we examine a problem stated in Gr\"{u}baum and Shephard's classic book on tiling theory, Tilings and Patterns, which asks the reader to find all unilateral and equitransitive tilings by squares of sizes [MATH] where [MATH]. The unilaterality condition requires that two squares of the same size in such a tiling may not intersect along an entire side, and the equitransitivity requires that two tiles of the same size in such a tiling must be in the same transitivity class with respect to the symmetry group of the tiling. These two conditions on tilings by squares allows for surprisingly interesting and complex tilings by squares.
