In this work we provide the answer to Gr\"{u}baum and Shephard's question for the case [MATH], as well as developing methods and computer algorithms that may be extended to the cases where [MATH].
tldr: A combinatorial geometry paper solving a tiling theory problem from Grünbaum and Shephard's classic text, finding all unilateral and equitransitive tilings by squares of sizes 1, 2, 3, and 4.
motivation: The work addresses an open question posed explicitly by Grünbaum and Shephard in 'Tilings and Patterns', concerning which tilings by squares of four distinct sizes satisfy the unilaterality and equitransitivity conditions.
method: The authors combine geometric and combinatorial reasoning with custom computer algorithms to enumerate and classify candidate tilings, developing techniques extendable to larger sets of square sizes.
result: All unilateral and equitransitive tilings by squares of sizes 1, 2, 3, and 4 are determined and catalogued, resolving the case n=4 of the question.
conclusion: The paper resolves the n=4 case of the Grünbaum–Shephard problem and provides generalizable methods and algorithms that could approach the n>4 cases.

title: Strong Legendre Regularity And Short-time Analysis Of Abnormal Curves
authors: Francesco Boarotto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study strictly abnormal sub-Riemannian extremals satisfying the Goh condition and a strong (i.e., coercive) generalized Legendre condition, imposed only at the Lebesgue points of the reference control. We prove that such a control is smooth, that the projected extended Hessian of the end-point map is uniformly coercive on the admissible set of variations for short times, and that the abnormal covector gives a quantitative separation of the end-point of the reference arc from the image of the admissible set under the nonlinear end-point map. As a consequence the reference arc is rigid and, for short times, it is a length minimizer: every admissible curve with the same end-points and no greater length is a reparametrization of the reference arc. In particular, among controls of constant speed the reference control is the unique length minimizer. All the estimates are uniform on the admissible set, and no assumption is made on the dimension of the manifold, on the growth vector of the distribution, or on the corank of the differential of the end-point map.
tldr: A pure control-theory/geometric analysis proving that strictly abnormal sub-Riemannian extremals satisfying the Goh condition and a coercive generalized Legendre condition are smooth and locally length-minimizing.
motivation: Understanding when abnormal extremals in sub-Riemannian geometry are rigid and length-minimizing is a long-standing question, typically hampered by assumptions on dimension, growth vector, or corank.
method: The authors impose a strong (coercive) generalized Legendre condition only at Lebesgue points of the reference control and then study the projected extended Hessian of the non-linear end-point map over admissible variations for short times.
result: They show the control is smooth, the projected extended Hessian is uniformly coercive, and the abnormal covector quantitatively separates the reference end-point from the image of the admissible set, yielding rigidity and short-time length minimality with estimates uniform on the admissible set.
conclusion: The results establish local optimality and uniqueness (among constant-speed controls) of such abnormal extremals without any assumptions on manifold dimension, growth vector, or corank of the end-point map differential.

title: Besov Spaces And Product Bmo Over Polydisc
authors: Kai Wang Chen Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the analytic Besov space [MATH] embeds continuously into Chang--Fefferman product BMO for every finite [MATH] and [MATH]. Consequently, every small Hankel operator in a finite Schatten class has a product BMO symbol. The proof uses smooth product wavelets and an estimate for dyadic rectangles. We also give a condition on Fej\'er means that yields a BMO symbol for a bounded Hankel operator on the polydisc.
tldr: The paper proves that analytic Besov spaces embed continuously into Chang–Fefferman product BMO on the polydisc, with consequences for Hankel operators in finite Schatten classes.
motivation: The authors aim to establish embedding relations between function spaces in several complex variables and to characterize symbols of Hankel operators via product BMO.
method: The proof relies on smooth product wavelets together with an estimate for dyadic rectangles, plus a Fejér-mean condition for boundedness of Hankel operators.
result: Analytic Besov space embeds continuously into product BMO for all finite parameters, implying every small Hankel operator in a finite Schatten class has a product BMO symbol; a Fejér-mean condition yields a BMO symbol for bounded Hankel operators.
conclusion: The work extends classical one-variable BMO/Hankel theory to the polydisc setting through product wavelet techniques.

title: Weakly Quasar-Convex Optimization
authors: Felipe Lara Abbas Khademi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces the class of weakly quasar-convex functions, a notion that simultaneously generalizes weak convexity (and hence convexity) and quasar-convexity. We establish the theoretical foundation for this new class by developing its basic calculus, deriving characterizations, and systematically investigating its closure and structural properties. Building on these tools, we analyze the proximal point algorithm for minimizing a weakly quasar-convex function under local quadratic growth, proving [MATH]-linear convergence of the iterates and [MATH]-linear convergence of the function values to a global minimizer, with iteration complexity [MATH]; we also give a fully computable, minimizer-free stopping rule via the proximal residual with matching complexity. Finally, we construct a weakly quasar-convex function, satisfying all our standing assumptions, that is neither weakly convex, quasi-convex, star quasi-convex, nor quasar-convex for any modulus, showing that our convergence theory applies to instances outside every prior framework in the literature.
tldr: The paper introduces weakly quasar-convex functions, develops their calculus and structural properties, and analyzes a proximal point algorithm with linear convergence under local quadratic growth.
motivation: The authors aim to unify weak convexity and quasar-convexity into a broader function class that captures optimization problems outside existing frameworks.
method: They establish basic calculus, characterizations, and closure properties for weakly quasar-convex functions, then apply these tools to prove convergence rates and a stopping rule for the proximal point algorithm.
result: The proximal point algorithm achieves linear convergence of iterates and function values to a global minimizer, with a matching complexity and a minimizer-free stopping rule based on the proximal residual.
conclusion: The new class is strictly more general than weak convexity, quasi-convexity, star quasi-convexity, and quasar-convexity, as demonstrated by an explicit example, expanding the scope of convergence guarantees for nonconvex optimization.

title: SoK: Are LLMs Reliable At Source Code Recovery? A Taxonomy And Empirical Evaluation
authors: Varun Kohli, Lee Bing Cheng, Nur Hazim Ghazali, Gao Yuze, Daryl Poon, Dinil Mon Divakaran
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective source recovery is critical to security applications such as malware analysis, vulnerability assessment, and legacy maintenance. Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping this field, shifting the paradigm away from rule-based heuristics to probabilistic and high fidelity semantic recovery of source code from assembly or classical decompiler-derived pseudo-C. However, despite rapid progress, the field suffers from fragmentation across numerous approaches as well as their non-unified evaluations, limiting objective comparisons. Further, existing works have limited coverage of embedded, IoT architectures and source languages beyond C/C++. In this work, we present the first Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) focused specifically on LLM-assisted binary-to-source recovery. We provide a granular design-centric taxonomy of LLM-assisted source recovery methods and systematic evaluations using seven key metrics along six evaluation dimensions. We evaluate state-of-the-art methods on 45,000 test samples derived from four standard and five embedded architectures, five optimization levels, and symbol stripping. We ablate the impact of design choices on recovery performance, including input representation, contextual enrichment, model scale, iteration and review roles using controlled in-house recovery pipelines and three off-the-shelf models. Finally, we test same-language and cross-language recovery capability covering four mature and two legacy languages. Our systematization and comprehensive evaluations provide key insights that guide future directions in this field.
tldr: This SoK systematizes and empirically evaluates LLM-based binary-to-source code recovery, providing a design-centric taxonomy and a large-scale benchmark across architectures, languages, and optimization levels.
motivation: LLM-assisted source recovery is fragmented across approaches with non-unified evaluations, limiting objective comparison, and existing work under-covers embedded/IoT architectures and languages beyond C/C++.
method: The authors construct a design-centric taxonomy of LLM-assisted source recovery methods and evaluate state-of-the-art approaches on 45,000 samples across nine architectures, five optimization levels, and symbol stripping, using seven metrics along six evaluation dimensions, plus ablations on input representation, context, model scale, and iterative review roles.
result: They characterize how design choices (input representation, contextual enrichment, model scale, iteration/review roles) affect recovery fidelity, and assess same-language and cross-language recovery over four mature and two legacy languages.
conclusion: The systematization and comprehensive evaluations yield insights to guide future research directions in LLM-assisted binary-to-source recovery.

title: Ltbd: Learnable Trust-Boundary Delimiters For Prompt Injection Defense
authors: Luman Zhao, Minghui Xu, Yue Zhang, Yijun Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform remarkably well on complex tasks, yet remain highly vulnerable to prompt injection attacks, where malicious instructions embedded in external data can override user intent. Existing defenses remain limited by model fine-tuning requirements, vulnerability to adaptive attacks, or reliance on brittle handcrafted prompts. We argue that a fundamental source of this vulnerability is the lack of an explicit representation of trust provenance. To address this, we introduce Learnable Trust-Boundary Delimiters (LTBD), a lightweight defense that explicitly encodes trust boundaries in the input while keeping the LLM parameters unchanged. LTBD uses a small number of learnable delimiters to distinguish trusted user instructions from untrusted external data, enabling the model to better respect the intended trust hierarchy. Experimental results show that LTBD substantially outperforms inference-time defenses and performs competitively with training-based approaches, while preserving benign-task utility and introducing negligible inference overhead. In particular, LTBD achieves 0.00% ASR on AlpacaFarm and only 0.11-0.19% ASR on TaskTracker. LTBD also remains effective under adaptive attacks, where adversaries have full knowledge of the defense and explicitly attempt to bypass it.
tldr: LTBD introduces lightweight learnable trust-boundary delimiters that encode trust provenance in the input to defend LLMs against prompt injection without fine-tuning the model.
motivation: LLMs are vulnerable to prompt injection because they lack an explicit representation of trust provenance, and existing defenses require fine-tuning, rely on brittle handcrafted prompts, or fail under adaptive attacks.
method: A small set of learnable delimiter tokens is optimized to mark boundaries between trusted user instructions and untrusted external data while keeping the LLM parameters frozen, teaching the model to respect the intended trust hierarchy.
result: LTBD achieves 0.00% attack success rate on AlpacaFarm and 0.11-0.19% on TaskTracker, outperforming inference-time defenses, competing with training-based methods, preserving benign utility, and remaining robust under adaptive attacks.
conclusion: Explicitly encoding trust boundaries via learnable delimiters offers an effective, low-overhead prompt injection defense, though the work lies entirely outside quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: The Mirror Theorem: Central Incidence Saturation In Keith Recurrences
authors: Federico Ignacio Zamponi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Keith numbers are integers that reappear in sliding-window recurrences generated from their own digits. We introduce Keith mirrors, a subclass defined by saturation at the center of the recurrence's incidence profile. For an even index m, let C_d(m) denote the sum of the two central incidence counts. We prove that the central deficit m-C_d(m) is exactly the distance from m to the interval [2d,2d+2], which forces every Keith mirror of order d>=3 in base B>=3 to return at 2d+2. A digit identity and analytic capacity bounds then reduce the classification to finitely many cases. Exact enumeration, independently checked against the original recurrence and incidence definition, yields precisely 35 mirrors of order at least three, while order two consists of two explicit infinite families. We also classify exactly eight cross-base triple alignments satisfying R=C=x_1+x_d and record the conditional reconstruction property induced by incidence symmetry.
tldr: The paper introduces 'Keith mirrors', a subclass of Keith numbers defined by saturation at the center of a sliding-window recurrence's incidence profile, and classifies them completely.
motivation: Keith numbers (integers that reappear in digit-generated sliding-window recurrences) are a classical curiosity of elementary number theory; the author aims to identify and classify a symmetric subclass with special incidence structure.
method: The central deficit m − C_d(m) is proven to equal the distance from m to the interval [2d, 2d+2], reducing the classification to finite analytic capacity bounds; exact enumeration is performed and cross-checked against the original recurrence definition.
result: Every Keith mirror of order d ≥ 3 in base B ≥ 3 returns at 2d + 2, yielding exactly 35 mirrors of order at least three, two infinite families at order two, and exactly eight cross-base triple alignments with R = C = x_1 + x_d.
conclusion: The mirror theorem provides a complete classification of centrally saturated Keith numbers and a conditional reconstruction property induced by incidence symmetry, with no apparent connection to physics or information theory.

title: Partition-theoretic Density Formulas: Radial Tauberian Theory And Non-radial Instability
authors: Mohammad F. Marashdeh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ono, Schneider and Wagner found a partition-theoretic analogue of Alladi's duality formula: for many sets [MATH], the series [MATH] over partitions into distinct parts with smallest part in [MATH] tends to the density of [MATH] as [MATH]. We determine when this happens. Radially, the summation kernel is a Gumbel density, and Wiener's theorem shows that for bounded [MATH] the associated series tends to [MATH] if and only if [MATH] has mean [MATH] on every interval [MATH]; natural density does not suffice. Multiplied by [MATH], the series tends to [MATH] if and only if [MATH] has [MATH] elements in each such interval; this gives a partition analogue of Alladi's theorem for Chebotarev sets of primes. Off the real axis the largest weights grow like [MATH] with [MATH]. Along [MATH], the formula for residue classes modulo [MATH] holds exactly when [MATH], an explicit Clausen-function threshold with [MATH], and it fails almost surely for random sets of bounded discrepancy. These results correct several published claims.
tldr: The paper studies partition-theoretic density formulas and radial Tauberian conditions for a partition analogue of Alladi's duality, correcting several published claims.
motivation: Ono, Schneider, and Wagner introduced a partition-theoretic analogue of Alladi's duality formula, but the exact conditions under which the relevant series converge to a density were not fully determined.
method: The author uses radial Tauberian theory, Wiener's theorem, Gumbel density kernels, and Clausen-function thresholds to analyze the limiting behavior on and off the real axis.
result: The series tends to the density under mean-value conditions on intervals, not merely natural density; a partition analogue of Alladi's theorem for Chebotarev sets is obtained, and off-axis weights grow with explicit exponents, while the residue-class formula holds only up to a Clausen-function threshold and fails for random sets of bounded discrepancy.
conclusion: The work characterizes when the partition-theoretic density formula holds, proves a sharp threshold in residue-class cases, and corrects several published claims in the literature.

title: What Forms Of Student Sensemaking Predict Mathematics Learning?: Student Perspectives On Opportunity, Comfort, And Utility
authors: Sarah E. Castleman, Richard Correnti, Christian D. Schunn
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Instructional practices that require student sensemaking of mathematics are considered critical to learning outcomes, yet strategies for measurement of this instruction at scale have yet to be established. This study aims at validating and exploring the predictive validity of three student survey measures: students' opportunity to engage with, comfort engaging with, and utility of engaging with instructional practices targeting sensemaking in mathematics. Using an initial sample of 1,955 US middle school student responses, we conducted exploratory factor analysis to establish sensemaking construct structure, identifying two distinct factors reflecting students' active and passive participation in mathematical sensemaking. We then analyzed data from an additional 3,170 surveys collected over two years in the same context to confirm measurement properties and evaluate the measures' predictive validity. The resulting measures capture students' reported opportunities to engage in sensemaking practices (Sensemaking Opportunity), their comfort with engaging in those practices (Sensemaking Comfort), and their perceived utility of those practices when tackling new or difficult math problems (Sensemaking Utility). While Sensemaking Comfort and Sensemaking Utility both showed strong predictive validity over two years, Sensemaking Utility provided the most reliable estimates of student sensemaking. These findings offer researchers and practitioners a psychometrically sound, scalable toolkit for monitoring sensemaking in mathematics classrooms with implications for both large-scale research on instructional quality and teachers' ongoing efforts to monitor and improve their practice.
tldr: This study develops and validates student survey measures of opportunity, comfort, and utility related to mathematical sensemaking in middle school classrooms.
motivation: Instructional practices that promote student sensemaking are considered critical for mathematics learning, but scalable measurement tools for such instruction are lacking.
method: Using exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis on survey responses from over 5,000 US middle school students collected over two years, the authors identify two factors (active and passive sensemaking) and assess predictive validity.
result: Sensemaking Comfort and Sensemaking Utility show strong predictive validity, with Sensemaking Utility providing the most reliable estimates of student sensemaking.
conclusion: The validated measures offer a psychometrically sound toolkit for monitoring mathematics sensemaking at scale, useful for research on instructional quality and teacher practice.

title: Isometric Rigidity Of Complete Pick Algebras On Monomial Varieties
authors: Hamidul Ahmed, B. Krishna Das, Chaman Kumar Sahu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a geometric rigidity theorem for a class of monomial varieties in finite-dimensional unit balls. Every ball automorphism mapping one such variety onto another is unitary, and whenever such an equivalence exists, it can also be realized by a permutation of the ambient coordinates. As a consequence, we obtain a complete isometric classification of the multiplier algebras of integrally generated complete Nevanlinna--Pick Dirichlet series kernels in terms of their defining weight and frequency data. We also obtain an explicit isometric classification for a class of complete Nevanlinna--Pick kernels on bounded Reinhardt domains.
tldr: The paper proves geometric rigidity and isometric classification results for complete Pick algebras on monomial varieties and related Nevanlinna–Pick kernels.
motivation: The authors aim to understand when ball automorphisms preserving certain monomial varieties must be unitary and how to classify multiplier algebras of complete Pick kernels by their defining data.
method: They use geometric rigidity arguments for monomial varieties in finite-dimensional unit balls, combined with operator-algebraic techniques for complete Nevanlinna–Pick Dirichlet series kernels.
result: Every ball automorphism mapping one such variety onto another is unitary and can be realized by ambient coordinate permutation, yielding explicit isometric classifications of multiplier algebras and certain complete Pick kernels on Reinhardt domains.
conclusion: The work provides a complete isometric classification of relevant complete Pick algebras, advancing the structure theory of these algebras on monomial varieties.

title: Backstepping Stabilization Of A Hyperbolic System With A Zero Characteristic Speed
authors: Wenhao Yang Zhiqiang Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the boundary stabilization of a linear hyperbolic system with a zero characteristic speed. We address a case that cannot be stabilized by proportional boundary feedback and develop a backstepping design for the critical setting where the zero-speed subsystem has no intrinsic dissipation. To this end, we construct a Volterra transformation leading to a nonstandard integro-differential target system. Its asymptotic stability in L2 is established by both the Lyapunov-LaSalle method and a spectral semigroup argument. The backstepping kernel equations are explicitly solved, yielding an explicit boundary feedback law that asymptotically stabilizes the original system. Numerical simulations are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed control design.
tldr: The paper develops a backstepping boundary control design for a linear hyperbolic system with a zero characteristic speed and no intrinsic dissipation in the zero-speed subsystem.
motivation: Such systems cannot be stabilized by standard proportional boundary feedback, motivating a tailored backstepping approach for the critical zero-speed case.
method: A Volterra transformation maps the original system to a nonstandard integro-differential target system; stability is proven via Lyapunov-LaSalle and spectral semigroup arguments, and kernel equations are solved explicitly.
result: The authors obtain an explicit boundary feedback law that asymptotically stabilizes the system in L2, supported by numerical simulations.
conclusion: The work provides a constructive control method for a previously unaddressable class of hyperbolic partial differential equations with a zero characteristic speed.

title: A Neural-Network Approach For The Stability Of Loosely-Coupled Fsi Simulations In Hemodynamics
authors: Francesca Renzi, Stefano Pagani, Paola F. Antonietti, Christian Vergara
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The development of accurate and efficient computational methods for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems remains an active research area due to its broad engineering and biomedical applications. Partitioned loosely coupled (LC) schemes are attractive for large-scale simulations because of their modularity and low computational cost. However, their applicability is limited by stability issues in high added-mass regimes, where fluid and structure densities are comparable, as in hemodynamics. In our recent work, we proposed an LC algorithm based on Dirichlet-Neumann interface coupling, the LC-DN-{\alpha} scheme, which improves the stability of the coupling through a stabilization parameter {\alpha}. Although theoretical stability has been demonstrated under suitable constraints on {\alpha}, its optimal value depends on the physical and numerical characteristics of the FSI problem and is difficult to determine in practice. In this work, we propose a data-driven strategy to automatically estimate the optimal value of {\alpha}. We develop a feed-forward neural network to predict {\alpha} from the descriptors of the FSI problem. The model is trained on a dataset of baseline FSI problems in large added-mass regimes and evaluated on more realistic configurations to assess robustness and generalization. Numerical results show that the proposed model generalizes across the considered FSI scenarios and provides robust estimates of {\alpha} under moderate variations in the problem setup, including changes in geometry and loading conditions, that do not completely alter the interaction mechanics represented in the training set. The methodology is intentionally developed and validated on simplified FSI problems, providing a proof of concept for data-driven strategies to improve the efficiency of partitioned FSI simulations and supporting their extension to more complex and realistic scenarios.
tldr: The paper develops a feed-forward neural network to automatically estimate the optimal stabilization parameter for a loosely coupled Dirichlet-Neumann scheme in fluid-structure interaction simulations of hemodynamics.
motivation: Partitioned loosely coupled FSI schemes are computationally efficient but suffer from stability issues in high added-mass regimes, and the optimal stabilization parameter depends on problem-specific physical and numerical characteristics and is difficult to determine manually.
method: A feed-forward neural network is trained on a dataset of baseline FSI problems in large added-mass regimes to predict the stabilization parameter α from problem descriptors, and evaluated on more realistic configurations to assess robustness and generalization.
result: The model generalizes across the considered FSI scenarios and provides robust estimates of α under moderate variations in geometry and loading conditions that do not completely alter the interaction mechanics.
conclusion: The methodology is a proof of concept for data-driven strategies to improve the efficiency of partitioned FSI simulations, supporting extension to more complex and realistic scenarios.

title: Poisson Representations Of Dunkl Harmonic Functions Satisfying A Carleson Condition
authors: Rafa{\l} {\l}y\.zwa Jacek Dziuba\'nski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that a smooth Dunkl harmonic function in the upper half-space whose Dunkl gradient satisfies a Carleson measure condition is the Poisson integral of a function in [MATH], defined using Euclidean balls. The result holds for arbitrary finite root systems and nonnegative multiplicities. The proof uses an estimate for increments from the origin, obtained from a finite-dimensional system indexed by the reflection group, together with the atomic characterization of the Dunkl Hardy space.
tldr: The paper proves that smooth Dunkl harmonic functions in the upper half-space whose Dunkl gradient satisfies a Carleson measure condition are Poisson integrals of functions in a Dunkl Hardy space.
motivation: This work addresses boundary-value and Poisson representation problems for Dunkl harmonic functions, extending classical harmonic analysis to the Dunkl setting with arbitrary finite root systems.
method: The proof uses an estimate for increments from the origin derived from a finite-dimensional system indexed by the reflection group, together with the atomic characterization of the Dunkl Hardy space.
result: A smooth Dunkl harmonic function satisfying a Carleson condition on its Dunkl gradient is shown to be the Poisson integral of a function in a Dunkl-type Hardy space defined via Euclidean balls.
conclusion: The result generalizes Poisson representation theorems to the Dunkl harmonic setting for arbitrary finite root systems and nonnegative multiplicities, with potential applications in related boundary-value problems.

title: SoK: Failure Modes In Common Criteria Product Evaluation - A Taxonomy And Design-for-Evaluability Guidance
authors: Punit Suketu Patel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Common Criteria (CC; ISO/IEC 15408) is the principal international framework for evaluating the security of IT products, and its certificates gate procurement across government, defense, and regulated industry. Yet evaluations routinely stall, fail, or yield certificates whose assurances do not survive real-world deployment. Prior work has approached this from two directions: economic critiques of misaligned incentives and "security theatre"; and recent data-driven studies that quantify vulnerabilities in already-certified products. Comparatively little systematizes the problem from the evaluator's operational vantage - recurring, cross-vendor failures against the Common Criteria work units themselves. This paper presents a systematization of knowledge (SoK) of failure modes in Common Criteria product evaluation. Drawing on the standard, the Common Evaluation Methodology (ISO/IEC 18045), public NIAP Protection Profiles, and published Security Targets and Certification Reports, we organize recurring failures into a lifecycle taxonomy spanning Security Target scoping, Protection Profile conformance, assurance evidence, cryptographic requirements, functional testing, vulnerability analysis, operational guidance, and post-certification configuration drift. We analyze their root causes, derive a design-for-evaluability framework that product teams can apply before evaluation begins, and identify open problems for cloud, continuous-delivery, and AI-enabled systems.
tldr: This SoK systematizes recurring failure modes in Common Criteria security product evaluations and proposes a design-for-evaluability framework.
motivation: Common Criteria certificates are widely used for procurement, but evaluations often stall or fail to provide durable assurance, and existing critiques lack an operational evaluator-centric systematization.
method: The authors synthesize the Common Criteria standard, Common Evaluation Methodology, public NIAP Protection Profiles, Security Targets, and Certification Reports into a lifecycle taxonomy of failure modes.
result: The taxonomy spans eight areas including Security Target scoping, Protection Profile conformance, assurance evidence, cryptographic requirements, testing, vulnerability analysis, operational guidance, and configuration drift, with root-cause analysis and a design-for-evaluability framework.
conclusion: The paper identifies open problems for cloud, continuous-delivery, and AI-enabled systems, aiming to help product teams prepare for evaluation and improve certification outcomes.

title: Ditto: A Context-aware Pickle-based Pre-Trained Model Scanner For Effective Security Audits
authors: Qiaolin Qin, Wanpeng Li, Benoit Baudry, Lorenzo de Carli, Heng Li, Ettore Merlo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pre-trained models (PTMs) are widely distributed as serialized binaries, but their reuse often exposes software supply chains to deserialization attacks. Despite the emergence of safer serialization formats, the unsafe Pickle format remains prevalent: our analysis of over 10,000 popular Hugging Face repositories reveals that 9.3% rely on Pickle. While many defense mechanisms have been proposed, state-of-the-art model scanners suffer from a coverage-precision gap, missing security-sensitive behaviors and generating excessive false alerts. In this paper, we introduce DITTO, the first stack-based, context-aware scanner for Pickle-based PTMs. DITTO faithfully tracks Pickle virtual machine state transitions and performs context-aware semantic analysis to infer model intentions. We also present PickleBench, a benchmark of 959 benign and 92 malicious real-world models, including extension registry attacks previously missed by existing tools. Across multiple evaluations, DITTO achieves 100% scanning coverage, a 0% false-negative rate, and a 0.7% false-positive rate, yielding an F1 score of 0.966, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art scanners. By minimizing false alerts while preserving detection accuracy, DITTO generates actionable security reports with contextual evidence, enabling safe PTM reuse and strengthening software supply chain integrity.
tldr: Ditto is a context-aware, stack-based scanner for detecting malicious behavior in Pickle-based pre-trained models to improve security audits.
motivation: Pre-trained models are widely distributed as Pickle binaries, exposing software supply chains to deserialization attacks, and existing scanners have a coverage-precision gap.
method: Ditto tracks Pickle virtual machine state transitions and performs context-aware semantic analysis to infer model intentions, and it is evaluated on PickleBench, a benchmark of real-world benign and malicious models.
result: Ditto achieves 100% scanning coverage, a 0% false-negative rate, a 0.7% false-positive rate, and an F1 score of 0.966, outperforming state-of-the-art scanners.
conclusion: By minimizing false alerts while preserving detection accuracy, Ditto generates actionable security reports and strengthens software supply chain integrity for safe pre-trained model reuse.

title: Branch: Bypassing Multi-Scanner Ai Guardrails
authors: Peter Garraghan William Hackett
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) as core reasoning engines, making them targets for prompt injection and jailbreaks. Guardrails monitor and validate model inputs and outputs, yet their isolated, task-focused detection leaves gaps in their classification making them susceptible to bypasses. In response, guardrail systems formed by multiple scanners have emerged that collaboratively detect different types of malicious instructions, whereby shared latent representations across classification boundaries render established bypassing techniques ineffective. We propose BRANCH, a bypassing methodology designed for multi-scanner guardrail systems. Our method leverages a branching tree search approach that dynamically applies adversarial perturbation against individual scanners, with subsequent perturbation optimization and technique selection based on overall improvement across all guardrail system scanners, effectively decoupling bypass evaluation from attack signal optimization. Our findings demonstrate that BRANCH achieves 100% attack success rate across 6 guardrail systems in 120 scenarios with 72% fewer queries and 4.5x reduced wallclock time compared to established techniques, while preserving semantic meaning within the bypass. We also show how bypasses generated by BRANCH transfer to 29 unseen guardrails, including 8 commercial black-box guardrails, improving attack success in some cases up to 100% with no additional optimization.
tldr: BRANCH is a branching tree search method for bypassing multi-scanner LLM guardrail systems via adversarial perturbations, achieving high attack success rates with fewer queries.
motivation: LLM guardrails are vulnerable to prompt injection and jailbreaks, and multi-scanner systems remain susceptible due to gaps in shared latent representations, motivating a dedicated bypass methodology.
method: BRANCH dynamically applies adversarial perturbations against individual scanners using branching tree search, optimizing perturbations and technique selection based on overall improvement across all guardrail scanners.
result: BRANCH achieves 100% attack success across 6 guardrail systems in 120 scenarios with 72% fewer queries and 4.5x reduced wallclock time, and transfers to 29 unseen guardrails including 8 commercial black-box systems.
conclusion: Multi-scanner guardrail systems can be effectively bypassed by decoupling bypass evaluation from attack signal optimization, raising security concerns for LLM deployments.

title: Optimal Multi-Item Auctions With I.i.d. Values
authors: Boyu Liu, Zhengyang Liu, Zihe Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study revenue-maximizing multi-item auctions under dominant-strategy incentive compatibility (DSIC) and ex-post individual rationality. Buyers have additive valuations, and all item values are independent draws from a common finite distribution. For every two-point distribution and arbitrary numbers of buyers and items, we give an explicit deterministic mechanism that is optimal among all randomized mechanisms satisfying these requirements, together with a polynomial-time algorithm for computing the optimal expected revenue. For general finite-support distributions, computing the exact optimal revenue is [MATH]-hard, both for a single buyer with an arbitrary number of items and for two items with an arbitrary number of buyers. For a single buyer, we also establish hardness of computing an optimal mechanism. Building on prior work, we also obtain exact and approximate algorithms under different parameter restrictions. Exact polynomial-time optimization is possible whenever any two of the buyer count, item count, and support size are fixed. When only the item count is fixed, a polynomial-time approximation scheme constructs a mechanism with expected revenue at least a [MATH] fraction of the optimum for every fixed [MATH]. All these algorithms satisfy DSIC and ex-post individual rationality.
tldr: The paper studies revenue-maximizing multi-item auctions with additive i.i.d. values, providing optimal mechanisms for two-point distributions and complexity results for general distributions.
motivation: Multi-item auction design is a central problem in algorithmic mechanism design, where optimal revenue maximization under DSIC and ex-post individual rationality is often computationally hard.
method: The authors construct explicit deterministic optimal mechanisms for arbitrary numbers of buyers and items when values follow any two-point distribution, and analyze computational complexity for general finite-support distributions.
result: They give a polynomial-time algorithm for the two-point case, prove NP-hardness for exact optimization in general settings, and provide exact/approximate algorithms under parameter restrictions.
conclusion: The work advances the understanding of optimal multi-item auction design, delineating tractable and intractable cases and providing efficient approximations.

title: On-Chain Archaeology Of Bitcoin Oracles: Evidence Of Use Under Limited Observability
authors: Giulio Caldarelli
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before Ethereum made the "oracle problem" a household term, Bitcoin already had oracles serving as feeds, key-release services, federated signers, and arbiters that carried real value on the main chain. This study traces their use and the changing evidence of oracle activity from early days through July 2026. We combine a complete census of Counterparty betting (1,149 bets), analysis of the full Bitcoin chain through block 958,628, and searches for documented keys from Reality Keys, Orisi, Bitrated, and Oraclize in an 854-million-row public-key index. We also recover DLC oracle records from an archived explorer and live Nostr relays. Two results emerge. First, early contracts remain on-chain, but many event descriptions have disappeared, and protocol encoding and API limitations complicate access to the surviving record. However, for modern DLCs, public oracle announcements can survive even when the contracts using them cannot be identified on-chain. In the script classes examined, the share of spends that reveal no script peaks at 81.9% in 2024 after excluding spends containing inscription data. Second, public registries can give a misleading picture of oracle use. In Counterparty, 95% of pre-2018 sources declaring an oracle fee were never bet on. In Bitrated, 0.1% of archived keys appear on-chain overall, compared with 10 of 19 keys captured in 2014. Sport dominates Counterparty's matched volume, while a daily price series dominates the archived DLC announcements. These findings show how protocol design and data preservation shape the historical record of Bitcoin oracle use.
tldr: This paper performs an on-chain archaeological analysis of Bitcoin oracle use from early Counterparty betting through modern DLC announcements, revealing how protocol design and data preservation shape the observable historical record.
motivation: Bitcoin hosted oracle-like services before Ethereum popularized the oracle problem, but their actual use and the reliability of public registries remain poorly understood due to limited on-chain observability and disappearing metadata.
method: The authors combine a complete census of Counterparty betting, analysis of the full Bitcoin chain through block 958,628, searches in an 854-million-row public-key index for documented oracle keys, and recovery of DLC oracle records from archived explorers and live Nostr relays.
result: Early contracts persist on-chain but many event descriptions are lost, while modern DLC oracle announcements can survive without identifiable on-chain contracts; public registries misrepresent oracle use, with 95% of pre-2018 Counterparty fee declarations never bet on and only 0.1% of archived Bitrated keys appearing on-chain overall.
conclusion: The findings demonstrate that protocol design and data preservation practices critically shape the historical record of Bitcoin oracle activity, cautioning against relying on public registries as accurate measures of use.

title: Grob: A Multi-Agent Architecture For Public-Trace Investigation Of Candidate Agentic Activity
authors: Cataldo Basile Chiara Bonfanti
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present GROB, a multi-agent architecture for investigating candidate autonomous-agent activity through public Internet traces when privileged telemetry is unavailable. The system performs controlled, read-only collection of public traces and preserves selected observations for later resolution. In a frozen September 2026 corpus, several collected traces became more informative as additional public evidence emerged. The strongest result concerns Census-labelled identifiers captured on 9 September. Public revision records later resolved these identifiers to specific Census requests from 16 - 17 June. Other results show weaker links between traces collected by GROB and evidence reconstructed or reported later. These links vary in strength, and only some can be tied to specific public records. The results show that sparse public traces can remain useful even before their significance is fully understood. Such evidence can support later reconstruction, but public traces alone do not establish organizational attribution. Execution identity presents a separate problem, as continuity of agent identity remains an active research question for autonomous language-model agents.
tldr: GROB is a multi-agent system that collects public Internet traces to investigate possible autonomous-agent activity without privileged telemetry.
motivation: Investigating autonomous-agent activity is difficult when internal or privileged telemetry is unavailable, so the authors explore whether sparse public traces can still provide useful evidence.
method: The system performs controlled read-only collection of public traces and preserves selected observations for later resolution, evaluated on a frozen September 2026 corpus.
result: Some traces became more informative as additional public evidence emerged, with the strongest case resolving Census-labelled identifiers to specific requests, though links varied in strength and only some tied to specific records.
conclusion: Sparse public traces can remain useful for later reconstruction, but public traces alone do not establish organizational attribution, and agent execution identity remains an open problem.

title: Host Attack Graph For Botnet Propagation
authors: Andrei Neagu, Mara-Cristina Sterian, Paul Irofti
abstract: ArXiv:2610.11640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Botnets represent the backbone of most modern cybersecurity attacks through which botmasters deploy distributed denial of service and advanced persistent threats against legitimate computer networks. In this paper we introduce the Host Attack Graph model and propose two botnet propagation strategies which we study across network topologies, target selection, and attack strategies together with their effectiveness in time. While strategy and botnet size are important for propagation, our study and simulations show that network topology and target selection should not be easily discarded. Implementation and benchmarks are available at [URL].
tldr: The paper introduces a Host Attack Graph model and studies botnet propagation strategies across network topologies, target selection, and attack timing.
motivation: Botnets underpin many modern cyberattacks, so understanding their propagation dynamics can inform defense and network design.
method: The authors define a Host Attack Graph and simulate two propagation strategies over different topologies and target-selection schemes.
result: Simulations show that network topology and target selection significantly affect propagation effectiveness over time, not just strategy and botnet size.
conclusion: The work highlights the importance of topology and target selection in botnet propagation and provides an implementation with benchmarks.

title: Polynomial $\mathcal{Z}$-contraction: A Unified Approach With Application
authors: Stojan N. Radenovi\'c Md Hasanuzzaman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we introduce polynomial [MATH]-contraction by unifying the ideas of polynomial contraction and [MATH]-contraction and also provide demonstrative examples to show the effectiveness and novelty. Chiefly, we prove two fixed point results for polynomial [MATH]-contraction employing simulation functions. Lastly, we utilize our main result to discuss the existence and uniqueness of solution for boundary value problem with a concrete example in [MATH] under suitable assumptions.
tldr: Introduces polynomial Z-contraction as a unification of polynomial contraction and Z-contraction, proving two fixed point results via simulation functions and applying them to a boundary value problem.
motivation: The paper aims to generalize existing contraction principles in metric fixed point theory by combining polynomial and Z-contraction ideas, motivated by applications to boundary value problems.
method: Defines a new class of contractions called polynomial Z-contractions and employs simulation functions to prove two fixed point theorems.
result: Establishes existence and uniqueness of solutions for a boundary value problem in a metric space, accompanied by a concrete example.
conclusion: The unified approach extends previous fixed point results and demonstrates applicability to differential equations, though it lies outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Multilevel Picard Approximations For McKean-Vlasov Stochastic Differential Equations With Jumps
authors: Ariel Neufeld, Tuan Anh Nguyen, Philipp Schmocker
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce multilevel Picard (MLP) approximations of McKean-Vlasov stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with jumps of finite or infinite activity. Under Lipschitz and integrability assumptions on the coefficients, we show that the MLP algorithm does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality when approximating the solution of the McKean-Vlasov SDE. The latter means that its computational cost grows at most polynomially in both the state-space dimension of the SDE and the reciprocal of the prescribed error tolerance. In two numerical experiments, we demonstrate the practical applicability of the MLP algorithm for two different McKean-Vlasov SDEs in dimensions up to 200.
tldr: Introduces multilevel Picard approximations for McKean-Vlasov SDEs with jumps, proving polynomial cost in dimension and error tolerance.
motivation: McKean-Vlasov SDEs with jumps arise in mean-field models but suffer from the curse of dimensionality in high dimensions, motivating efficient numerical schemes.
method: The authors develop a multilevel Picard algorithm combining Picard iteration with multilevel Monte Carlo to handle finite and infinite activity jumps.
result: Under Lipschitz and integrability assumptions, they prove the computational cost grows at most polynomially in state dimension and inverse error, and demonstrate it numerically up to 200 dimensions.
conclusion: The proposed MLP algorithm avoids the curse of dimensionality for McKean-Vlasov SDEs with jumps and is practically applicable.

title: When Ai Finds Hidden Messages, Does It Report?
authors: William Guey, Rashik Jahangir, Pierrick Bougault, Vitor D. de Moura, Wei Zhang, Jos\'e O. Gomes
abstract: ArXiv:2610.10620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an assistant encounters a message for another AI, does it tell its user? Four fixed model-provider deployments perform simulated source tasks in 1,280 ordinary-note and 128 enhanced-note sessions. Harmless and harmful messages have matched plaintext and ROT13 versions, with no-message controls. Observers receive no decoder or decoded meaning; a requested reference code incentivizes inspection. Asking for reports increases rule-detected notifications identifying another AI as recipient by 53.1 percentage points for harmless ROT13 messages and 54.7 for harmful ones. This is a joint inspection, recognition, and notification effect; missing-response bounds are 38.3--77.3 and 36.7--78.1 points. Model-based trace checks identify eleven ordinary plaintext cases where agents interpret the message but do not notify their user. Seven encoded omissions are verified with enhanced notes; ordinary encoded omissions remain unverified. Seven simulated filename disclosures coexist with accurate review-status answers, and two answers use a planted false count. Interpretation, notification, and authorized task performance are distinct outcomes.
tldr: This study investigates whether AI assistants report hidden messages intended for other AI systems, finding that explicit reporting prompts increase notifications but omissions still occur.
motivation: As AI agents may encounter encoded messages, understanding whether they notify users is important for safety, oversight, and transparency in multi-agent deployments.
method: Four fixed model-provider deployments performed 1,280 ordinary-note and 128 enhanced-note sessions with harmless and harmful messages in matched plaintext and ROT13 versions, no-message controls, no decoder, and a requested reference code to incentivize inspection.
result: Asking for reports increased rule-detected notifications by 53.1 percentage points for harmless ROT13 messages and 54.7 for harmful ones; model-based trace checks found eleven ordinary plaintext cases where agents interpreted but did not notify, and seven encoded omissions were verified with enhanced notes.
conclusion: Interpretation, notification, and authorized task performance are distinct outcomes, and AI agents may not reliably disclose hidden messages, raising concerns about transparency and oversight.
